label: Capstone
title: Mastery Capstone: Synthesis, Debate Prep & Final Exam
tagline: Five roads, one summit — explaining and defending the whole case
oneSentence: Feser’s five proofs begin from five different undeniable features of reality — change, composition, abstract truths, the gap between what things are and that they are, and the intelligibility of things — and, by one shared two-stage method, each arrives at a cause that must be purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence itself, a necessary intellect and a necessary being; since there can be only one such reality, the five are independent paths to the single God of classical theism, whose nature chapter 6 unfolds and whose critics chapter 7 answers.
bigPicture:
The first nine modules of this course took Feser’s book apart piece by piece. This capstone puts it back together. Its goal is not to add new material but to let you see the book the way its author intends it to be seen: as **one cumulative case** built from five independent demonstrations, a systematic account of the divine nature, and a clearing-away of the standard objections. If you can explain how those pieces fit — why each proof works on its own, why they all land on the same God, what they do and do not claim, and how to answer the twenty objections you are most likely to meet — you have mastered the book.

Three ideas hold the whole thing together. First, **every proof has the same shape**: Stage 1 reasons from an everyday starting point to something that fits a precise description (a purely actual actualizer, an absolutely simple cause, a necessarily existing intellect, subsistent existence itself, a necessary being), and Stage 2 shows that anything fitting that description must be one, unchanging, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, all-powerful, intelligent and all-knowing. Second, **the four causal proofs are about dependence here and now**, not about a first moment of time: they turn on hierarchical causal series, in which intermediate causes have only borrowed power, and which therefore require an underived source even if the universe had no beginning. Third, **the five descriptions pick out one and the same reality**: whatever is purely actual is simple, whatever is simple is purely actual, both are identical with subsistent existence itself, and all three hold if and only if something exists necessarily — and there cannot in principle be two of any of them.

The capstone is also your final exam and debate lab. You will find a comparison table of the five proofs, a numbered convergence argument, a twenty-item objection handbook drawn from the whole book (with chapter references), a long practice conversation with a sharp skeptic, a sixty-six-term whole-book vocabulary, a 70-question final exam, twenty-one essay prompts, ninety-four flashcards, and an eight-week plan for consolidating everything. Treat it as the place where understanding becomes fluency: you should leave able to pick the right proof for the person in front of you and to defend it without distortion or bluster.

Finally, keep Feser’s own framing in view. He presents these arguments as *demonstrations*, not probabilistic hypotheses; he claims the most common objections rest on misunderstandings; and he insists the real debate is not between atheism and theism but among theists of different kinds, beginning exactly where natural theology leaves off. You do not have to agree with all of that to master the book — but you do need to be able to state it accurately, which is what this capstone trains.
objectives: Describe the two-stage structure shared by all five proofs and explain why it answers the objection that a first cause need not be God.
State each proof’s starting point, key principle, conclusion and characteristic distinction from memory, and reconstruct any one of them step by step.
Explain why the four causal proofs concern hierarchical (per se) causal series operating here and now, and why they are therefore indifferent to whether the universe had a beginning.

Show, using the identity arguments of chapter 6, why the purely actual actualizer, the One, the necessary intellect, subsistent existence itself and the necessary being must be one and the same being.
List at least eight things the proofs do not claim (e.g., that everything has a cause, that the universe began, that God is a being among beings) and correct each misreading.
Summarize how chapter 6 completes the case — proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, analogy, the divine attributes, conservation, concurrence and miracles.
Answer at least twenty major objections from the whole book, naming the chapter that handles each and anticipating the objector’s follow-up.
Choose and adapt the most suitable proof for different listeners (scientist, mathematician, analytic philosopher, believer, casual skeptic) and present it without the common presentation traps.
Explain what Feser means by a demonstration and why controversy about an argument does not show that it fails.

summary.heading: The book’s project: natural theology without exegesis
summary.plain: Feser wants to show that you can reason your way to God using ordinary logic and careful thinking, without appealing to the Bible or any religious authority. He doesn’t spend time interpreting what famous philosophers of the past ‘really meant’; he borrows their best ideas and argues for them directly. Every argument chapter follows the same pattern, so once you learn the pattern, the book becomes much easier to follow.
summary.body:
Natural theology asks what unaided reason — apart from any claim of divine revelation — can know about whether God exists, what he is like, and how he is related to the world. Feser’s earlier books approached these questions by expounding Aquinas, which meant long stretches of textual interpretation and some seventy pages of general metaphysics before any argument for God appeared. *Five Proofs* deliberately does something else. It offers no exegesis of any historical thinker; it introduces background metaphysics only when an argument needs it; and it defends five arguments, only two of which appear in Aquinas in anything like this form. The proofs are *inspired* by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas and Leibniz, and Feser thinks they capture what is essential in those thinkers, but he presents them in his own way and does not claim any of those figures would endorse every detail.

The intended reader is a layperson willing to be eased into abstraction. Feser’s image is of starting in the shallow end of the pool and ending, in every chapter, in the deepest part. Chapters 1–5 each follow the same pattern: an **informal statement** of the argument in two stages, a **more formal statement** in numbered steps (which is not meant to stand alone — it recaps the informal discussion), and a long section of **objections rebutted**, where much of the most technical material lives. Chapter 6 then examines God’s nature and his relationship to the world systematically, and chapter 7 answers the most common objections to natural theology in general.

Feser is openly confident. He argues that the most common objections are feeble and overrated, that what was for most of Western history the mainstream view — that God’s existence can be rationally demonstrated — should be the mainstream view again, and that the real debate is not between atheism and theism but among Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, purely philosophical theists and others. That debate begins where natural theology stops, and the book deliberately does not enter it.
summary.takeaway: *Five Proofs* is a self-contained argument, not a history lesson: five proofs built on one pattern, meant to show atheism is false and leave the real debate to theists of different kinds.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest thing to grasp here is what kind of book this is, because it changes how you should evaluate everything in it. Feser is doing **natural theology**: arguing for conclusions about God from premises that any reasonable person could in principle check, without citing revelation. And he is doing it **without exegesis** — he is not claiming ‘this is what Aristotle meant’ or ‘this is what Aquinas said’.

Why does that matter? Try a thought experiment. Suppose someone gives you an elegant geometry proof and says it is ‘inspired by Euclid’. Would it refute the proof to point out that Euclid wrote it differently, or that Euclid believed the Earth was the center of the universe? Obviously not. The proof stands or falls on its own steps. Likewise, when critics say ‘Aristotle’s physics is obsolete’ or ‘Aquinas didn’t argue exactly that’, they may be correct and still say nothing against Feser’s arguments. Feser makes exactly this point in chapter 1: the essential kernel of the argument can be separated from its ‘outdated husk’ of celestial spheres.

Two nuances. First, the **formal statements are not meant to stand alone**. They compress pages of careful explanation into numbered steps. If you read, say, chapter 1’s step 11 (‘a hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely’) without the informal discussion of cups, desks and paintbrushes, you will almost certainly misread ‘hierarchical’ as ‘happening at the same time’ or ‘first’ as ‘earliest’. Second, Feser does not claim his historical sources would endorse every detail; two proofs appear in Aquinas in something like this form, three do not.

How does this feed the capstone’s convergence argument? Step 25 says that a being with the attributes the proofs establish ‘is just what it is for God to exist’. That step is credible precisely because Feser is not inventing a new God; he is using the concept shared by a long tradition of pagan, Jewish, Muslim and Christian thinkers. And step 26 stops at that God — the book deliberately goes no further.

The usual confusion: people often think ‘natural theology’ means worshipping nature, or that it competes with faith. It means neither. It is the part of theology that reason alone can do, and on Feser’s view (chapter 6) it is what makes faith reasonable rather than blind.

checks.q: What most distinguishes *Five Proofs* from Feser’s earlier books on natural theology?
options: It defends only arguments found in Aquinas
It avoids textual exegesis and introduces background metaphysics only as needed
It relies on scientific evidence rather than philosophy
It argues from the Bible as well as reason
checks.explanation: His earlier books expounded Aquinas and required long metaphysical preliminaries; this one argues directly, with metaphysics introduced along the way. Three of the five proofs are not Aquinas’ arguments in this form.

checks.q: Why does Feser warn that the formal statements should not be read on their own?
options: Because they contain errors corrected in the informal sections
Because they are written for professional logicians only
Because they summarize concepts, like ‘hierarchical series’, whose meaning is explained only in the informal discussion
Because they are optional and can be skipped
checks.explanation: The numbered steps recap the informal presentation; key terms carry meanings established there, so reading the steps alone invites misunderstandings.

checks.q: According to the Introduction, where does the ‘real debate’ lie once natural theology has done its work?
options: Among theists of different kinds — Jews, Christians, Muslims, philosophical theists and others
Between atheists and agnostics
Between science and religion
Between Aristotelians and Platonists
checks.explanation: Feser says the real debate is not atheism versus theism but begins where natural theology leaves off, among varieties of theism — a debate the book does not enter.

summary.heading: The shared two-stage structure
summary.plain: Each argument happens in two steps. First Feser shows that something very special must exist — for example, a cause that doesn’t depend on anything. Then he asks what such a thing would have to be like, and shows it must be one, unchanging, all-powerful, all-knowing and good — in other words, what people have always meant by God. So you can’t say ‘fine, there’s a first cause, but who says it’s God?’ without dealing with that second step.
summary.body:
Every proof is built in two stages. **Stage 1** reasons from some evident feature of the world to the existence of something that fits a precise description:

- Aristotelian: a *purely actual actualizer* (Unmoved Mover).
- Neo-Platonic: an *absolutely simple or noncomposite cause* (the One).
- Augustinian: a *necessarily existing intellect* in which abstract objects exist.
- Thomistic: a cause that is *subsistent existence itself*, whose essence just is existence.
- Rationalist: an *absolutely necessary being*, whose existence is explained by its own nature.

**Stage 2** argues that anything fitting the description must have the key divine attributes: unity (there can be only one), immutability, eternity, immateriality and incorporeality, perfection, full goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience, being the uncaused cause of everything else. Each chapter’s formal statement ends the same way: to exist with these attributes is simply what it is for God to exist.

This structure matters rhetorically and logically. The most common lazy reply to ‘first cause’ arguments is that even if they reach *some* first cause, nothing shows it is God. In Feser’s book that gap is closed inside every chapter, and at greater length in chapter 6. The two stages are one continuous deduction: the attributes are not tacked on by faith but drawn out of the very description Stage 1 establishes.

Note two further common features. Four of the proofs — Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, Rationalist — are *causal* and concern what keeps things in existence **here and now**; the Augustinian proof is not causal at all but starts from the reality of abstract objects. And all five are offered as **demonstrations** — deductions meant to follow necessarily from premises that can be established with certainty — rather than as ‘best explanation’ hypotheses competing with scientific theories.
summary.takeaway: Stage 1 reaches something fitting a precise description; Stage 2 deduces the divine attributes from that description — so the supposed gap between ‘first cause’ and ‘God’ is closed inside every proof.
summary.deepDive:
The hard idea is why you can legitimately deduce so much from a single description. Here is an analogy from arithmetic. Suppose you prove there exists ‘the smallest prime number’. You haven’t yet said which number it is — but from the description alone you can deduce that it is 2, that it is even, that it is the only even prime. A precise description is a mine of implications. Stage 1 of each proof delivers a precise description; Stage 2 mines it.

Watch it work in chapter 1. From **pure actuality** (step 14), Feser gets **uniqueness** (steps 15–18: nothing could differentiate two purely actual beings), **immutability** (19–21: no potency, so no change), **eternity** (22–23: what cannot change is not in time), **immateriality** (24–27: matter is changeable), **perfection** and **goodness** (28–32: imperfection and badness are unrealized potential), and **omnipotence** (33–37: all power to actualize derives from it). Notice the order: eternity depends on immutability, and immateriality depends on both. That is why a critic must attack a specific inference, not just announce a ‘gap’.

A nuance many readers miss: **intellect does not follow from pure actuality alone**. It needs an extra premise, the principle of proportionate causality (chapter 1, step 38): the cause of every possible thing must contain the forms of those things, and since it cannot contain them concretely, it contains them as an intellect does (steps 39–44). In the Augustinian proof the order is reversed — Stage 1 already gives an intellect, and Stage 2 derives pure actuality from its necessity (chapter 3, step 19). In the capstone’s convergence argument, this appears as steps 21–23.

The last premise of each formal statement — that for there to be such a cause ‘is just what it is for God to exist’ (e.g., chapter 1, step 49; convergence step 25) — is not a trick definition. It matches the concept of God held by classical theists across traditions.

The usual confusion: people often think Stage 2 is decoration, attributes ‘projected’ onto a bare first cause out of wishful thinking. But every attribute is inferred, and the inferences can be checked one by one. Another confusion is to treat Stage 1 alone as ‘the proof of God’ and then complain that it proves too little.

checks.q: In chapter 1, which additional premise, beyond pure actuality, is needed to show that the first cause has intellect?
options: The principle of sufficient reason
The principle that a hierarchical series needs a first member
The claim that change is real
The principle of proportionate causality
checks.explanation: Intellect is derived by combining the PPC with the fact that the first cause causes every possible thing: their forms must be in it, abstractly, as in a mind.

checks.q: How does the Augustinian proof’s Stage 2 differ in order from chapter 1’s?
options: It reaches intellect in Stage 1 and then derives pure actuality from the intellect’s necessity
It skips Stage 2 entirely
It derives intellect last, after omnipotence
It derives the attributes from PSR rather than from its conclusion
checks.explanation: The Augustinian Stage 1 already concludes to a necessary intellect; Stage 2 shows such an intellect must be purely actual, from which the other attributes follow.

summary.heading: The common toolkit: concepts the whole book relies on
summary.plain: A few ideas show up again and again in the book. The most important: things can really change because they have hidden capacities that get switched on; nothing can switch on its own capacity; and when something only works because something else is making it work right now — like a tool in a hand — there has to be something that works without being made to. Learn these handful of ideas well and every chapter becomes readable.
summary.body:
A handful of ideas introduced early recur everywhere, and fluency with them is most of what mastery requires.

- **Actuality and potentiality.** Change is the actualization of a potential; a potential is neither nothing nor yet actual (the hot coffee really can become cold, but cannot become chicken soup). This answers Parmenides’ worry that change would be something coming from nothing.
- **The principle of causality.** A potential cannot actualize itself; only what is already actual can actualize it. Note what it does *not* say: not that ‘everything has a cause’, only that whatever goes from potential to actual does.
- **Linear vs. hierarchical causal series.** In a linear (per accidens) series — the air conditioner switched on by you, which keeps running after you leave — each member has its own power, and Feser grants such series might extend back infinitely. In a hierarchical (per se) series — cup held up by desk, desk by floor, floor by foundation — every member other than the first has its power only derivatively, like a brush in a painter’s hand. Such a series must have a **first** member, where ‘first’ means *underived*, not *earliest*. Even an infinitely long brush handle could not move itself.
- **The principle of proportionate causality (PPC).** Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually or eminently (the $20 bill in my wallet, in my bank account, or in my power to print it). The PPC is what lets Stage 2 infer intellect and omniscience.
- **The principle of sufficient reason (PSR).** Everything is intelligible: there is an explanation for the existence and attributes of whatever exists, found either in the thing’s own nature or in something else. Every cause is an explanation, but not every explanation is a cause, which is why something can be *self-explanatory* without being *self-caused*.
- **The uniqueness argument.** For there to be two of anything, something must distinguish them — a specific difference, a parcel of matter, some perfection one has and the other lacks. Anything so distinguishable has parts or potentiality. Hence there can be only one purely actual, simple, self-existent being.
- **Analogical predication.** Terms like ‘good’, ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ apply to God neither univocally (in exactly our sense) nor equivocally (in an unrelated sense) but analogically — literally, yet not in exactly the same way.
summary.takeaway: Master act and potency, the principle of causality, hierarchical series, the PPC, PSR, the uniqueness argument and analogy, and you hold the keys to every chapter.
summary.deepDive:
The single hardest tool is the **hierarchical causal series**, and the best way to get it is by contrast. Picture a row of dominoes: once the first is pushed, each falls on the next by its own weight, and the first domino could be removed from the scene without stopping the rest. That is like a **linear** series. Now picture a clock’s gear train driven by a spring: the last gear turns only while the middle gears turn, and they turn only while the spring drives them. Remove the spring and everything stops at once. That is a **hierarchical** series — every member except the first has only borrowed power, like a brush in a painter’s hand.

Feser adds three qualifications that are easy to miss. First, what makes a series hierarchical is not that its members act at the same instant (that is only a helpful illustration) but that their power is **derivative**. Second, ‘first’ means **underived**, not earliest; even an infinitely long gear train would need a spring. Third, Feser does *not* reject all infinite series. He grants that linear series might run back forever and has no quarrel with infinite mathematical series, which involve no causation at all.

A subtle point from chapter 1’s footnote on Al, Bob and Chuck: members of a linear series (a grandfather, father and son) have their begetting power in their own right *relative to one another*, but none of them could exist or act for an instant without the hierarchical series of actualizers that keeps their bodies in being. So every linear series rests on hierarchical ones — which is why Feser can grant a beginningless universe and lose nothing.

The other tools each play a role in the capstone’s convergence argument: act and potency and the hierarchical series drive steps 1–10; the uniqueness argument secures step 19; the PPC secures step 21; the sense/reference distinction and analogy make step 20 intelligible. PSR, meanwhile, is different from the principle of causality: a cause must be distinct from its effect, but an explanation can lie in a thing’s own nature.

The usual confusion: people often hear ‘first cause’ and imagine the first domino. Feser’s first cause is the spring — and it would be needed even if the row of dominoes had no beginning.

checks.q: Which of these is the best example of a hierarchical (per se) causal series?
options: A row of falling dominoes
A grandfather, father and son
An infinite series of numbers
A clock’s gear train turned by a spring, where every gear turns only while the spring drives it
checks.explanation: In the gear train each intermediate member has only borrowed power at every moment. Dominoes and generations are linear; numbers involve no causation.

checks.q: Does Feser deny that any series can be infinite?
options: Yes — all infinite series are impossible
No — he allows that linear causal series and mathematical series may be infinite, and denies only that hierarchical series can lack an underived first member
Yes, but only for series in time
No — he allows hierarchical series to be infinite without any first member
checks.explanation: Feser grants a beginningless linear series for argument’s sake; his claim concerns series in which power is derivative.

checks.q: What does the uniqueness argument rely on?
options: The principle that for two things of a kind to differ there must be some differentiating feature, which a purely actual or simple being cannot have
Observations showing that only one god is worshipped
The principle of sufficient reason alone
The claim that the universe is finite
checks.explanation: Plurality requires a differentiator (specific difference, matter, a perfection lacked), and any such feature is a part or a potency.

summary.heading: Proof 1 compressed: the Aristotelian proof (chapter 1)
summary.plain: Things change — your coffee gets cold. But nothing can change itself; something already real has to make the change happen. More importantly, your coffee only exists at all right now because tinier things are holding it together right now, and those depend on still tinier things. That chain can’t consist only of things that are being held up; something must be doing the holding without needing to be held. That ‘something’ turns out to have to be God.
summary.body:
**Starting point:** change is real. The coffee cools, the leaf falls, the puddle grows, the swatted fly dies. Even a lifelong hallucination would involve a succession of experiences, and even arguing that change is illusory involves moving from premise to conclusion. Aristotle’s analysis of change as the actualization of potential defuses Parmenides.

**Key moves.** Any potential that is actualized must be actualized by something already actual. Series of changers stretched through time (coffee cooled by air, air by air conditioner, air conditioner by your finger) might for all the argument cares run back forever — Feser grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for argument’s sake. But every such change presupposes a *thing* that changes, and that thing’s very existence at each moment involves the concurrent actualization of potentials: the water in the coffee exists only because its matter is actually water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen, which in turn depends on the arrangement of atoms, which depends on subatomic particles, and so on. That is a hierarchical series of actualizers of existence, and it must terminate in something that can actualize without being actualized — something with no potentiality at all, **pure actuality**. It is not merely unmoved but *unmovable*: a ‘first’ actualizer with unactualized potentials would need something further to actualize them and so would not be first.

**Stage 2.** Being purely actual, it cannot change (immutable), so it is outside time (eternal); material things are changeable, so it is immaterial and incorporeal; imperfection and badness are failures to actualize potential, so it is perfect and fully good; there is nothing to distinguish two purely actual beings, so it is unique; all power to actualize derives from it, so it is omnipotent; and since by the PPC the forms of everything it can cause must pre-exist in it — not concretely, as in a cat or a tree, but abstractly, as in a mind — it has intellect and, since nothing is outside its range, omniscience. The formal statement runs to **fifty steps**.

**Signature objections:** ‘What caused God?’ (a straw man — the principle concerns what goes from potential to actual); Hume on conceiving uncaused events; Kant on extending causality beyond experience; Russell’s claim that physics has no causes; Newton’s law of inertia; Einstein’s block universe; quantum indeterminacy and radioactive decay; ‘outdated science’ (Eddington’s two tables); whether hierarchical series are real; and why the mover must be unmovable.
summary.takeaway: Because change — and even the existence of changing things here and now — involves actualized potential, there must be a purely actual actualizer, and Stage 2 shows it is God.
summary.deepDive:
The pivotal move, and the one most readers skate past, is the shift **from change to existence**. Steps 1–5 of chapter 1’s formal statement concern change. Step 6 notes that any change requires a thing that changes; step 7 then says that thing’s very **existence at a given moment** presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for existence. From there on, the regress is a regress of actualizers of *existence*.

Work through Feser’s example slowly. The matter in your coffee could exist as separate hydrogen and oxygen; right now it exists as water instead. Why? Not because of how it got here — that is a past event. Not because nothing has yet split it — that concerns how it might cease. Saying ‘chemical bonding’ merely restates the question, because the atoms could be bonded otherwise; appealing to atomic structure pushes the question down a level. So the water’s existence depends on the atoms’ potential being actualized now, which depends on the subatomic level being actualized now, and so on — a hierarchical series (step 11), which must end in something that actualizes without being actualized (steps 12–14).

This shift does three jobs. It makes the argument indifferent to whether the universe had a beginning. It explains why the first actualizer must be **unmovable**, not merely unmoved: since it actualizes *existence*, any unactualized potential in it would need some further actualizer. And it grounds the capstone’s convergence steps 1–2.

A nuance: in a footnote Feser admits that his water example treats water as an aggregate of atoms, whereas on Aristotelian hylemorphism atoms exist in water only ‘virtually’. He avoids relying on that controversial theory — but notes the argument can be restated in its terms: prime matter depends on form for concrete existence, and form on matter, so there would be a vicious circle unless something outside the composite actualized it.

The usual confusion: people often picture the Unmoved Mover as the one who gave the first push long ago. Aristotle himself believed the world had no beginning; his Unmoved Mover was never a starter motor but the ever-present source of actuality. Aristotle’s own version was entangled with celestial spheres, but, as Feser stresses, the kernel does not depend on that husk.

checks.q: Which step of chapter 1’s formal argument moves the discussion from change to existence?
options: Step 1: change is a real feature of the world
Step 4: no potential is actualized unless something actual actualizes it
Step 11: a hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely
Step 7: a substance’s existence at any moment presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for existence
checks.explanation: Steps 1–5 concern change; steps 6–8 shift to the existence of the changing substance, which is what the hierarchical regress then concerns.

checks.q: Why doesn’t ‘chemical bonding’ answer the question of what keeps the coffee’s water in existence now?
options: Because chemistry is outdated science
Because bonding occurred only in the past
Because the atoms have the potential to be bonded in other ways, so appealing to bonding just restates the question of what actualizes this potential rather than another
Because water is not made of atoms
checks.explanation: Feser says the appeal rephrases rather than answers; appealing to atomic structure only pushes the question down a stage.

summary.heading: Proof 2 compressed: the Neo-Platonic proof (chapter 2)
summary.plain: Everything around us is made of parts — chairs, bodies, molecules. A thing made of parts only exists if its parts are held together, and it can’t hold itself together. So everything with parts depends, right now, on something else. That dependence has to end in something with no parts at all, which therefore needs nothing to hold it together — and Feser shows this ‘partless’ thing must be God.
summary.body:
**Starting point:** the things of our experience are composite. A chair has legs, screws, seat and cushion; your body has limbs, organs and cells. In one sense the parts are understood through the whole, but in another the whole is less fundamental, because it exists only if its parts exist and are combined in the right way. That dependence is not merely temporal — it holds at every moment, even for something that had always existed or came to be all at once.

**Key moves.** A composite cannot be the cause of its own parts’ being combined; that would be an explanatory vicious circle, the chair lifting itself by its metaphysical bootstraps. So at any moment a composite depends on something else — screws, friction, molecular bonds, a suitable room temperature — and those factors are composite too, yielding a hierarchical series. The principle is completely general: it applies whether the parts are physical (legs, atoms) or metaphysical (form and matter, essence and existence). Such a series must have a first member, and the first member cannot be composite in any way, or it would need a cause itself. So there must be an absolutely **simple or noncomposite** cause — what Plotinus called **the One**.

**Stage 2.** Two simple causes would need a distinguishing feature, which would be a part; so the One is unique. Change means gaining or losing a feature, so it is immutable; it neither begins nor ends, so it is eternal. Using a fourfold division borrowed from William Vallicella — everything is a mind, a mental content, a material thing or an abstract object — the One is not abstract (abstract objects are causally inert), not material (material things have parts), not a mental content (contents depend on minds), so it is a mind or more like a mind than anything else. Having no potential part, it is purely actual, so everything said of the Unmoved Mover applies — and indeed **the One and the Unmoved Mover are identical**. The formal statement has **thirty-eight steps**.

This chapter also introduces two tools crucial later: Frege’s distinction between **sense and reference** (‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ differ in sense but both name Venus), which explains how God’s many attributes can be one reality; and **analogical predication**, illustrated by the literal but non-identical ‘good’ in ‘good wine’ and ‘good man’. Physics’ wave-particle duality shows we should expect the ultimate level of reality to strain our concepts.

**Signature objections:** a further part might unify the parts (it just adds another item to be unified, regress); unity might be an irreducible or brute fact (either self-causation, which is incoherent, or no explanation at all, not an alternative explanation — and, as Lloyd Gerson notes, the proof has offered one); laws of nature might explain composition (laws plus what they govern are just another composite).
summary.takeaway: Whatever has parts depends at every moment on something that combines them, so everything composite depends on a cause with no parts at all — the One.
summary.deepDive:
The hard idea is how general ‘composite’ is meant to be. Feser starts with chair legs and body parts, but step 3 of the formal statement (‘this composition of parts requires a concurrent cause’) applies to parts of *any* kind: physical parts, atoms, even conditions like room temperature, and also **metaphysical** parts — form and matter, essence and existence. On Aristotelian analysis form is a mere abstraction without matter, and matter is mere potential without form; each depends on the other, so something outside them must account for their union. The same goes for essence and existence. So even a thing with no physical parts may be composite in the relevant sense.

Try a thought experiment Feser himself suggests: imagine a chair that has **always existed**. There was no moment of assembly. Does it still depend on its parts? Yes — at every moment its existence presupposes that its legs, seat and screws exist and are combined in the right way. The dependence is atemporal (ontological), not a matter of history. And the chair cannot be the cause of that combination, or it would be both the result and the source of its own composition — lifting itself by its metaphysical bootstraps.

Why must the first cause be *absolutely* simple (step 8)? Because any first member with parts of any kind would itself need a cause of its composition, and so would not be first. Hence the One has no physical parts, no form-matter composition, no essence-existence composition.

This feeds the capstone’s convergence steps 3–4 and, more deeply, steps 11–13: anything with parts has potency, and anything with potency has parts, so the One is the Unmoved Mover.

Two nuances. The argument that the One is a mind (steps 22–29) is borrowed from William Vallicella, and Plotinus himself actually placed intellect in a second divine reality after the One — Feser follows the general Neo-Platonic approach, not every detail. And ‘simple’ does not mean ‘tiny’ or ‘easy to understand’: a fundamental particle has no smaller parts but still has distinct attributes and comes and goes, so it is not simple in Feser’s sense.

The usual confusion: people often equate ‘composite’ with ‘complex’ in the design-argument sense. A pebble or a drop of water serves this proof as well as an eye.

checks.q: Would a chair that had always existed still require a cause of its composition, according to chapter 2?
options: No, because it was never assembled
Yes, because at every moment its existence depends on its parts existing and being combined, whether or not it ever began
Only if it was made by a carpenter
No, because eternal things are necessary
checks.explanation: The dependence of a whole on its parts is atemporal; history is irrelevant.

checks.q: Which kinds of parts does the Neo-Platonic principle ‘whatever is composite requires a cause’ cover?
options: Only visible physical parts
Only atoms and molecules
Only parts that were assembled over time
Parts of any kind, including metaphysical ones like form and matter or essence and existence
checks.explanation: Feser stresses the principle is completely general, applying whatever the parts are.

checks.q: Why isn’t a single fundamental particle ‘simple’ in the sense the proof requires?
options: Because it is too small to observe
Because it has distinct attributes and comes into and goes out of existence, so it involves parts and potentiality
Because physics says particles are waves
Because it has a beginning in time
checks.explanation: Chapter 6 notes that even fermions and bosons, though not made of smaller particles, have distinct attributes and exhibit potentiality.

summary.heading: Proof 3 compressed: the Augustinian proof (chapter 3)
summary.plain: Some truths — like 2 + 2 = 4 — seem to be true whether or not anyone thinks about them, and they don’t depend on the physical world either. But things like numbers, ideas and truths seem to be the kind of thing that only exists in a mind. So if they are real and don’t depend on our minds, they must exist in a mind that is always there and can’t fail to exist. That eternal mind turns out to be God.
summary.body:
**Starting point:** there are abstract objects — universals (redness, triangularity), propositions (what ‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’ both express), numbers, and possible worlds (ways things could have been). They exist at least as objects of thought, but they cannot be seen, touched or erased.

**Stage 1 in outline.** Feser gives six direct arguments for **realism** about such objects — the one-over-many argument, the argument from geometry, from mathematics generally, from the nature of propositions, from science, and from possible worlds — plus indirect arguments against the rivals. **Nominalism** (only general words, no universals) faces Russell’s regress (resemblance is itself a universal) and the fact that words are themselves universals (one word type, many tokens). **Conceptualism** (universals are mind-made) cannot explain shared meaning and communication, and **psychologism** undermines itself because any account of how minds build logic must use logic. So some realism is true. But which? **Platonic realism** puts abstract objects in a ‘third realm’ outside minds and matter — yet such objects would be causally inert (so how could we know them, or they explain anything?), would be paradoxically both universal and individual (animality itself would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which no individual can be), and would make trees and people mere imitations. **Aristotelian realism** — universals exist in things, and as abstract only in minds that abstract them — is better but cannot ground truths and possibilities that would hold even if no material world or human minds existed (pure possibles like unicorns, necessary truths of mathematics). What remains is **Scholastic realism**: abstract objects exist in an infinite, eternal, *divine* intellect.

**Stage 2.** Human, alien and even angelic minds are contingent, so the grounding intellect must exist necessarily. Abstract objects form an interlocking system — grasping one universal requires grasping others, and every proposition stands in logical relations to every other — so they must exist in one intellect that grasps them all, a ‘conceptually omniscient’ being (Robert Adams’ phrase). A necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual (otherwise its existence would depend on something actualizing it), which brings uniqueness and all the other attributes; and if it failed to know some contingent truth it would have unactualized potential, so it is omniscient in the full sense. Greg Welty’s six conditions for a theory of abstract objects (objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude, simplicity) point the same way. The formal statement has **twenty-nine steps**.

**Signature objections:** divine ideas would not really be ‘abstract’ (begs the question against the Aristotelian understanding of abstraction); Brian Leftow on ‘deity theories’ making God depend on water being H₂O (compare: arithmetic doesn’t depend on rocks); Patrick Grim’s Cantorian argument that there is no set of all truths (proves too much, needs no set, and ignores divine simplicity); and Scholastic critics like Peter Coffey who deny the argument can come *before* God’s existence is known.
summary.takeaway: Objective, necessary, eternal truths and universals can exist only in a mind, and only a necessarily existing mind that grasps them all can ground them — the divine intellect.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest step is eliminating **Platonism** and seeing why abstract objects are tied to minds (chapter 3, steps 10–11). Many thoughtful people are happy to say numbers just ‘exist’, full stop, in no particular place. Why not?

Feser’s sharpest argument uses **animality**. Every actual animal is either rational (a human) or nonrational (a dog). Animality itself, precisely because it is universal and applies to both, can include neither rationality nor nonrationality. But no individual existing thing can be neither rational nor nonrational. So animality cannot exist as an individual thing in its own right — a Platonic Form. Where, then, does animality-without-rationality-or-nonrationality exist? Only as the intellect abstracts it: in the world it exists always tied to rationality (in Socrates) or nonrationality (in Fido); considered in abstraction, it exists only in a mind. As David Oderberg puts the Aristotelian point, we do encounter squareness — in square things — but never squareness in the abstract, because the abstract is what the mind abstracts.

Next comes the move beyond Aristotelian realism (steps 12–13). Consider **pure possibles**. Before any material world or human mind existed, it was possible that they would exist. What grounded that possibility then? Not the essence of any existing material thing (there were none), and not a human mind (there were none). Similarly for necessary truths that would hold if every finite mind vanished. So there must be a necessarily existing intellect (steps 14–15), and because abstract objects form an interlocking web of logical relations, one intellect grasping all of them (steps 16–18).

Then the bridge to the rest of the book: a necessarily existing intellect cannot depend on being actualized, so it is purely actual (step 19) — hence unique (20–21) — and if it failed to know some contingent truth it would have an unrealized potential, so it is omniscient in the full sense (24–25). In the capstone argument these are steps 5–6 and 18.

A nuance: Feser admits the debate over abstract objects is 2,300 years old and that he can only present its main lines.

The usual confusion: people often think the Augustinian proof makes mathematics depend on God’s arbitrary choice. It does not; that is voluntarism. Truths are grounded in the divine intellect and nature, which is why they are necessary.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, can animality not exist as a Platonic Form?
options: Because animals are material and Forms are not
Because animality itself would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which no individual existing thing can be
Because Plato never discussed animality
Because animality is merely a word
checks.explanation: As universal, animality must apply to rational and nonrational animals and so include neither; but anything existing as an individual must be one or the other.

checks.q: Does the Augustinian proof make necessary truths depend on God’s arbitrary will?
options: Yes — God could have made 2 + 2 = 5
Yes, but only for mathematical truths
No — they are grounded in the divine intellect and nature, not in arbitrary will (which is voluntarism)
No — they exist independently of God in a third realm
checks.explanation: Feser rejects voluntarism (Leftow’s view about some necessities) and grounds necessities in God’s nature, via divine simplicity.

checks.q: What moves the argument from a ‘conceptually omniscient’ intellect to a fully omniscient one?
options: Its pure actuality: failing to know some contingent truth would be an unactualized potential
Observation of the world’s order
The principle of sufficient reason
Welty’s plenitude condition
checks.explanation: Chapter 3, steps 24–25; Feser also notes that the actual is a subset of the possible.

summary.heading: Proof 4 compressed: the Thomistic proof (chapter 4)
summary.plain: Knowing what something is doesn’t tell you whether it exists — you can know exactly what a unicorn is and still not know if there are any. So for everything around us, existing is something extra, not built into what it is. Nothing can give itself existence, so everything must be receiving its existence, right now, from something else. That chain must end in something whose very nature is simply to exist — and that is God.
summary.body:
**Starting point:** for each thing we know, we can distinguish its **essence** (what it is — say, rational animal) from its **existence** (that it is). The question is whether this distinction is merely verbal, like ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’, or real.

**Three arguments for a real distinction.** (1) You can know what a lion, a pterodactyl and a unicorn are without knowing which exists, which is extinct and which never existed; if existence were the same as essence, knowing the essence would reveal the existence. Judging lions not to exist is a false judgment, but it is not a *misconception* of what a lion is, whereas judging a lion not to be a cat would be. (2) Things are contingent; if their existence were identical with their essence, they would exist by nature and could not fail to exist. (3) Something whose essence just is existence could only be one — it could not be differentiated either as a species within a genus or as an individual within a species (each would be ‘existence itself PLUS something’, and so not existence itself) — whereas there are, or could be, many stones, dogs and people. And there is no middle option on which existence is merely one *part* of an essence. A real distinction need not mean separability: the radius and circumference of a circle are really distinct but inseparable.

**Key moves.** A thing whose essence is distinct from its existence cannot give itself existence — it would have to exist before it exists. So its existence must be imparted by something else, and not just when it began but **at every moment**, or it would simply blink out of existence (Fido needs this here and now). If the cause is itself an essence-existence composite, it too needs a cause here and now, generating a hierarchical series that must terminate in something whose essence just *is* existence: what Aquinas calls **subsistent existence itself**.

**Stage 2.** There can be only one such thing; everything else has essence distinct from existence and depends on it; it exists necessarily and is uncaused; essence and existence relate as potency and act, so subsistent existence itself is purely actual — and therefore identical with the Unmoved Mover and possessed of all the attributes. The formal statement has **thirty-six steps**.

**Signature objections:** Hume’s ‘why need a first cause if each member is explained?’ (irrelevant to hierarchical series — an infinite series of IOUs never yields real money; Barry Miller’s point that the explanatory sentence can only be completed by naming a first member); fallacy of composition (not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious — Lego — and in any case the argument starts from one thing, not the universe); Anthony Kenny’s two notions of existence (assumes real distinction means separability, and that quantifier-style ‘specific existence’ is the only respectable notion; see John Knasas and Gyula Klima); the aspirin/acetylsalicylic-acid objection that the distinction is merely conceptual (a complete grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would include its being acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence ever includes its existence); and doubts about real essences (answered from the unity of natural kinds, the practice of physics described by Nancy Cartwright, Brian Ellis on chemistry, and Crawford Elder’s argument that conventionalism about essence is incoherent).
summary.takeaway: Nothing we encounter exists by its own nature, so each thing must receive existence at every moment from something whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself.
summary.deepDive:
Start with the idea that trips most people up: a **real** distinction that is **not separable**. Feser does not claim that a dog’s essence floats around somewhere waiting for existence, or that existence is a kind of stuff poured into essences. There is no such thing as an essence existing apart from existence, or existence apart from any essence. Yet the two are really distinct — the way a circle’s radius and circumference are really distinct though you can never have one without the other.

Now the thought experiment that powers the argument. Suppose Fido’s existence *were* identical with his essence. Then three absurdities follow. You could know Fido exists just by understanding what a dog is (but you can’t — lion, pterodactyl, unicorn). Fido would exist by his nature and so could never fail to exist (but he is mortal). And there could be only one dog — because something whose essence is existence could not be differentiated from another such thing, either as a species within a genus or as an individual within a species; each would be ‘existence itself plus something’, and so not existence itself (formal steps 2–11). Feser also closes the escape route of making existence merely one *part* of an essence: then the whole thing would depend on that part, making existence the true essence after all.

With the real distinction in hand, the rest moves quickly. Nothing can impart existence to itself — it would have to exist before it existed (steps 12–16). And since the distinction persists every moment, the need for existence to be imparted persists every moment (step 17): without a sustaining cause Fido would ‘blink out’. The regress of existence-givers is hierarchical and ends in **subsistent existence itself** (steps 19–23). Essence relates to existence as potency to act, so subsistent existence is purely actual (31–32) — the capstone’s steps 7–8 and 14–15.

A nuance: for the Thomist, existence is not a property or accident, since a thing must exist before it can have properties — which is why Kenny’s framework, in which existence is either a quantifier or a trivial ‘going on being what one is’, misses the target.

The usual confusion: people often think the Thomistic proof is about Fido’s origin. It is about his existing *now* — the proof would go through even if dogs had begotten dogs forever.

checks.q: Which example does Feser use to show that a real distinction need not involve separability?
options: Aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid
The morning star and the evening star
A circle’s radius and its circumference
A lion and a unicorn
checks.explanation: Radius and circumference (and triangularity and trilaterality) are really distinct but inseparable — as essence and existence are.

checks.q: Why must a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence be caused to exist at every moment, not just when it began?
options: Because the distinction between its essence and existence persists at every moment, so existence must be imparted as long as it exists
Because God chooses to re-create everything constantly
Because matter decays over time
Because of the second law of thermodynamics
checks.explanation: Formal step 17: since the real distinction remains at every moment, including here and now, existence must be imparted here and now.

checks.q: For the Thomist, is existence a property or accident that a thing has?
options: Yes — the most basic property
Yes — an accident added after the thing exists
It is the same thing as the thing’s essence
No — a thing must exist in order to have properties or accidents at all
checks.explanation: Feser notes (following Oderberg) that existence is neither a Fregean second-order predicate nor a property or accident.

summary.heading: Proof 5 compressed: the rationalist proof (chapter 5)
summary.plain: We always assume there’s a reason why things are the way they are — in daily life and in science. If that’s right, then there must be a reason why anything that didn’t have to exist does exist. Pointing to other things that also didn’t have to exist, even an endless chain of them, never finishes the explanation. Only something that exists by its own nature — something that couldn’t fail to exist — can finish it, and that is God.
summary.body:
**Starting point:** the principle of sufficient reason — everything that exists has an explanation for its existence and its attributes. Everyday life and science always assume it; even unsolved murders have explanations of why they are unsolved.

**Why believe PSR?** Inductively, it is as well confirmed as anything: we find explanations when we look, and a world without PSR would be full of inexplicable events. More decisively, it can be defended by *reductio*. Denying it would mean we have no reason to trust that our perceptions connect to the world (a point from Alexander Pruss and Robert Koons), and — pushing further — no reason to think our beliefs are caused by the good reasons we take ourselves to have, so denying PSR undercuts any grounds for denying it. Explanations that end in a ‘brute fact’ are illusory: a book resting on a shelf that stays up for no reason at all has not really been explained. And Michael Della Rocca shows that critics who use ‘explicability arguments’ elsewhere have no principled, non-question-begging way to exempt the existence of things from them.

**Key moves.** Anything is explained either by another (contingent) or by its own nature (necessary); PSR rules out a third option of being explained by nothing. Contingent things exist. Even if every contingent thing were caused by an earlier one in a beginningless series, universe or multiverse (Hume’s suggestion), the existence of the series itself would remain unexplained — contingency, like the redness of Lego blocks rather than the weight of stones, carries over from parts to collection — and specific features would remain unexplained too (Leibniz’s infinitely recopied geometry book: why *this* content?). Appealing to a contingent cause of the series only starts a higher-order series with the same problem. Alternatively, and without mentioning the universe at all, ask why any single contingent thing persists at this moment; a simultaneous regress of contingent causes can never answer. Only a **necessary being** can end the regress.

**Stage 2.** A necessary being must be purely actual, noncomposite and subsistent existence itself — any potency, parts or essence-existence distinction would make its existence depend on something else. Therefore it is unique and identical with the realities reached by the other proofs. Feser adds that the deep reason things are contingent is that they are act-potency mixtures, composite, and essence-existence composites, and the deep reason they need causes is that otherwise they would be unintelligible. The formal statement has **twenty-seven steps**.

**Signature objections:** ‘rationalism’ implies innate ideas (no — only commitment to intelligibility, understood in a Thomistic way); the ‘big conjunctive contingent fact’ (assumes propositions are Platonic objects needing their own explanation, and that explanation requires logical entailment, which even scientific explanation does not); quantum mechanics (quantum events are made intelligible by quantum laws); ‘why not the universe as the necessary being?’ (it changes and has parts); and ‘What caused God?’ (the rationalist proof makes no exception: God has an explanation, in his own nature).
summary.takeaway: If everything is intelligible, then the existence of contingent things — even an endless series of them — must be explained by something that exists by its own nature.
summary.deepDive:
The deepest part of this chapter is the defense of **PSR by self-undermining** (formal steps 4–5, and step 6’s claim that there is no principled way to reject PSR while accepting genuine explanations). Walk through it with an example. Right now you believe some claim — say, that the Earth orbits the Sun — and you think you believe it *because* of good evidence. Notice that this involves two things: there are good reasons for the belief, and those reasons are what actually cause you to hold it. Now suppose PSR is false: things can happen for no reason at all. Then your belief might have popped into your head for no reason, and the feeling that you hold it on good grounds might also have arisen for no reason. You would have no way to rule that out. And the same would go for your belief that PSR is false. So denying PSR removes the grounds for any belief, including the denial. That is a **reductio**: PSR is not proved from something more certain but shown undeniable because its denial destroys itself.

Feser adds the ‘book on a shelf’ point: an explanation resting on a brute fact is no explanation, since the brute foundation has nothing to pass on — exactly like an instrument that is the instrument of nothing.

Notice the two routes to the necessary being. The Leibniz–Clarke route (steps 11–14) asks why the whole series of contingent things exists. The second route (steps 15–17) asks only why *this* contingent thing persists *now* — no talk of the universe as a whole, so the fallacy-of-composition objection has nothing to grab.

Two nuances. Feser’s PSR is Thomistic: it does not demand explanations for propositions as extra objects, and it does not require that explanations logically entail what they explain. And in a footnote he prefers to ask ‘why are there any contingent things?’ rather than ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’, since if a necessary being exists it is false that there could have been nothing at all. He also distinguishes the strict sense of ‘necessary being’ from Aquinas’ broader sense, in which naturally incorruptible angels count as necessary.

In the capstone, this chapter supplies steps 9–10 and, through Stage 2, steps 16–17.

The usual confusion: people think PSR means determinism or ‘everything has a cause’. It means only that everything has an explanation — in God’s case, in his own nature.

checks.q: Why does Feser prefer ‘Why are there any contingent things?’ to ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’
options: Because the second question is unanswerable by science
Because ‘something rather than nothing’ suggests there could have been nothing at all, which is false if a necessary being exists
Because Leibniz never asked it
Because nothing is a kind of physical stuff
checks.explanation: The footnote in chapter 5: what is purely actual, simple, necessary, etc. could not have failed to exist, so it is not true that there could have been nothing.

checks.q: Which of the rationalist proof’s routes to a necessary being avoids any claim about the universe as a whole?
options: The route from the whole infinite series of contingent things
The route from Leibniz’s geometry books
The route from why any particular contingent thing persists in existence at this moment
The route from the Big Bang
checks.explanation: Formal steps 15–17 consider only the persistence of one contingent thing and the simultaneous regress of its causes.

checks.q: Does Feser’s version of PSR require that an explanation logically entail what it explains?
options: No — it requires only that the explanation make the explanandum intelligible, as scientific explanations do without entailment
Yes — otherwise it would not be sufficient
Yes, but only for contingent facts
No — PSR requires no explanations at all for contingent things
checks.explanation: Feser cites Pruss: scientific explanations, such as the Sun’s gravity explaining orbits, do not strictly entail their explananda.

summary.heading: Why the five converge on one and the same God
summary.plain: The five arguments describe their conclusion in five different ways — the thing that doesn’t need to be ‘switched on’, the thing with no parts, the eternal mind, the thing whose nature is to exist, the thing that can’t fail to exist. Feser shows that anything fitting one of these descriptions must fit all of them, and that there can only be one such thing. So the five arguments aren’t pointing to five gods; they are five roads to the same destination.
summary.body:
A critic might grant each proof and still ask whether they reach five different ultimate realities. Feser answers explicitly in the stage 2 sections and systematically at the start of chapter 6. The key is a set of two-way entailments:

1. **Purely actual ⇔ absolutely simple.** Anything with parts is a mixture of act and potency, because parts only potentially compose the whole until something combines them; so what is purely actual has no parts. Conversely, anything simple cannot have any potency, since it would then have an actual ‘part’ and a potential ‘part’. So the Unmoved Mover (ch. 1) and the One (ch. 2) coincide.
2. **Purely actual ⇔ subsistent existence itself.** Essence and existence relate as potency to act, so a purely actual being cannot have an essence distinct from its existence; and something whose existence depended on actualizing a potency would have derived existence and so not be existence itself. So the ch. 1 and ch. 4 conclusions coincide — and, through step 1, the ch. 2 conclusion as well (a simple being cannot have an essence-existence composition; subsistent existence can have no parts of any kind).
3. **Purely actual, simple, subsistent ⇔ absolutely necessary.** Contingency implies potency to be actualized, parts to be combined, or existence added to essence; and a necessary being can have none of these. So the ch. 5 conclusion coincides with the others.
4. **The necessary intellect is purely actual.** A necessarily existing intellect cannot depend on any actualization, so the ch. 3 conclusion coincides as well — which also explains why the other proofs could infer intellect via the PPC.
5. **There cannot be two.** Any plurality requires differentiation — genus plus specific difference, or form plus matter — and hence parts and potency. So there is, in principle and not merely in fact, only one such being.

The result: the five proofs are ‘distinct paths to one and the same God’, not arguments for five deities. Frege’s morning star/evening star distinction shows why this is not mysterious: ‘purely actual’, ‘simple’, ‘necessary’, ‘subsistent existence’ and ‘supreme intellect’ differ in sense but share a single referent. The convergence also strengthens the case in a non-probabilistic way: each proof is meant to succeed alone, but seeing how their conclusions interlock shows that the attributes are not a grab bag but facets of one idea, and it lets one proof supply what another leaves implicit (for example, the Augustinian proof explains *how* the first cause has intellect).
summary.takeaway: Pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity entail one another, and only one being can have them — so all five proofs reach the same God.
summary.deepDive:
The trickiest link is the claim that **anything with potency is composite** (convergence step 12). Why should having an unrealized capacity count as having ‘parts’? Because ‘part’ here means any really distinct constituent, and actuality and potentiality are really distinct (chapter 6 argues this in defending the analogy of being). A being that is actual in some respects and potential in others is thus built of two constituents, an actual one and a potential one — which is why the simple and the purely actual coincide (step 13).

Feser tests the link against a clever objection at the start of chapter 6. Suppose the first cause is purely actual in its *existence* but has potentials in its *activity* — say, a potential to cause this world or that. He answers twice. First, by **agere sequitur esse**: action follows being, so a thing whose existence is purely actual cannot act in a less than purely actual way — where would those potentials come from? Second, such a cause would have parts (an actual part and a potential part), and whatever has parts needs a cause, so it would not be first.

Now a thought experiment to feel the force of **uniqueness** (step 19). Try to imagine two purely actual beings, A and B. What makes them two? Not location — they are immaterial. Not a difference in some feature — any feature one has and the other lacks would be a perfection lacked, i.e., a potency, or an added part. Not a ‘bare’ difference with no ground; ‘two’ requires something by which they are two. Once the grounds are stripped away, the ‘two’ collapse into one.

The Fregean image then makes step 20 intuitive: ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ have different senses but one referent. So do ‘purely actual actualizer’, ‘the One’, ‘necessary intellect’, ‘subsistent existence’ and ‘necessary being’.

A nuance worth noticing: the convergence holds at the level of the *descriptions*. Even if a critic defeated one proof, the identity of the others’ conclusions would remain; the case is robust (step 27). And each chapter’s Stage 2 already makes these identifications locally (e.g., chapter 2, steps 33–35; chapter 4, steps 31–33).

The usual confusion: people often read ‘cumulative case’ as ‘five weak probabilities adding up’. The convergence is itself deduced; it explains why the arguments agree rather than hoping they do.

checks.q: How does Feser answer the suggestion that the first cause might be purely actual in existence but have potentials in its activity?
options: He concedes it but says it doesn’t matter
He appeals to the Bible
He argues from agere sequitur esse (action follows being) and from the fact that such potentials would give it parts, requiring a cause
He appeals to quantum mechanics
checks.explanation: Chapter 6 (Unity) gives both replies: a purely actual existence cannot ground potential activity, and having potential and actual ‘parts’ would make it caused.

checks.q: If a critic refuted the Augustinian proof, would the convergence of the other four conclusions be undermined?
options: No — the identity of the other conclusions depends on the biconditionals among pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity, not on the Augustinian proof
Yes — all five stand or fall together
Yes — the convergence depends on the divine intellect
Only the Thomistic proof would be affected
checks.explanation: The convergence is a relation among descriptions; defeating one route leaves the others and their identity intact — which is why the case is robust.

summary.heading: What the proofs do NOT claim
summary.plain: A lot of popular criticism attacks arguments Feser doesn’t make. He doesn’t say ‘everything has a cause’, he doesn’t say the universe must have had a beginning, and he doesn’t treat God as a giant being inside the universe. He also doesn’t claim to prove any particular religion. Knowing what isn’t being claimed is half the battle in understanding what is.
summary.body:
Most popular criticism attacks arguments Feser never makes. Before defending the case, be able to disown the caricatures:

- **Not that everything has a cause.** The principles are that whatever goes from potential to actual, whatever is composite, or whatever has essence distinct from existence needs a cause; the PSR says everything has an *explanation*, which for God lies in his own nature. Chapter 7 shows that no major defender of cosmological arguments ever used the premise ‘everything has a cause’.
- **Not that the universe had a beginning.** Every causal proof grants, for argument’s sake, a beginningless universe or multiverse. Only the kalām argument (not defended here) tries to prove a beginning.
- **Not a premise about the universe as a whole.** The proofs start from any single thing — a cup of coffee, a stone, Fido. That God causes *everything* is a conclusion, not a premise, so the fallacy of composition charge misfires.
- **Not ‘first’ in time.** The first cause is first in the sense of underived, the source of the borrowed power of every other cause.
- **Not a god of the gaps or a probabilistic hypothesis.** They are demonstrations from starting points any possible empirical theory must presuppose; parsimony and ‘better explanation’ talk does not apply.
- **Not a design argument.** None appeals to complexity, fine-tuning or Paley-style functional order; a pebble or a drop of water would do as a starting point.
- **Not the ontological argument.** God’s necessity is not ‘existence by definition’; Aquinas rejects the ontological argument while accepting the cosmological ones.
- **Not that God is ‘a being’ alongside others.** God is not the biggest item in the inventory, not a member of the genus ‘gods’, but subsistent being itself from which everything else derives its being.
- **Not the truth of any particular religion.** The proofs establish a cause that is one, simple, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good; whether God has revealed himself (the Trinity, prophets, scripture) is a further question.
- **Not that every intelligent hearer will be convinced.** A demonstration is a valid deduction from premises that can be shown true; that people dispute it no more refutes it than disputes refute any other philosophical argument.
summary.takeaway: Most popular objections attack claims the proofs never make — ‘everything has a cause’, a beginning of time, the universe as a premise, a god of the gaps, a being among beings.
summary.deepDive:
The subtlest item on this list is the one about **the universe as a whole**, because it sounds as if Feser both does and doesn’t make claims about it. Here is the resolution: claims about the whole universe appear in the proofs only as **conclusions**, never as **premises**.

Work through it. The Aristotelian proof starts from one cup of coffee. It shows that this one cup’s existence here and now requires a purely actual actualizer. Then Stage 2 shows that there can be only one purely actual actualizer. Then — and only then — it observes that what was true of the coffee is true of every material thing, so everything depends on that one actualizer. ‘The universe has a cause’ is a *consequence*. That is why the fallacy-of-composition objection, which accuses the argument of inferring from parts to whole, misses: there is no such inference at the start. (Feser adds, for the Thomistic proof, that the space-time universe would need a cause anyway, since it too has an essence distinct from its existence; and for the rationalist proof, that contingency transfers from parts to whole like color.) In the capstone argument, steps 1, 3, 7 and 9 all begin from particular things; step 24 draws the universal conclusion.

A second subtle item: ‘not the ontological argument’. Kant claimed any argument to a necessary being secretly needs the ontological argument. But the necessity Feser attributes to God is not ‘existing by definition’, the way a bachelor is unmarried by definition; it is the metaphysical necessity of what is purely actual, simple and identical with its own existence. Aquinas rejected the ontological argument while defending cosmological ones, which already shows they can come apart.

A third: ‘not a being among beings’. This is less a disclaimer than a positive thesis. God is not the biggest item in the inventory of the universe but the source from which anything in the inventory has being at all.

The usual confusion: people think Feser’s refusal of ‘everything has a cause’ is a clever dodge invented to escape ‘what caused God?’. Chapter 1 answers that the ‘potential to actual’ formulation has been the claim for over two thousand years, and chapter 7 cites a Thomist making the same complaint in 1889.

checks.q: In the Aristotelian proof, is ‘the universe as a whole has a cause’ a premise or a conclusion?
options: A premise, needed to get the argument started
Neither — the proof says nothing about the universe
A premise borrowed from cosmology
A conclusion, drawn after showing a single thing depends on the one purely actual actualizer
checks.explanation: Feser says the claim about the universe is a consequence of the argument, not a premise; any old object will do as a starting point.

checks.q: Which kind of cosmological argument, not defended in the book, does try to show that the universe had a beginning?
options: The kalām cosmological argument
The Leibnizian argument
The Neo-Platonic argument
The Thomistic argument from essence and existence
checks.explanation: Chapter 7 notes that only the kalām version is concerned to show the universe began.

summary.heading: How chapter 6 completes the case (I): principles and attributes
summary.plain: Chapter 6 asks: if God exists, what is he like? Using a few basic principles — for instance, that a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have, and that what a thing does reflects what it is — Feser shows God must be one, without parts, unchanging, outside time, all-powerful, all-knowing, good, free and loving. He also explains that our words for God (‘good’, ‘wise’) are used literally but in a stretched sense, and that God is ultimately beyond our full understanding.
summary.body:
Chapter 6 infers from the world, considered as effect, to the nature of its cause, using three background principles. The **PPC** (formally, virtually, eminently) is defended against John Cottingham’s ‘heirloom’ charge and his helium and sponge-cake counterexamples: those concern only material ingredients, not total causes; the principle never required that causes hand on their own form; and even naturalists like Paul Churchland rely on it, while evolution respects it (genes, mutations and environment jointly contain what emerges). **Agere sequitur esse** — action follows being — says what a thing does reflects what it is; even John Searle implicitly uses it against property dualism. The **analogy of being** is defended by showing that potency must have being in a sense analogous to actuality’s (Parmenides and Heraclitus each deny one side incoherently). Analogy comes in two main kinds — of *attribution* (healthy George, healthy food) and of *proper proportionality* (seeing a tree, seeing a theorem) — and both are literal, not metaphorical. Without analogy, talk of God would collapse into anthropomorphism or empty negation.

The attributes then follow:

- **Unity** — including the proof, above, that all five paths reach one God.
- **Simplicity** — nonnegotiable for classical theism (pagans, Jews, Muslims, Christians; Lateran IV and Vatican I; Luther and Calvin). Denying it makes God a ‘superangel’ in need of a cause. Alvin Plantinga’s objection that simplicity makes God a property rests on his broad notion of ‘property’, Platonist view of properties and univocal predication, all rejected by classical theists; Thomas Morris’s necessary-versus-contingent-properties objection is met with Peter Geach’s and Barry Miller’s ‘Cambridge properties’ (God’s being Creator is like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato when Plato grows).
- **Immutability** — acting and being alive do not essentially require being changed; to think otherwise is a **fallacy of accident**.
- **Immateriality and incorporeality**; **eternity** understood as strict timelessness — God causes a whole temporal world in one act, as an author conceives a whole story, and eternity is not a point in time that could be ‘simultaneous’ with Socrates and Obama.
- **Necessity** — not linguistic convention (J. N. Findlay), and not refuted by imagining a world with nothing in it (David Schrader), since God is not imageable and essence determines modality, not the reverse.
- **Omnipotence** — the power to actualize any potential; the stone paradox describes no genuine capacity.
- **Omniscience** — via the PPC and the author analogy; God knows the world by knowing himself as its cause. Foreknowledge no more removes freedom than an author’s writing removes a character’s free choice; God is not a hypnotist inside the story.
- **Perfect goodness** — goodness is actuality relative to a thing’s nature; badness is **privation**, so the PPC does not put evil in God.
- **Will** — free, since nothing outside or inside God compels one creation over another; there is no obligation to create, and no ‘best possible world’.
- **Love** — willing the good of another, which requires no passive emotion.
- **Incomprehensibility** — we know that God is and much of what he is not, and we can speak analogically, but we cannot comprehend him the way we understand things by their parts.
summary.takeaway: Proportionate causality, action-follows-being and analogy let us infer from the world to a God who is one, simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient, good, free and loving — yet never fully comprehended.
summary.deepDive:
The knottiest issue in this half of the chapter is how **simplicity** squares with God’s having many attributes and with contingent truths about him. Three tools untangle it.

First, **sense and reference plus analogy**. ‘God’s power’ and ‘God’s knowledge’ differ in sense but refer to one reality; and the words apply to God analogically. Power and knowledge are distinct in us because we are composite; nothing forces them to be distinct in a simple being.

Second, the **right metaphysics of predication**. Plantinga’s critique treats every predicate as a ‘property’ and properties as Platonic abstract objects; on those assumptions, ‘God is identical with his properties’ turns God into an abstract object. Classical theists distinguish a thing’s essence, its properties (which flow from its essence), its accidents and its mere relations — all as constituents of the thing, not Platonic entities.
