Third, **Cambridge properties**. Take the contingent truth ‘God created Adam’. Does simplicity make this identical with God’s necessary wisdom? No. Compare: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows — a new truth about Socrates with no change in Socrates. ‘Creator of Adam’ is like that: it reflects a change in the world, not in God. Simplicity identifies God’s *real* properties with one another, not his Cambridge properties.

Now a worked example of how the attributes answer puzzles. Is God obliged to create the best possible world, and if he can’t do otherwise, is he free? Feser denies there is any best possible world: if a world with trees is better than one without, a world with more forests is better still, without limit — so ‘the best world’ is like ‘the largest number’. And God’s perfection flows from what he is, not what he makes, like a perfect diamond whether or not it cuts glass.

These results feed the capstone’s convergence steps 21–23 and explain why step 20’s identity is coherent.

The usual confusion: people think ‘simple’ means God has only one feature, or that analogical talk is metaphor or evasion. Feser insists analogy is literal (attribution and proper proportionality) and that it is required even outside theology — physics must speak of curved space and wave-like particles.

checks.q: Thomas Morris argues that simplicity is inconsistent with God’s having both necessary properties (omnipotence) and contingent ones (having created the world). How does Feser reply?
options: He denies that God created the world
Contingent truths like ‘God created the world’ are mere Cambridge properties, whereas simplicity identifies only God’s real properties
He concedes that God is composite in this respect
He says omnipotence is contingent too
checks.explanation: Following Geach and Miller: God’s having created the world involves a real change only in the world, like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato.

checks.q: Why does Feser deny that there is a best possible world?
options: Because the actual world is already best
Because goodness cannot be compared
Because for any world with some degree of goodness (e.g., x forests), a better one is possible (x + 1 forests), without limit
Because God cannot know which world is best
checks.explanation: Like ‘the largest number’, ‘the best world’ describes nothing, so God cannot be obliged to create it.

checks.q: When we say ‘God has power’ and ‘the sun has power’, with God as the source of all causal power, which kind of analogy is at work?
options: Improper (metaphorical) proportionality
Univocal predication
Equivocal predication
Analogy of attribution, with God as primary analogate
checks.explanation: Chapter 6: creatures have power only derivatively from God, as food is ‘healthy’ by relation to a healthy person.

summary.heading: How chapter 6 completes the case (II): God, the world and miracles
summary.plain: God didn’t just start the world long ago; he keeps it in existence every moment, the way a singer keeps a song going by singing. Things in the world really do cause things, but only because God is empowering them as they act. That rules out the idea that God is the world, the idea that only God really acts, and the idea that God set things up and walked away. A miracle, on this view, isn’t God ‘breaking’ nature but lifting it beyond its normal abilities or holding back its normal effect.
summary.body:
The causal proofs imply **divine conservation**: nothing other than God could exist for an instant unless he were sustaining it, so creation is ongoing, not a past event. This rules out ‘existential inertia’ — the idea that things tend to stay in existence on their own — because no composite, act-potency, essence-existence thing could have such a feature, and its defenders never say what would give it one. Because the world is composite, changing and contingent while God is simple, immutable and necessary, the proofs also rule out **pantheism** (God is the world) and **panentheism** (God is changed by the world).

Combining conservation with *agere sequitur esse* yields **concurrence**. **Occasionalism** says only God causes anything; but if creatures truly did nothing, they would not truly exist, and the proofs themselves started from real changes and real composites — occasionalism kicks away the ladder it climbed. **Mere conservationism** says creatures act independently once God keeps them in being; but what cannot exist independently cannot act independently, and the view drifts toward deism. So secondary causes are real but secondary: the chalk makes the square blue, you make there be a square at all; the moon shines, but only with the sun’s light. Human freedom fits like a child whose hand is guided by a parent teaching him to write — the child can resist or cooperate, but the letter appears only with the parent’s guidance.

Finally, **miracles**. On the Aristotelian view, laws of nature describe the tendencies things have by their natures, so they are not broken; a miracle is not a violation but either an *elevation* of nature beyond its own powers or a *suspension* in which God refrains from conserving or concurring with some causes (the three young men unburnt in the furnace). God cannot literally ‘intervene’ in a world that is his own continuous work; better images are the musician improvising beyond the score, the director’s cut, or an author’s second edition. Miracles matter because they would be the rational bridge from natural to revealed theology — the sign that a purported revelation truly comes from God — and natural theology already constrains religions: any that deny God’s unity, distinctness from the world, intellect, will, immateriality or infinite power are thereby shown false.

Two further points round out the chapter. First, natural theology gives a practical test of religious claims: a religion that denies God’s unity, identifies him with the world, makes him impersonal, material, or finite in power or knowledge is thereby shown false; and a religion that claims revelation but cannot back that claim with a miracle in the strict sense gives us no reason to take it seriously. Second, a short appendix asks whether God is male. Being immaterial, God is not an animal and so is literally neither male nor female. But because he has intellect and will, ‘it’ would be misleading; and because his relation to the world is active rather than receptive, unchanging, independent and distinct — more like a father’s role than a mother’s in procreation — Feser argues that masculine language is the least misleading, whereas maternal imagery would suggest a changeable God continuous with the world, as in pantheism or panentheism.
summary.takeaway: God keeps everything in being and empowers every act at every moment, which rules out pantheism, occasionalism and deism and makes miracles elevations or suspensions rather than violations.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is **concurrence**: how can one effect be fully produced by a creature and also by God, without the two competing? The key is that they are causes **on different levels**, not two causes side by side splitting the work.

Feser’s images help. When you draw a blue square with blue chalk, you and the chalk both cause the effect, but in different respects: the chalk accounts for the square’s being *blue*, you account for there being any square at all. Swap red chalk and you get a different effect, so the chalk contributes something real; stop pressing and you get no effect, so it acts only through your action. The moon shines by reflected sunlight: its surface really shapes the light we see, but without the sun there is no light at all. God concurs with every creature’s action somewhat like that.

Now the application to freedom. A parent teaching a child to write guides the child’s hand; the child can resist or cooperate, and the child’s choice makes a real contribution, yet the letter appears only with the parent’s guidance. Divine concurrence with free choices is analogous (Feser borrows this from David Oderberg). The author-and-story analogy from the first half of the chapter reinforces the point: the author is not a hypnotist inside the story.

Two nuances Feser adds. Occasionalism cannot rescue itself by leaning on the Augustinian proof, since that proof does not reach God as the source of all causal power — only the causal proofs do, and those are the proofs occasionalism undercuts by denying that creatures act. And a miracle need not *add* anything; it can *subtract*, as when God refrains from conserving or concurring with some factor, so fire does not burn the three young men in the furnace. That is a suspension of a law, like a law temporarily taken off the books, not a violation of one left on them.

This section corresponds to the capstone’s convergence step 24.

The usual confusion: people picture God and nature as rivals — ‘either nature did it or God did’. On Feser’s view that is a category mistake; God is not one cause alongside others but the source of the causal power of all of them. That is also why miracles are not the main evidence for God; the ordinary course of nature is.

checks.q: In Feser’s blue-chalk example of concurrence, what does the chalk contribute?
options: Nothing — only the hand acts
The square’s being blue, a real contribution, though it produces nothing without the hand’s action
The existence of the square as a whole
The chalkboard
checks.explanation: Secondary causes make a real contribution to the character of the effect but act only with the primary cause’s action.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, can’t the occasionalist appeal to the Augustinian proof instead of the causal proofs?
options: Because the Augustinian proof is unsound
Because the Augustinian proof denies that God exists necessarily
Because the Augustinian proof does not start from causality, so it does not reach God as the source of all causal power
Because Augustine was not an occasionalist
checks.explanation: Chapter 6, note 79: only the causal proofs give the occasionalist the idea of God as source of all causal power — and those proofs start from real creaturely causes.

checks.q: How does Feser classify a miracle like the young men not being burned in the fiery furnace?
options: As a violation of the law that fire burns
As an elevation of fire’s powers
As a preternatural effect produced by an angel
As a suspension — a subtraction in which God refrains from conserving or concurring with some factors, so the normal effect does not follow
checks.explanation: Feser supplements Ramelow: some miracles subtract rather than add; this is suspension, not breach, of natural law.

summary.heading: How chapter 7 completes the case: the objections and their diagnosis
summary.plain: Chapter 7 goes through the most common reasons people give for rejecting arguments for God. Feser argues that the most famous one — ‘if everything has a cause, what caused God?’ — attacks a version of the argument that no serious thinker ever gave. Other objections, like ‘only science gives knowledge’ or ‘evil disproves God’, get careful answers too. The message: to reject the arguments, you have to deal with what they actually say.
summary.body:
Chapter 7 revisits, from new angles, the objections that have come up throughout and adds several more. Its central diagnosis is historical: the famous ‘basic cosmological argument’ — everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, God — was never defended by any major proponent, from Plato and Aristotle through Aquinas, Leibniz and Clarke to recent writers; even critic Robin Le Poidevin concedes no one held it. Following W. Norris Clarke, Feser traces the straw man through Russell back to the Mills and ultimately to Hume, who confused the rationalist claim that everything has a *sufficient reason* (Descartes and Spinoza spoke loosely of God as self-caused) with the claim that everything has an *efficient cause distinct from itself*.

The chapter then works through: ‘What caused God?’ (in each proof, the feature that makes things need a cause is precisely what God lacks, so the question asks what caused the uncausable); ‘maybe the universe, Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events or laws are the necessary being’ (each is a mixture of act and potency, composite, contingent; laws are either descriptions, Platonic entities, divine decrees or tendencies of natures, and none is ultimate; and a necessary universe would be pantheism, not atheism); ‘not everything has a cause’ (chance presupposes causal regularities, like the farmer finding buried treasure; quantum events are indeterministic, not unintelligible; Hume’s conceivability test fails); ‘why assume a beginning or a terminus?’; the fallacy of composition (Grayling and Hume are the ones who commit it — sticks, mirrors, Leibniz’s books); ‘why think the first cause is God?’ (Aquinas devoted around a hundred dense pages of the *Summa* to exactly this); ‘this does not prove the Trinity’ (true and irrelevant); Kant’s charge that cosmological arguments presuppose the ontological one (God’s necessity is metaphysical, grounded in pure actuality, not definitional); ‘god of the gaps’ and Lawrence Krauss’s universe ‘from nothing’ (a quantum vacuum and laws of physics are not nothing); **scientism** (self-refuting or trivial; science abstracts from everything unquantifiable, so its success no more shows nothing else exists than a metal detector’s success shows only metal exists; Hume’s fork refutes itself); brute-fact laws (violates PSR, ad hoc, and makes all higher explanations illusory); Dawkins’ ‘the designer is more complex’ (aimed at design arguments; these proofs agree complex things need causes, which is why they conclude to a simple one); ‘one god further’ (a category mistake, like treating triangularity as one more drawn triangle); ‘the God of the philosophers is not the God of religion’ (irrelevant, and false — compare the layman’s crude but real belief in atoms); the problem of evil (Mackie’s logical version fails because some goods — forgiveness, mercy, courage, compassion — logically require evils; Rowe’s evidential version fails against anyone who has independent proof of a good God; an afterlife could outweigh all suffering); divine hiddenness (Schellenberg; most people have in fact believed in the divine); the ‘rationalization’ charge (ad hominem — and Thomas Nagel confessed to hoping there is no God); and ‘it can’t be a proof if so many doubt it’.
summary.takeaway: Chapter 7 shows the standard objections mostly target a caricature born of a historical misreading, and that the serious ones — scientism, brute facts, evil, hiddenness — do not defeat the demonstrations.
summary.deepDive:
The most instructive thread is Feser’s diagnosis of why ‘What caused God?’ feels devastating yet misses. It has two layers.

The **logical** layer: rewrite the question in each proof’s own terms. For the Aristotelian proof it becomes ‘What actualized the potentials of that which has no potentials?’; for the Neo-Platonic, ‘What combined the parts of that which has no parts?’; for the Thomistic, ‘What joined the essence and existence of that whose essence is existence?’; for the rationalist, ‘What gave a reason for existing to that which has its reason in itself?’ Put that way, the question is not hard; it is incoherent. The proofs do not exempt God from a rule; they identify the feature that generates the need for a cause and show there must be something lacking it.

The **historical** layer: following W. Norris Clarke, Feser argues the straw man came from a confusion. Descartes and Spinoza spoke of God as ‘self-caused’, meaning that God is self-explanatory — he has his sufficient reason in himself. Hume read ‘cause’ as ‘efficient cause distinct from its effect’ and credited the tradition with ‘everything has an efficient cause’ — a principle the tradition always denied. Russell, via the Mills, popularized the result. Clarke even concedes that *if* someone held ‘every being has a cause’, the refutation would be devastating — which should have made critics suspicious that no one held it. Note the irony Feser points out: Descartes himself is immune to the objection, because he did not deny that God has a ‘cause’ in his sense.

A second instructive case is ‘maybe the universe is the necessary being’. Feser’s reply has a twist: if the universe really were necessary, uncaused and self-explanatory, it would have divine attributes, and the result would be **pantheism**, not atheism.

In the capstone argument, these replies rest on steps 11–20: the stopping point of explanation is principled because only what is purely actual, simple, self-existent and necessary can be it.

The usual confusion: people think chapter 7’s tone means Feser dismisses critics wholesale. His real claim is narrower — that *specific* popular objections misread the arguments — and he engages serious critics (Mackie, Rowe, Schellenberg, Kenny, Plantinga) in detail. When you use this material, keep his substance and drop the heat.

checks.q: According to Norris Clarke’s account, why is even Descartes not vulnerable to ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
options: Because Descartes did not deny that God has a ‘cause’ — he called God self-caused, meaning self-explanatory
Because Descartes was an atheist
Because Descartes argued only from design
Because Descartes held that nothing has a cause
checks.explanation: Descartes’ argument makes no exception for God; he meant something like PSR, blurring cause and sufficient reason.

checks.q: Why would the claim that the universe is a necessary, self-explanatory being, if true, fail to vindicate atheism?
options: Because the universe would then have begun
Because the universe would then have distinctively divine attributes, yielding pantheism rather than atheism
Because necessary beings cannot exist
Because science would be refuted
checks.explanation: Feser notes the objection would show that God exists and is identical with the world — a view many Hindus accept but atheists cannot.

checks.q: What is Feser’s dilemma against scientism?
options: Science is either deterministic or random
Science is either Newtonian or quantum
Science is either inductive or deductive
The claim that only science gives knowledge is either self-refuting (not itself scientific) or trivial (if ‘science’ is stretched to include philosophy)
checks.explanation: And on the trivial horn, natural theology could itself count as ‘science’, so scientism loses its force against it.

summary.heading: Demonstration, controversy and the burden of proof
summary.plain: Feser calls his arguments ‘demonstrations’: if the starting points are true, the conclusion must be true, and the starting points are things no future discovery could overturn. That doesn’t mean everyone will be convinced right away — plenty of good arguments are argued about for centuries. What it means is that a critic has to point to a specific false premise or a specific bad step, not just say ‘some people disagree’.
summary.body:
The book closes by clarifying what it means to call these arguments **demonstrations**. A demonstration, in the classical sense, is a deduction whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are certain, where that certainty can be shown by metaphysical analysis. This makes it more secure than a scientific inference in two respects: it is not probabilistic or ‘best explanation’ reasoning where some rival hypothesis might turn out correct, and its premises cannot be overturned by further empirical discovery because they concern what any empirical inquiry presupposes. The Aristotelian proof illustrates this: its starting premise (change occurs) is known through experience, so the argument is not a priori, yet no future experience could overturn it, since any future experience would itself be a change. The other premises (the principle of causality, the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress) are defended metaphysically — for instance, the principle of causality follows from PSR, and PSR can be defended by *reductio*.

It follows that controversy is not refutation. Nothing about a demonstration requires that every reader, or even every fair-minded and informed reader, immediately see its force; significant philosophical work may be needed to defend its premises. Feser also notes a double standard: an argument for materialism or against free will is not declared to have ‘failed’ merely because critics exist, yet arguments for God are often treated as dead the moment Hume is mentioned. What a demonstration needs is that, when all is said and done, it can be defended against every objection claiming the premises are doubtful or the conclusion does not follow — which is what the book claims to have done for all five proofs.

For you as a defender, this has practical consequences. Put the burden where it belongs: a critic must show *which* premise is false or *where* the inference fails, not merely gesture at an alternative, a probability or a famous name. And be scrupulous yourself — present the premises accurately, concede what the arguments do not show, and never pass off confidence as proof.
summary.takeaway: A demonstration is a valid deduction from premises no empirical discovery could overturn; it can be controversial without failing, and the burden is on the critic to show where it goes wrong.
summary.deepDive:
The puzzling idea here is how an argument can **start from experience** and yet be **immune to empirical overturning**. Isn’t anything learned from experience revisable by more experience?

Take the Aristotelian proof’s first premise, ‘change occurs’. We know it through experience — so the argument is not a priori. But consider what it would take to overturn it empirically. You would need some future observation showing that no change occurs. Yet having that observation, after not having had it, would itself be a change. Any possible evidence against the premise instantiates it. Distinguish carefully: we can discover that *this or that* apparent change is illusory (the ‘moving’ train was the one next to ours); we cannot coherently discover, on empirical grounds, that *all* change is illusory. That is the special status Feser claims for the starting points of all five proofs: change, composition, contingency, abstract truths and the demand for explanation are presupposed by any empirical theory.

The other premises are defended not by experiment but by metaphysical analysis — the principle of causality from what potentiality is (and from PSR), the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress from the nature of derivative power, PSR by *reductio*. That is why Feser can say the premises are certain without saying they are obvious to everyone. Significant philosophical work may be needed to see them.

Now the double standard he highlights, with help from Hilary Putnam: no philosophical argument — not Frege’s, not Quine’s, not an argument for materialism — convinces every rational person who hears it, yet only arguments for God are declared ‘failed’ as soon as someone objects or Hume is mentioned. Controversy shows an argument needs defending, not that it is unsound.

In the capstone, this is the basis of step 27: the case is robust because each route is a demonstration, so a critic must refute each one, premise by premise.

The usual confusion: people think ‘demonstration’ means a mathematical-style proof from self-evident axioms, or a proof that compels instant agreement. Feser means neither; he means a sound deduction whose premises can be shown true and cannot be undermined by further observation.

checks.q: Why is the Aristotelian proof not a priori, yet not open to empirical refutation?
options: Because its premises are definitions
Because it relies on revelation
Because its first premise (change occurs) is known through experience, but any future experience that seemed to refute it would itself be a change
Because it has been confirmed by physics
checks.explanation: We can reject particular instances of change as illusory, but not all change on empirical grounds (chapter 7’s closing section).

checks.q: What, according to Feser, does the fact that an argument is controversial show?
options: That it is unsound
That significant philosophical work may be needed to defend it — not that it fails as a demonstration
That it is merely probable
That its conclusion is false
checks.explanation: A demonstration need only be defensible against every objection; fair-minded readers may still fail to see its force.

summary.heading: Choosing the right proof for the right conversation
summary.plain: You don’t need to present all five arguments to anyone. Pick the one that starts from something your listener already cares about — a scientist might like the argument from change, a mathematician the argument from mathematical truth. Explain that one well, with everyday examples, and only then mention that four other roads lead to the same place.
summary.body:
The five proofs are logically independent, so you never need all five at once. (This section is course advice rather than Feser’s text.) Match the entry point to the listener’s existing commitments:

- **Scientists and engineers** usually respond best to the **Aristotelian** proof (everyday change, cups on desks, the difference between how something got here and what keeps it here now) or the **Neo-Platonic** proof (‘what holds this together right now?’). Be ready with the ‘absence from the equations is not absence from reality’ point.
- **Mathematicians, logicians, programmers and Platonist-leaning thinkers** often find the **Augustinian** proof compelling, because they already believe that 2 + 2 = 4 would be true without us. The real work is moving them from Platonism to a divine intellect.
- **People who ask ‘why is there anything at all?’** or who love explanation — including many who know the Leibniz–Clarke tradition from debates — are natural audiences for the **rationalist** proof. Start with PSR and the self-undermining character of denying it.
- **Philosophy students and the metaphysically curious** tend to relish the **Thomistic** proof; its central idea (a thing does not have its existence by its own nature) is the deepest in the book.
- **Believers who think of God as a very powerful person among persons** benefit most from chapter 2 and chapter 6: simplicity, analogy and the category mistake in ‘one god further’.
- **Casual skeptics raised on New Atheist talking points** first need the caricatures removed: no ‘everything has a cause’, no Big Bang premise, no god of the gaps. Often the most persuasive single move is showing that ‘What caused God?’ misunderstands every proof.

Whatever proof you pick, run it through the same five-part checklist: an everyday starting example, the key principle stated precisely, the hierarchical ‘here and now’ point, the Stage 2 attributes, and the one or two objections that listener is likeliest to raise. Then, if the conversation goes well, show how the others converge on the same conclusion — the moment many listeners realize they are not facing a single clever argument but a whole tradition’s worth of converging reasoning.
summary.takeaway: Pick the one proof that meets your listener where they already stand, run it through a fixed checklist, and only then show how the others converge.
summary.deepDive:
The hard part of choosing a proof is **diagnosing the hidden premise** your listener already holds, because that premise usually decides which road is shortest. (This section is course advice, not Feser’s text, but it applies his material.)

Three diagnoses cover most conversations. The first is **scientism**: the listener assumes that anything real is something physics could in principle describe. Leading with the Augustinian proof here often stalls, because they will simply deny that numbers are real. Better to start with the Aristotelian proof’s water molecule — a physical example — and let the ‘absence from the equations is not absence from reality’ point emerge naturally. The second is **Platonism**: the listener already believes mathematical truths are objective and necessary. Here the Augustinian proof starts halfway up the mountain. The third is **theistic personalism**, common among believers: God pictured as a very powerful person inside the universe. Here the Neo-Platonic proof and chapter 6 on simplicity do the most good.

A worked example. A software engineer says, ‘Numbers are just symbols we manipulate.’ Ask: ‘If every computer and every person vanished, would it stop being true that there are infinitely many primes?’ If she says no, she is a realist and you can proceed with chapter 3. If she says yes, she is a nominalist or conceptualist; you can explore Russell’s resemblance regress — or switch roads and ask what keeps her laptop’s silicon existing as silicon right now.

Two cautions. First, meeting people where they stand is not tailoring the truth. Each proof is presented in the book as a demonstration in its own right; don’t present it as weaker (‘just a possibility’) or stronger (‘this settles which religion is true’) than it is. Second, more is not better: one proof understood beats five half-understood. The convergence (capstone step 27) is best used afterwards, to show the listener that the conclusion they have just reached is not an isolated trick but where every road leads.

The usual confusion: people think persuasion means finding the cleverest argument. Usually it means finding the argument whose first premise the listener already accepts — and then going slowly.

checks.q: A listener assumes that only what physics can describe is real. Which opening is most promising?

The problem of evil

The Aristotelian proof, starting with what keeps a physical thing (like the water in coffee) existing right now

argument.name: The Convergence Argument: Five Paths to One God
argument.overview:
This is not one of Feser’s own numbered arguments but a synthesis of the whole book, built from the formal statements of chapters 1–5 and the unity section at the start of chapter 6. It has three stages.

**Stage A** restates, in compressed form, the conclusion of each of the five proofs. Each pair of steps compresses a long argument; consult the chapter modules for the full formal statements (50, 38, 29, 36 and 27 steps respectively). Each proof is meant to succeed on its own.

**Stage B** shows that the five conclusions describe one and the same being. It relies on two-way entailments among pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity, plus the argument that none of these can be had by more than one thing.

**Stage C** draws out what follows: a single being with the full set of divine attributes, sustaining and empowering everything else at every moment — which is what classical theism means by God.

> Remember that ‘cumulative’ here does not mean ‘probabilistic’. The case does not add up five weak arguments into one stronger bet; it shows five independent demonstrations arriving at the same place, and it explains *why* they must.

stages.title: Stage A — Five independent routes
stages.gist: Each proof, from its own starting point, establishes a being fitting a distinctive description: purely actual actualizer, absolutely simple One, necessary intellect, subsistent existence itself, necessary being.

stages.title: Stage B — One referent
stages.gist: Pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity entail one another; a necessary intellect is purely actual; and there cannot in principle be two such beings. So the five conclusions name one being.

stages.title: Stage C — The God of classical theism
stages.gist: That one being has every attribute derived by any route, conserves and concurs with all things, and is therefore God — reached by five distinct paths.

steps.text: Change is real, and every change presupposes a thing that changes, whose existence at each moment requires the concurrent actualization of its potential to exist.
steps.why: Chapter 1: change cannot coherently be denied (denying it is itself a change), and change is the actualization of potential. The coffee’s water exists here and now only because its matter’s potential to be water is being actualized, via atoms, via subatomic particles, and so on.
steps.example: The coffee on your desk cools (a change), but even to be there cooling it must exist as coffee — its matter actually water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen, which depends right now on how its atoms and particles are actualized.
steps.challenge: Why can’t the water simply go on existing by itself, with no concurrent actualizer (‘existential inertia’)?
steps.answer: The water is a mixture of act and potency — its matter could exist otherwise — so its being water now is an actualized potential needing an actualizer. Chapter 6 adds that no composite, act-potency thing could have existential inertia, and its defenders never say what would give it that feature.

steps.text: So there exists a purely actual actualizer — an Unmoved (indeed unmovable) Mover.
steps.why: Chapter 1: the regress of concurrent actualizers of existence is hierarchical, and a hierarchical series must end in something with underived power that can actualize without being actualized, i.e., something with no potency at all.
steps.example: The cup is held by the desk, the desk by the floor, the floor by the foundation; a series whose members only pass on borrowed power must bottom out in something that holds without being held.
steps.challenge: Why not an infinite regress of actualizers, each actualized by the next?
steps.answer: In a hierarchical series every member other than the first has only derivative power, so adding more members never supplies the power; an infinitely long brush handle still cannot move itself (chapter 1, step 11).

steps.text: The things of our experience are composite, and a composite exists at any moment only if its parts are combined at that moment by a cause distinct from it.
steps.why: Chapter 2: the whole depends on the parts being put together; it cannot be the cause of its own composition without vicious circularity. This holds for physical parts and metaphysical ones (form and matter, essence and existence).
steps.example: A chair exists only while its legs, frame, seat and screws exist and are held together — by screws and friction, by molecular bonds, by a room cool enough not to set it alight.
steps.challenge: The chair just is its parts; there is no further fact of their being combined that needs a cause.
steps.answer: The same parts could exist scattered in a pile or assembled as a table, so their being arranged as this chair is a further fact; and the chair cannot cause its own composition without being both cause and effect of it — lifting itself by its bootstraps (chapter 2).

steps.text: So there exists an absolutely simple, noncomposite cause — the One.
steps.why: Chapter 2: the regress of composing causes is hierarchical and must have a first member, and any composite first member would need a cause of its own; so the first member has no parts of any kind.
steps.example: The regress of composers — screws, molecules, atoms — must end in something that has no parts to be put together: the One.
steps.challenge: Why not stop at the simplest physical particles?
steps.answer: Fundamental particles still have distinct attributes and come into and go out of existence, so they involve potency and parts in the relevant sense; laws governing them plus the things governed form yet another composite (chapters 2 and 6).

steps.text: Abstract objects — universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds — are real, are not dependent on the material world or on human (or any contingent) minds, and cannot exist in a Platonic ‘third realm’.
steps.why: Chapter 3: direct arguments for realism, decisive problems for nominalism and conceptualism, the causal inertness and incoherence of Platonic Forms, and the inability of Aristotelian realism alone to ground necessary truths and pure possibilities.
steps.example: The Pythagorean theorem was true before any human existed; unicorns were possible before any mind conceived them; ‘Schnee ist weiss’ and ‘Snow is white’ express one proposition.
steps.challenge: A Platonist can accept all this and say abstract objects exist necessarily in no mind at all.
steps.answer: Third-realm objects would be causally inert — so how could they make things what they are, or be known by us? — and a Form would have to be both universal and an individual, as animality itself would be neither rational nor nonrational (chapter 3, steps 10–11).

steps.text: So abstract objects exist as ideas in a necessarily existing intellect that grasps their entire interlocking system.
steps.why: Chapter 3: the only remaining home for abstractions is an intellect; contingent intellects cannot ground necessary and eternal truths; and because abstract objects are logically interconnected, one intellect must grasp them all (a ‘conceptually omniscient’ being).
steps.example: Grasping humanness requires grasping animality and rationality; ‘all men are mortal’ and ‘Socrates is a man’ entail ‘Socrates is mortal’ — every universal and proposition is tied to every other in a single web.
steps.challenge: Why not several necessary minds, each holding a different region of abstract objects?
steps.answer: Abstract objects form an interlocking system, since every proposition stands in logical relations to every other, so one intellect must grasp them all; and a necessary intellect is purely actual, of which there can be only one (chapter 3, steps 16–21).

steps.text: In each thing we experience, essence is really distinct from existence, so that each such thing must have existence imparted to it by another at every moment it exists.
steps.why: Chapter 4: we can know essences without knowing existence; things are contingent; and something whose essence is existence could only be one. Nothing can impart existence to itself, and the need for existence to be imparted persists as long as the distinction does — here and now.
steps.example: Told only what lions, pterodactyls and unicorns are, you cannot say which exists, which is extinct and which never existed; and Fido would ‘blink out’ unless existence were imparted to him now.
steps.challenge: The distinction is merely conceptual, like knowing aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does.
steps.answer: A complete grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would reveal that it is acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence reveals that lions exist; contingency and plurality give further independent grounds (chapter 4, following Klima).

steps.text: So there exists a cause whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: Chapter 4: a regress of causes that are themselves essence-existence composites is hierarchical and must terminate in something that need not receive existence because it is existence.
steps.example: The regress of causes imparting existence to Fido here and now must end in something that does not receive existence because it just is existence: Aquinas’ subsistent existence itself.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t the first cause simply have existence as one part of its essence, rather than being existence itself?
steps.answer: Feser shows this middle option collapses: if the whole depended on existence as one part of its essence, existence would be the true essence, returning us to a being whose essence is existence (chapter 4).

steps.text: The principle of sufficient reason is true, and neither any contingent thing nor any series of contingent things (even an infinite one) can explain why contingent things exist or why any particular contingent thing persists now.
steps.why: Chapter 5: PSR is inductively confirmed and denying it undermines perception, reasoning and explanation; contingency transfers from parts to collection; appeal to further contingent causes merely relocates the problem.
steps.example: Even an endless series of copies of a geometry book, each copied from the last, leaves unexplained why the series exists and why it contains geometry; and a stone’s persisting this moment is not explained by what formed it long ago.
steps.challenge: PSR is false — reality can simply end in brute facts, such as the universe or its fundamental laws.
steps.answer: Denying PSR undercuts our grounds for trusting perception and reasoning, including the reasoning against PSR; an explanation resting on a brute fact is illusory, like a book on a shelf that floats for no reason; and critics cannot principledly exempt existence from explicability arguments (chapter 5).

steps.text: So there exists an absolutely necessary being, whose existence is explained by its own nature.
steps.why: Chapter 5: explanation is either by another or by one’s own nature; PSR excludes explanation by nothing; so the regress must end in something necessary.
steps.example: Only something whose own nature explains its existence — which depends on nothing outside itself — can end the regress of contingent explanations.
steps.challenge: The necessary being might be the universe itself, or abstract objects like numbers.
steps.answer: The universe changes, has parts and could have been otherwise, so it cannot be necessary; and numbers can exist necessarily only derivatively, as ideas in a necessary mind (chapter 5 and its note on chapter 3).

steps.text: Whatever has parts of any kind is a mixture of actuality and potentiality.
steps.why: Chapter 6 (Unity), drawing on chapter 2: parts only potentially compose a whole until something actually combines them, and this is true even if the whole has always existed.
steps.example: A chair’s legs, seat and screws only potentially make up a chair until something holds them together as one.
steps.challenge: A composite that has always existed never needed its parts combined, so it has no unactualized potency.
steps.answer: The dependence is atemporal: at every moment the whole presupposes that its parts are combined, so even an everlasting composite needs an ontologically (not temporally) prior cause (chapters 2 and 6).

steps.text: Whatever has any potentiality is thereby composite, having an actual ‘part’ and a potential ‘part’.
steps.why: Chapter 2 (stage 2) and chapter 6: a simple being must be at least partly actual in order to exist and cause, and any added potency would be a second constituent.
steps.example: A being that is actually in one state but able to become otherwise has two really distinct constituents: what it actually is and what it merely could be.
steps.challenge: Calling a potentiality a ‘part’ is only a metaphor; a thing with capacities need not have parts.
steps.answer: ‘Part’ here means any really distinct metaphysical constituent, and potency is really distinct from act, as Feser argues in defending the analogy of being (chapter 6); so a being with both is not absolutely simple.

steps.text: So something is purely actual if and only if it is absolutely simple: the conclusions of steps 2 and 4 describe the same kind of being.
steps.why: Follows from 11 and 12. This is why chapter 2 concludes that the One and the Unmoved Mover are in fact identical — one reality approached from composition rather than from change.
steps.example: Chapter 1’s Unmoved Mover and chapter 2’s One turn out to be the same kind of being, reached once from change and once from composition.

steps.text: In anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, essence and existence are related as potency to act.
steps.why: Chapter 4 (stage 2): Fido’s essence by itself is only a potential dog; only when existence is imparted is there an actual dog.
steps.example: Fido’s essence, considered by itself, is only a possible dog; only when existence is imparted to it is there an actual Fido.
steps.challenge: An essence is just a description or definition, not a potency of anything.
steps.answer: Given the real distinction, a thing’s essence is precisely what receives existence and is actualized by it; the distinction is between aspects of the thing itself, not between our descriptions (chapter 4, steps 31–32).

steps.text: So something is purely actual if and only if it is subsistent existence itself: the conclusions of steps 2 and 8 describe the same kind of being — and, given 13, so does step 4.
steps.why: From 14: pure actuality leaves no room for an essence that merely potentially exists; and if subsistent existence depended on any actualization it would have derived existence and not be existence itself. A simple being cannot have an essence-existence composition, and subsistent existence can have no parts of any other kind either.
steps.example: A being that just is existence cannot be waiting for any potential to be actualized, and a purely actual being cannot have an essence that merely potentially exists.
steps.challenge: Something could be existence itself yet have unactualized potentials for activity, such as the potential to create this world or another.
steps.answer: By agere sequitur esse, a being whose existence is purely actual cannot act in a less than purely actual way; and potential activities would give it an actual and a potential part, making it caused and so not first (chapter 6, Unity).

steps.text: To be contingent is to depend for existence on the actualization of some potency, on the combining of parts, or on existence being added to an essence.
steps.why: Chapters 4–6: these are exactly the ways something can fail to exist of itself. Chapter 5 identifies them as the underlying reason why contingent things are contingent.
steps.example: A pile of stones depends on each stone’s atoms not dissipating and on the stones being gathered together — it is contingent on potencies actualized, parts combined and existence received.
steps.challenge: A thing could be contingent merely because it has an external cause, without any of these metaphysical features.
steps.answer: Chapter 4 answers that we still need to know why such a thing needs or could have a cause at all; if existence were part of what it is, nothing else would be needed to cause it and nothing in it could make it cease.

steps.text: So something is absolutely necessary if and only if it is purely actual, simple and subsistent existence itself: the conclusion of step 10 describes the same kind of being as steps 2, 4 and 8.
steps.why: From 16 in both directions: a purely actual, simple, self-existent being has nothing it depends on; a necessary being can have no potency, parts or distinct essence without becoming dependent (chapter 5, stage 2; chapter 6, Unity).
steps.example: A necessary being has nothing it depends on — no potential awaiting actualization, no parts awaiting combination, no existence awaiting bestowal.
steps.challenge: Numbers and logical truths exist necessarily but are neither purely actual nor God, so necessity doesn’t imply pure actuality.
steps.answer: Chapter 3 argues that abstract objects cannot exist apart from a mind; their necessity is derivative, a consequence of the necessity of the infinite mind that entertains them (chapter 5, note).

steps.text: A necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual.
steps.why: Chapter 3 (stage 2): if its existence presupposed the actualization of some potential, it would exist contingently on that actualization — contradicting its necessity.
steps.example: The intellect that grounds all necessary truths cannot owe its existence to anything being actualized in it, or it would exist only contingently on that actualization.
steps.challenge: An intellect might exist necessarily yet still pass from thought to thought, as ours do.
steps.answer: Passing from thought to thought is actualization of potency, which would make the intellect depend on an actualizer; and any truth it failed to know would be an unactualized potential, so it must be purely actual and fully omniscient (chapter 3, steps 19 and 24–25).

steps.text: There cannot in principle be more than one being that is purely actual (equivalently: simple, subsistent existence itself, absolutely necessary).
steps.why: Chapters 1, 2, 4 and 6: two such beings would need a differentiating feature — a specific difference, a parcel of matter, a perfection one lacks — and any such feature is a part or a potency, which such a being cannot have.
steps.example: Two dogs differ by their matter; two species differ by their specific differences. A purely actual being has neither, so there is nothing that could make it two.
steps.challenge: Two purely actual beings might just be numerically distinct, without differing in any feature.
steps.answer: For there to be two, there must be something by virtue of which they are two rather than one; Feser argues that any such differentiator — genus-plus-difference, matter, a perfection lacked — would be a part or a potency, so a ‘bare’ numerical difference makes no sense here (chapters 1, 4 and 6).

steps.text: So the purely actual actualizer, the One, the necessary intellect, subsistent existence itself and the necessary being are one and the same being.
steps.why: From 13, 15, 17, 18 and 19: all five descriptions apply to one kind of being, and there can be only one of that kind. Like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’, the descriptions differ in sense but share a single referent (chapter 2’s Fregean point).
steps.example: ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ turned out to be one planet; ‘purely actual actualizer’, ‘the One’, ‘necessary intellect’, ‘subsistent existence’ and ‘necessary being’ likewise name one reality.
steps.challenge: Showing the five descriptions apply to the same kind of being doesn’t show they apply to the same individual.
steps.answer: Step 19 shows that kind can have only one member, so sameness of kind here guarantees sameness of being.

steps.text: Whatever is in an effect is in its total cause formally, virtually or eminently (the principle of proportionate causality).
steps.why: Chapters 1 and 6: a cause cannot give what it does not in some way have — the $20 in my wallet, in my account, or in my power to print it. Defended against Cottingham’s counterexamples in chapter 6.
steps.example: I can give you $20 because I have a bill in my wallet (formally), money in my account (virtually), or the power to have bills printed (eminently).
steps.challenge: Effects often have what their causes lack — a sponge cake has a sponginess found in none of its ingredients (Cottingham).
steps.answer: The PPC concerns the total cause, including the mixing and baking, not just the ingredients, and it allows virtual and eminent containment rather than an ‘heirloom’ handing-down of features (chapter 6).

steps.text: So this one being contains the forms of all possible things in the way an intellect does, and knows all things: it has intellect and omniscience.
steps.why: From 20 and 21 (chapter 1, stage 2; chapter 6, Omniscience): as the cause of every possible thing, it must contain their forms, but not concretely (it is immaterial), so abstractly, as in a mind. Step 6 reaches the same result directly, and knowledge of contingent truths follows from pure actuality (chapter 3).
steps.example: The forms of cats and trees pre-exist in their first cause somewhat as a house pre-exists as a plan in an architect’s mind — not concretely, since the cause is immaterial, but as ideas.
steps.challenge: Unintelligent causes can produce intricate effects, as natural processes produce complex life, so the first cause needn’t be an intellect.
steps.answer: The first cause causes every possible thing, so the forms of all possible things must be in it somehow; being immaterial, it cannot have them concretely, and the only other way to have forms is abstractly, as an intellect does. Evolution respects the PPC, since genes, mutation and environment jointly contain what emerges (chapters 1 and 6).

steps.text: Being purely actual and simple, this one being is also immutable, eternal (timeless), immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, fully good, omnipotent, uncaused and the cause of everything other than itself.
steps.why: Stage 2 of every chapter: no potency means no change, hence no time and no matter; perfection and goodness are actuality, badness is privation; all power to actualize derives from it; being unique, everything else is composite and depends on it.
steps.example: What cannot change is not in time; what is outside time is not material; what lacks no actuality is perfect and good; what is the source of all actualizing is all-powerful.
steps.challenge: Pure actuality sounds static and inert, not living, good or powerful.
steps.answer: Pure actuality is fullness of act, not inactivity; to infer that anything which acts or lives must change is a fallacy of accident, since what is essential to acting is producing an effect and to life is acting from within (chapter 6, Immutability).

steps.text: Nothing other than this being could exist for an instant, or act at all, unless it were conserving that thing in being and concurring with its activity.
steps.why: Chapter 6 (Conservation and concurrence): the causal proofs concern dependence here and now; and by agere sequitur esse, what cannot exist independently cannot act independently. This rules out existential inertia, pantheism, panentheism, occasionalism and deism.
steps.example: The moon gives light only by reflecting the sun; the blue chalk makes the square blue only as your hand presses it — so creatures really act, but only as God concurs.
steps.challenge: Once created, things could keep existing and acting on their own, as the deist or mere conservationist says.
steps.answer: Nothing composite or contingent could exist for an instant without a sustaining cause, and by agere sequitur esse what cannot exist independently cannot act independently; both views undercut the very dependence that led to God (chapter 6).

steps.text: For there to exist a single, simple, purely actual, necessary, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good cause of all other things, which conserves them in being, is just what it is for God to exist.
steps.why: The final premise of each chapter’s formal statement: this is what classical theism — pagan, Jewish, Muslim and Christian — has meant by ‘God’. It is not a stipulation smuggled in; it is the traditional concept.
steps.example: The being described is the God affirmed by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna and Aquinas — the God of classical theism.
steps.challenge: This is the abstract God of the philosophers, not the God ordinary believers worship — so calling it ‘God’ is a stipulation.
steps.answer: Chapter 7 replies that even if true this would be irrelevant — atheism would still be false — and that it is not true: many religions identify the God of reason with the God of revelation, and ordinary believers hold the same God less sophisticatedly, as laymen believe in atoms.

steps.text: So God exists.
steps.why: From 20, 22–25. And he exists as one God, not five: the proofs are distinct paths to one and the same reality.
steps.example: Five trails from five valleys — change, composition, abstract truth, essence and existence, explanation — end on one summit.
steps.challenge: Even granting this, it doesn’t show that any particular religion is true.
steps.answer: True and irrelevant, Feser says: the proofs aim to establish one central tenet shared by many religions; which kind of theism is true is a further question, where miracles would be the bridge (chapters 6 and 7).

steps.text: So the case is robust: to escape it, a critic must refute each of the five demonstrations independently, and the convergence explains why their conclusions interlock rather than being a coincidence.
steps.why: Since steps 1–10 are independent routes and steps 11–20 show why they coincide, defeating one proof leaves four; and the interlocking conclusions show that the divine attributes are facets of one idea (pure actuality, subsistent being) rather than an arbitrary list. This last step is the course’s framing of the book’s cumulative force.
steps.example: A critic who finds a flaw in the Augustinian proof still faces the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic and rationalist demonstrations — and an explanation of why all of them agree.
steps.challenge: Five flawed arguments don’t add up to one good one; this is just piling on.
steps.answer: The case is not probabilistic: each proof is offered as a demonstration that must be refuted on its own terms, and the convergence is itself deduced (steps 11–20), so the agreement is explained rather than hoped for (chapter 7 on demonstration).

comparison.startingPoint: Change is real — potentials are actualized (the coffee cools); and the things that change exist here and now only by the concurrent actualization of their potential to exist.
comparison.keyPrinciple: The principle of causality — no potential actualizes itself; plus the thesis that a hierarchical series of actualizers must have an underived first member.
comparison.conclusion: A purely actual actualizer (Unmoved, indeed unmovable, Mover), which Stage 2 shows is one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, omnipotent, intelligent and omniscient.
comparison.keyDistinction: Actuality vs. potentiality; linear (per accidens) vs. hierarchical (per se) causal series.
comparison.bestFor: Science-minded listeners; people who assume the argument is about the Big Bang; anyone who likes concrete, everyday examples and step-by-step causal reasoning.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ — or ‘physics (inertia, quantum mechanics, relativity) shows change can occur without a cause.’
comparison.quickReply: The principle concerns what goes from potential to actual, not ‘everything’; what is purely actual has nothing to be actualized. And physics abstracts from causation by method — absence from the equations is not absence from reality; its own evidence rests on changing experiences.

comparison.startingPoint: The things of our experience are composite — made of parts (legs and screws, organs and cells, form and matter, essence and existence) that must be combined at every moment for the whole to exist.
comparison.keyPrinciple: Whatever is composite requires a concurrent cause of the combination of its parts; nothing can compose itself, and the regress of composers is hierarchical.
comparison.conclusion: An absolutely simple, noncomposite first cause — the One — which is unique, immutable, eternal, a mind, purely actual, and identical with the Unmoved Mover.
comparison.keyDistinction: Composite vs. absolutely simple; temporal vs. atemporal (moment-to-moment) dependence of a whole on its parts.
comparison.bestFor: Engineers, builders and systems thinkers who find ‘what holds this together right now?’ natural; also ideal for teaching divine simplicity to believers.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘Maybe a thing’s parts are unified by one of its parts, or the unity is just a brute fact, or laws of nature explain it.’
comparison.quickReply: A unifying part is one more item needing to be unified (regress); a brute fact is not an alternative explanation but no explanation — and one has been offered; laws plus the things they govern form yet another composite.

comparison.startingPoint: Universals, propositions, numbers and possible worlds are real and are not dependent on the material world or on human minds (2 + 2 = 4 would be true if no humans existed).
comparison.keyPrinciple: Abstract objects can exist only in things or in intellects (there is no Platonic third realm); necessary, eternal, interlocking truths require a necessary, eternal intellect that grasps them all.
comparison.conclusion: A necessarily existing, conceptually omniscient divine intellect — which, being purely actual, is unique, fully omniscient, omnipotent, good, immutable, immaterial and eternal.
comparison.keyDistinction: Realism vs. nominalism and conceptualism; Platonic vs. Aristotelian vs. Scholastic realism.
comparison.bestFor: Mathematicians, logicians, programmers and Platonist-leaning skeptics who already believe in objective, necessary truths.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘Why not simple Platonism — abstract objects existing necessarily in no mind at all?’
comparison.quickReply: Third-realm objects would be causally inert, so they could neither explain why things instantiate them nor be known by us; and a Form would have to be both universal and a particular (animality itself neither rational nor nonrational). Only an intellect can house what is abstract — and only a necessary one can ground necessary truths.

comparison.startingPoint: In each thing we experience, essence (what it is) is really distinct from existence (that it is) — we can know what a lion or unicorn is without knowing whether it exists.
comparison.keyPrinciple: Nothing whose essence is distinct from its existence can give itself existence; it must receive existence from another at every moment, and the regress of such causes is hierarchical.
comparison.conclusion: A cause whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself — which is unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual, the cause of all else, and has all the divine attributes.
comparison.keyDistinction: Essence vs. existence; real vs. merely conceptual distinction (real need not mean separable).
comparison.bestFor: The metaphysically curious, philosophy students, and anyone who asks why anything exists rather than not; people comfortable with abstract reasoning.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘The distinction is merely conceptual (like aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid), or existence is just the logical quantifier’ (Kenny).
comparison.quickReply: A complete grasp of aspirin reveals it is acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence reveals its existence; contingency and plurality confirm the real distinction. Kenny assumes real distinction means separability and that quantifier-existence captures everything — both beg the question.

comparison.startingPoint: The principle of sufficient reason: everything has an explanation, either in its own nature or in something else.
comparison.keyPrinciple: Neither a contingent thing nor any series of contingent things (even infinite) can explain why contingent things exist or why any one persists now; only something necessary can end the regress.
comparison.conclusion: An absolutely necessary being, explained by its own nature, which must be purely actual, simple and subsistent existence itself — hence the same God reached by the other proofs.
comparison.keyDistinction: Contingent vs. necessary; cause vs. sufficient reason (self-explanatory is not self-caused).
comparison.bestFor: Lovers of explanation and science, people who ask ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’, and debate settings where the Leibniz–Clarke argument is already familiar.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘PSR is false: the universe or the fundamental laws may simply be brute facts.’
comparison.quickReply: Denying PSR undercuts trust in perception and in our own reasoning, including the reasoning against PSR; brute-fact foundations make every explanation built on them illusory (a book on a shelf that floats for no reason); and there is no principled line for where explanation may stop (Della Rocca).

keyTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that investigates what unaided reason, apart from revelation, can know about God’s existence, nature and relation to the world.
keyTerms.example: The five proofs and chapter 6’s derivation of the divine attributes are natural theology; the doctrine of the Trinity is not.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *theologia*, ‘an account of God’; the phrase *theologia naturalis* comes down from the Roman scholar Varro via Augustine’s *City of God*, meaning theology grounded in nature and reason.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Revealed theology — which reasons from what God is believed to have revealed (scripture, creeds), whereas natural theology uses only premises available to unaided reason.

keyTerms.definition: The mainstream conception of God in Western philosophy and religion — God as absolutely simple, immutable, eternal, purely actual, subsistent being itself — defended by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas and others.
keyTerms.example: Contrasted with ‘theistic personalism’, which treats God as a very great person within a genus of persons.
keyTerms.origin: A modern label for the mainstream tradition of Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Anselm, Maimonides, Avicenna, Averroes and Aquinas; ‘classical’ because it was the historic default.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism — which also calls God personal but treats him as a member of the genus ‘person’ and so denies or weakens divine simplicity.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality is the way a thing really is; potentiality is a real but unrealized capacity to be otherwise. Change is the actualization of a potential.
keyTerms.example: Hot coffee is actually hot and potentially cold — but not potentially chicken soup.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *energeia* / *entelecheia* (actuality) and *dynamis* (potency); Latin *actus* and *potentia*. Introduced to answer Parmenides.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical possibility — a potency is a real capacity rooted in something actual (this coffee can cool), not merely whatever is non-contradictory.

keyTerms.definition: Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. It concerns what goes from potential to actual, not ‘everything’.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s potential coldness cannot make itself actual; the cool air or an ice cube does.
keyTerms.origin: The Scholastic formulation of Aristotle’s analysis of motion; Feser abbreviates it ‘PC’ in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Everything has a cause’ — PC covers only what goes from potential to actual, which is why it makes no arbitrary exception for a purely actual God.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which every member other than the first has its causal power only derivatively, from the one before it; it must have a first member with underived power.
keyTerms.example: Cup held up by desk, desk by floor, floor by foundation; a stone pushed by a stick pushed by a hand.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *per se*, ‘through itself’ or ‘essentially’: the members are essentially ordered to one another. The per se / per accidens distinction is Scholastic (Aquinas, Scotus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A merely simultaneous series — simultaneity is a helpful illustration, but what defines the series is that later members’ power is derivative or instrumental.

keyTerms.definition: A series ordered through time in which each member has its own causal power once it exists; Feser grants such a series could, in principle, have no beginning.
keyTerms.example: Grandfather begets father, who begets son — the son is begotten even if the grandfather is long dead.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *per accidens*, ‘incidentally’: each member’s causal power is only accidentally related to the earlier members.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Any infinite series is impossible’ — Feser allows that linear series might regress infinitely; only hierarchical series cannot.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that is first because its causal power is underived, not because it comes earliest in time.
keyTerms.example: Even an infinitely long paintbrush handle needs a painter; the painter is ‘first’ however long the handle.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *causa prima*; ‘first’ in the sense of primary or underived, as in the Scholastic contrast between primary and secondary causes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The kalām argument’s ‘first moment’ — a temporally first event. Feser’s first cause could exist even if there were no first moment.

keyTerms.definition: A cause with no potentiality whatsoever, which can actualize other things without being actualized itself.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of chapter 1’s argument from the existence of the coffee here and now.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s ‘unmoved mover’ (*Physics* VIII, *Metaphysics* XII); Aquinas’ *actus purus*, ‘pure act’. Feser also calls it an ‘unactualized actualizer’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A merely unmoved mover — one that happens not to be moved while acting but has unrealized potentials; Feser argues the first actualizer must be unmovable.

keyTerms.definition: To be composite is to have parts (physical or metaphysical) that must be combined; the One is the absolutely simple, noncomposite first cause of all composites.
keyTerms.example: A chair needs its legs, screws and seat held together; the One has no parts to hold together.
keyTerms.origin: Plotinus’ *to hen*, ‘the One’, in the *Enneads*; the notion of a noncomposite first principle is central to Neo-Platonism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Complexity in the design-argument sense (many parts functioning together). For the Neo-Platonic proof even a pebble or a drop of water is composite.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God has no parts of any kind — no matter and form, no genus and difference, no essence distinct from existence, no distinct attributes; his power, intellect and goodness are one reality under different descriptions. God is accordingly called ‘simple’ or ‘noncomposite’.
keyTerms.example: ‘God’s power’ and ‘God’s intellect’ differ in sense but have one referent, like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *simplicitas*, literally ‘without folds’. Affirmed by Augustine, Anselm and Aquinas, and taught by the Fourth Lateran Council and the First Vatican Council.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Simple’ as ‘easy to understand’ — Feser notes God is hard to understand precisely because he is simple (partless).

keyTerms.definition: Universals, propositions, numbers and possible worlds — objects of thought that are not material and cannot be perceived by the senses.
keyTerms.example: The proposition that snow is white, expressed by both ‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *abstrahere*, ‘to draw away’: the intellect draws a common feature away from the individualizing conditions of particular things.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imaginary or fictional objects — numbers and propositions are real and objective, discovered rather than made up.

keyTerms.definition: Platonic: abstract objects exist in a mind-independent ‘third realm’. Aristotelian: universals exist in things, and as abstract only in minds. Scholastic: Aristotelian realism plus the thesis that abstract objects exist in an infinite divine intellect.
keyTerms.example: The Augustinian proof eliminates the first two and concludes to the third.
keyTerms.origin: Named after Plato (Forms in a separate realm), Aristotle (universals in things), and the medieval Scholastics, who added Augustine’s thesis that the divine intellect contains the exemplars of all things.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Realism in the everyday sense that the external world exists — here the dispute concerns the status of universals and other abstract objects.

keyTerms.definition: A thing’s essence is what it is; its existence is the fact that it is. In everything except God these are really distinct.
keyTerms.example: You can know what a unicorn is without knowing whether any exist.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *essentia* (from *esse*, ‘to be’) and *esse* / *existentia*. The distinction is the centerpiece of Aquinas’ early work *De Ente et Essentia* (On Being and Essence).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence vs. accident — accidents are features a thing can gain or lose while remaining what it is; existence is neither part of the essence nor an accident added to an already existing thing.

keyTerms.definition: A real distinction reflects a difference in things themselves; a conceptual one only a difference in how we think or speak. A real distinction need not involve separability.
keyTerms.example: ‘Bachelor’/‘unmarried man’ is merely conceptual; a circle’s radius and circumference are really distinct though inseparable.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *distinctio realis* vs. *distinctio rationis* (a ‘distinction of reason’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Separability — a real distinction need not mean the two items could exist apart (radius and circumference).

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ description of a being whose essence just is existence, which therefore need not and could not receive existence from anything.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of chapter 4’s regress of causes imparting existence to Fido here and now.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas’ *ipsum esse subsistens*, ‘subsisting being itself’ or ‘the very act of being, subsisting’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The sum of all existing things, or ‘existence in general’ as an abstract concept — it is the unique concrete being whose essence is to be.

keyTerms.definition: A contingent thing depends on something outside itself and could fail to exist; a necessary being (in the strictest sense) exists by its own nature and depends on nothing. ‘Contingency’ and ‘necessity’ name the corresponding conditions.
keyTerms.example: Stones, trees, universes and multiverses are contingent; only what is purely actual, simple and subsistent existence is necessary in the strict sense.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *contingere*, ‘to happen’ or ‘to befall’, and *necessarius*, ‘unavoidable’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical necessity (true by definition) — God’s necessity is metaphysical, grounded in pure actuality; also Aquinas’ broader sense in which angels are ‘necessary’ because naturally incorruptible.

keyTerms.definition: Everything is intelligible: whatever exists has an explanation of its existence and attributes, either in itself or in something else. Something that has its explanation in its own nature is ‘self-explanatory’.
keyTerms.example: Even an unsolved murder has an explanation, including of why it remains unsolved.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Leibniz (*principium rationis sufficientis*); Thomists such as Garrigou-Lagrange state it as ‘everything is intelligible’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality — PSR demands an explanation, which may lie in a thing’s own nature; PC demands a cause distinct from its effect.

keyTerms.definition: A supposed fact with no explanation at all, neither in itself nor in anything else. PSR denies there are any.
keyTerms.example: Mackie and Russell suggested the most fundamental laws of nature are brute facts; Feser argues that would make all explanations resting on them illusory.
keyTerms.origin: A modern analytic term; Russell (in his debate with Copleston) and J. L. Mackie held that the universe or its most basic laws might simply be brute.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unknown explanation — a brute fact has no explanation at all, not merely one we have not found.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually or eminently.
keyTerms.example: The $20 you receive was in my wallet (formally), my bank account (virtually), or my power to print money (eminently).
keyTerms.origin: A Scholastic principle (a cause cannot give what it does not have); Descartes’ variant is often called the ‘causal adequacy principle’, the version John Cottingham criticizes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ‘heirloom’ view that causes hand on their own features — the PPC allows virtual and eminent, not only formal, containment.

keyTerms.definition: ‘Action follows being’: what a thing does reflects and cannot exceed what it is.
keyTerms.example: Stones don’t grow or reproduce because they are not living things; a thing that could not act independently of God could not exist independently of him.
keyTerms.origin: Latin Scholastic maxim, ‘acting follows being’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The PPC — the PPC concerns efficient causes and what they produce; agere sequitur esse concerns a thing’s nature (formal cause) and its own activities.

keyTerms.definition: Using a term in senses that are neither identical (univocal) nor unrelated (equivocal) but related; it remains literal. Two kinds: analogy of attribution and analogy of proper proportionality.
keyTerms.example: ‘Good wine’ and ‘good man’; ‘seeing a tree’ and ‘seeing that a theorem is true’.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *analogia*, ‘proportion’; systematized by Aquinas and later by Cajetan.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphor — ‘George is a lion’ is improper (metaphorical) proportionality; the analogy used of God is proper proportionality or attribution, which are literal.

keyTerms.definition: A ‘change’ in something that consists only in a change in something else related to it, not a real change in the thing itself.
keyTerms.example: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows; God becomes Creator when the world comes to be, with no real change in God.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Peter Geach after Cambridge philosophers (Russell, McTaggart) whose criterion of change counted such cases; Barry Miller applies it to God.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Real change — in which the thing itself gains or loses a feature by actualizing a potential.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that a feature that merely happens to accompany something in our experience belongs to it essentially.
keyTerms.example: ‘Every actualizer we know changes as it acts, so any possible actualizer must change’ — like concluding every possible president must be under seven feet tall.
keyTerms.origin: One of the fallacies in Aristotle’s *Sophistical Refutations*; Latin *fallacia accidentis*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hasty generalization — the fallacy of accident specifically treats a contingent (accidental) correlation as if it were essential.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of a feature a thing should have given its nature; on the classical view, all badness is privation.
keyTerms.example: Blindness is the lack of sight in an eye; a tree’s weak roots are a privation, its lack of wings is not.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *privatio*, ‘deprivation’ (Greek *sterēsis*); the classical account of evil runs from Plato and Plotinus through Augustine to Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere absence or negation — a stone’s lack of sight is a negation, not a privation; blindness in an animal is a privation because sight is due to it.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that nothing could continue to exist for an instant unless God were sustaining it in being; creation is ongoing, not a past event. God is said to ‘conserve’ or ‘sustain’ things in being.
keyTerms.example: Answers the ‘existential inertia’ view that things tend to stay in existence on their own.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *conservare*, ‘to preserve’; the Scholastic doctrine that creation is continuous, not a one-time event.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deism’s one-time creation — on conservation, God’s creative causality is at work at every moment.

keyTerms.definition: The view that creatures are real (secondary) causes but can act only with God’s cooperation at every moment — the middle ground between occasionalism and mere conservationism.
keyTerms.example: You and the blue chalk jointly produce a blue square: the chalk makes it blue, you make there be a square.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *concurrere*, ‘to run together’; developed by Aquinas and later Scholastics; Feser draws on Alfred Freddoso’s modern treatment.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Occasionalism — which denies that creatures are real causes at all; concurrence affirms real but secondary creaturely causality.

keyTerms.definition: Recent views that treat God as the unique member of a genus of persons, differing from us only in lacking our limitations, and so deny or weaken divine simplicity.
