keyTerms.example: Plantinga’s and Swinburne’s views, as classified by Brian Davies; Feser argues such a ‘god’ would be a superangel needing a cause.
keyTerms.origin: ‘Theistic personalism’ is Brian Davies’ label; ‘neo-theism’ is Norman Geisler’s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Affirming that God is personal — classical theists also attribute intellect and will; what distinguishes theistic personalism is treating God as a member of a genus and rejecting simplicity.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge, so that any worthwhile philosophy must be implicit in science.
keyTerms.example: Alex Rosenberg’s argument from the predictive success of physics; Feser compares it to inferring that only metal exists from the success of metal detectors.
keyTerms.origin: Originally a pejorative label; Alex Rosenberg embraces the term for his own view.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science itself — Feser’s objection is to the philosophical thesis that science is the only knowledge, not to science.

keyTerms.definition: A deduction whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are certain and cannot be overturned by further empirical inquiry, as opposed to a probabilistic or best-explanation argument.
keyTerms.example: ‘Change occurs’ is known through experience, but no future experience could overturn it, since that experience would itself be a change.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *apodeixis* (*Posterior Analytics*); Latin *demonstratio*, as when Aquinas says God’s existence can be demonstrated.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A proof that compels immediate universal assent, or a purely a priori proof — these demonstrations can start from experience and can be controversial.

keyTerms.definition: An event with a supernatural cause that either elevates a nature beyond its own powers or suspends its operation by God’s refraining from conserving or concurring — not a ‘violation’ of natural law.
keyTerms.example: A resurrection adds to nature’s course; the three young men unburnt in the furnace involve a subtraction.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *miraculum*, ‘object of wonder’ (from *mirari*, to wonder).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hume’s ‘violation of a law of nature’, or a merely preternatural marvel an angel might produce — a miracle strictly has God alone as its cause.

keyTerms.definition: Parmenides argued that change is impossible because it would require something to come from nothing; Heraclitus (on the traditional reading) held that only change is real and nothing is stable. Both deny one side of the act/potency distinction.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s coldness is ‘nothing’ while it is hot, so (says Parmenides) it can never come to be; Aristotle replies that it was there potentially.
keyTerms.origin: Pre-Socratic Greek philosophers of the 5th century BC; Aristotle’s act/potency theory is his response.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Skepticism about the senses (Descartes’ dream hypothesis) — Parmenides denies change even as experienced, which Feser shows is self-refuting.

keyTerms.definition: Qualitative (a change in a quality), local (change of place), quantitative (change of size or amount) and substantial (one kind of thing becoming another).
keyTerms.example: Coffee cooling; a leaf falling; a puddle growing; a swatted fly dying — Feser’s opening examples in chapter 1.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s classification in the *Physics* and *Categories*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Cambridge change — which is not a real change in the thing at all.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that acts only by power it derives from another cause acting through it; the intermediate members of a hierarchical series are instrumental.
keyTerms.example: The brush in the painter’s hand; the stick pushing a stone; the desk holding up the cup only because the floor holds it.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *causa instrumentalis*; the painter-and-brush image goes back to Aristotle and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An inert or unreal cause — instrumental causes really act (the chalk colors the square), but not independently.

keyTerms.definition: The Aristotelian view that physical substances are composites of form (what makes a thing the kind of thing it is) and matter (which ties form to a particular). Prime matter by itself is pure potentiality.
keyTerms.example: Copper conducts electricity because of its form; this lump and that lump are two because of their matter.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *hylē* (matter) + *morphē* (form); Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mind-body (Cartesian) dualism — form and matter are not two things but two principles of one substance.

keyTerms.definition: A genus is a broader kind; the specific difference is what distinguishes one species within it. Things that fall under a genus are composite, which is why God cannot belong to one.
keyTerms.example: Human being = animal (genus) + rational (specific difference).
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle and Porphyry’s logic; ‘species’ and ‘genus’ in the traditional logical rather than biological sense.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Biological genus and species — Feser uses the terms in their older, broader logical sense.

keyTerms.definition: The view that there are no universals (or other abstract objects), only general words applied to many particular things.
keyTerms.example: The nominalist says there is no redness, only the word ‘red’ applied to stop signs and fire engines — inviting Russell’s resemblance regress.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *nomen*, ‘name’; associated with medieval thinkers such as Ockham and with modern empiricism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceptualism — which admits universals exist but only as human mental constructions.

keyTerms.definition: Conceptualism holds that universals exist but are wholly constructed by the human mind; psychologism reduces the laws of logic and mathematics to facts about human psychology.
keyTerms.example: The claim that logic is just how evolution happened to wire our brains — which Feser argues undermines itself, since defending it requires logic.
keyTerms.origin: Psychologism was Frege’s target in defending the objectivity of logic; Kant’s view is a less radical relative.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelian realism — which also says abstract universals exist in minds, but insists they are abstracted from real features of things, not invented.

keyTerms.definition: What a declarative sentence expresses — the content that is true or false — as opposed to the words used to express it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’ are two sentences expressing one proposition; erasing every such sentence would not make the proposition false.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *propositio*, ‘something put forward’; the sentence/proposition contrast is central to Frege.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Sentence — a sentence is a linguistic, conventional item; a proposition is not.

keyTerms.definition: A complete way things could have been, constrained by logic rather than by the actual laws of physics.
keyTerms.example: A world in which Mars has three moons, or in which unicorns exist; but no world in which 2 + 2 = 5.
keyTerms.origin: An idea going back to Leibniz; central to 20th-century modal logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A physically real parallel universe (as in multiverse cosmology) — possible worlds are ways things could be, not places you could visit.

keyTerms.definition: An objection to Platonic Forms: if individual men are men by participating in the Form of Man, and the Form is itself an individual, a further Form seems needed to explain it, and so on without end.
keyTerms.example: Form of Man → Super-Form of Man → Super-Super-Form… — a regress Plato himself raised in the *Parmenides*.
keyTerms.origin: Plato’s dialogue *Parmenides*; later named by Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s ‘more telling’ objection that animality itself would have to be neither rational nor nonrational — a separate argument against Forms as individuals.

keyTerms.definition: A being that eternally understands all essences, possibilities and necessary truths; the Augustinian proof’s Stage 1 intellect, before Stage 2 shows it also knows all contingent truths.
keyTerms.example: The necessary intellect that grasps the whole interlocking system of universals and propositions, including infinitely many mathematical truths.
keyTerms.origin: Robert Merrihew Adams’ phrase, in his book on Leibniz.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Full omniscience — knowing contingent truths too, which Feser derives from pure actuality (no unactualized potential to know).

keyTerms.definition: Greg Welty’s view — essentially Scholastic realism — that abstract objects are divine ideas, defended as best meeting six conditions: objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude and simplicity.
keyTerms.example: Only an omnipotent mind’s idea of Socrates-as-carpenter could make it true that Socrates could have been a carpenter (relevance).
keyTerms.origin: Greg Welty, in the anthology *Beyond the Control of God?* (2014).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceptualism in Feser’s sense — Welty uses ‘conceptualism’ more broadly, but the disagreement is only terminological.

keyTerms.definition: Brian Leftow’s label for views on which what is possible and necessary is grounded in God’s nature; Scholastic realism is one.
keyTerms.example: Leftow worries that if God’s nature grounds ‘water = H₂O’ being necessary, God depends on water; Feser compares arithmetic ‘depending’ on rocks.
keyTerms.origin: Brian Leftow, *God and Necessity* (2012).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Voluntarism — Leftow’s own view that some necessities depend on God’s will; deity theorists ground them in God’s nature.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that a state of affairs does not obtain because it would be inexplicable, a ‘brute fact’. Michael Della Rocca argues that accepting such arguments anywhere commits one to PSR.
keyTerms.example: Materialists argue consciousness must be physical because otherwise it would be inexplicable — an EA.
keyTerms.origin: Michael Della Rocca, ‘PSR’ (2010).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inference to the best explanation — an EA rules out an option for being inexplicable, not for being less likely.

keyTerms.definition: The conjunction of all true contingent propositions, used in an objection claiming PSR cannot be satisfied: neither a necessary nor a contingent proposition could explain it.
keyTerms.example: Raised in various forms by James Ross, Peter van Inwagen and William Rowe; Feser answers that propositions are not extra objects needing explanation and explanation need not be entailment.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary philosophy of religion; the ‘BCCF’ label is common in the literature rather than Feser’s own.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Leibnizian question of why the series of contingent things exists — which concerns concrete things, not a conjunction of propositions.

keyTerms.definition: The thesis that things, once they exist, tend to remain in existence on their own unless something destroys them, so that no sustaining cause is needed.
keyTerms.example: Defended in different ways by John Beaudoin, Mortimer Adler and Bede Rundle; Feser replies that no composite, contingent thing could have such a feature.
keyTerms.origin: Named by analogy with Newton’s law of inertia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical inertia — which concerns a body’s motion, presupposing its existence; existential inertia concerns existence itself.

keyTerms.definition: Anthony Kenny’s two notions: ‘specific existence’, expressed by the logical quantifier (there is an x such that…); and ‘individual existence’, what an individual has while it lasts.
keyTerms.example: ‘There are cats’ (specific) vs. ‘The Great Pyramid still exists but the Library of Alexandria does not’ (individual).
keyTerms.origin: Anthony Kenny, *Aquinas on Being* (2002); specific existence corresponds to Frege’s view of existence.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Thomist’s existence as act (*esse*) — what makes it the case that something falls under a concept, which Feser argues neither of Kenny’s notions captures.

keyTerms.definition: Essentialism holds that at least natural substances have real, mind-independent essences; conventionalism holds that all essences are products of our concepts or language.
keyTerms.example: Chemistry’s discrete elements (Brian Ellis) and physics’ search for natures under controlled conditions (Nancy Cartwright) support essentialism; Crawford Elder argues conventionalism about the mind’s own essence is incoherent.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle thought it absurd even to try to prove that things have natures; ‘new essentialism’ is a recent movement in philosophy of science.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ‘essentialism’ criticized by Étienne Gilson — the rationalist attempt to read reality off abstract essences, which Feser’s essentialism does not involve.

keyTerms.definition: Hume’s thesis that all objects of inquiry are either ‘relations of ideas’ (conceptual truths) or ‘matters of fact’ (empirical truths).
keyTerms.example: The scientistic claim that philosophy is either natural science or mere conceptual analysis is a version of the fork — and, like it, is itself neither.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, *An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The analytic/synthetic distinction as such — Feser’s complaint is that the fork claims these two exhaust all knowledge, which is self-refuting.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that a whole has a property merely because its parts have it, when the property does not transfer.
keyTerms.example: Each brick weighs a pound, so the wall weighs a pound — fallacious; each Lego block is red, so the wall is red — valid.
keyTerms.origin: A traditional informal fallacy (Aristotle discusses composition and division).
keyTerms.confuseWith: All part-to-whole reasoning — whether an inference is fallacious depends on the property; contingency transfers like color.

keyTerms.definition: The view that only God is a genuine cause; creatures do nothing, and God produces effects on the ‘occasion’ of creaturely events.
keyTerms.example: On occasionalism the sun does not melt the ice; God melts it when the sun is out.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with some medieval Islamic theologians and with the Cartesian Nicolas Malebranche.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Concurrence — which agrees nothing acts without God but insists creatures are real secondary causes.

keyTerms.definition: Mere conservationism: God keeps creatures in existence but they act independently of him. Deism: God created the world but does not sustain or act in it.
keyTerms.example: On mere conservationism God keeps the cue ball in existence, but the cue ball moves the eight ball on its own.
keyTerms.origin: ‘Deism’ from Latin *deus*; a movement of the 17th–18th centuries.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Concurrence — which denies that anything created can act without God’s cooperation at every moment.

keyTerms.definition: Pantheism identifies God with the world; panentheism holds the world is in God, or God in the world, in such a way that God is affected or changed by it.
keyTerms.example: Some Hindu thinkers accept pantheism — which is why Feser says a ‘necessary universe’ would yield pantheism, not atheism; process theology is panentheist.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *pan* (all) + *theos* (God); *en* (in).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine conservation and omnipresence — God is intimately present to all things as their sustaining cause while remaining distinct and unchanged.

keyTerms.definition: A cosmological argument that tries to show the universe began to exist and therefore has a cause; the only major version concerned with a beginning.
keyTerms.example: Defended today by William Lane Craig; Feser mentions it only to note that his own proofs do not depend on a beginning.
keyTerms.origin: Arabic *kalām*, ‘speech’ or ‘discussion’, the name for medieval Islamic dialectical theology (e.g., al-Ghazali).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s causal proofs, which grant a beginningless universe and argue from present, hierarchical dependence.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that God exists from the concept of God alone — for Descartes, that a supremely perfect being must have existence, since existence is a perfection.
keyTerms.example: Kant and Grayling claim cosmological arguments secretly presuppose it; Feser notes Aquinas rejected it while accepting cosmological arguments.
keyTerms.origin: Anselm of Canterbury’s *Proslogion* (11th century); named by Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The metaphysical necessity of God in the five proofs — grounded in pure actuality, not in ‘existence by definition’.

keyTerms.definition: Univocal: a term used in exactly the same sense in two applications. Equivocal: a term used in completely unrelated senses.
keyTerms.example: ‘Fido is a dog’, ‘Rover is a dog’ (univocal); a baseball bat and a bat in the attic (equivocal).
keyTerms.origin: Latin *univocus* (‘one-voiced’) and *aequivocus* (‘equally voiced’, i.e., same word, different things).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication — the literal middle ground, which is how terms apply to God and creatures.

keyTerms.definition: Frege’s distinction between the way an expression presents its object (sense) and the object itself (reference).
keyTerms.example: ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ differ in sense but both refer to Venus — as God’s ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ refer to one simple reality.
keyTerms.origin: Gottlob Frege, ‘On Sense and Reference’ (1892); German *Sinn* and *Bedeutung*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A real distinction in the thing — distinct senses do not imply distinct parts in what is referred to.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of God by saying what he is not: not composite, not changing, not material, not in time or space.
keyTerms.example: ‘Immutable’, ‘immaterial’ and ‘incorporeal’ all tell us what God is not — real knowledge, but not the whole story.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *apophasis*, ‘denial’; prominent in Pseudo-Dionysius and Maimonides.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Agnosticism about God’s nature — Feser holds negative theology must be supplemented by analogical positive knowledge, or even the proofs’ claims could not be stated.

keyTerms.definition: Barry Miller’s notion of something that differs absolutely, not merely in degree, from a series that nonetheless points toward it.
keyTerms.example: A speed of zero is not the slowest speed but no speed at all, yet the ordering of speeds points to it; God’s will and goodness are limit cases of creaturely appetite and goodness.
keyTerms.origin: Barry Miller, *A Most Unlikely God* (1996).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A limit simpliciter (like the speed of light), which differs only in degree from what it limits.

keyTerms.definition: A defense shows that God and evil are logically compatible; a theodicy tries to explain why God actually permits the evils there are.
keyTerms.example: Pointing out that courage requires danger is part of a defense; claiming to know why a particular child suffered would be theodicy.
keyTerms.origin: ‘Theodicy’ was coined by Leibniz from Greek *theos* (God) + *dikē* (justice); older Thomist works used it for natural theology generally.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Pastoral comfort — neither a defense nor a theodicy is meant to console a sufferer.

keyTerms.term: Logical vs. evidential problem of evil
keyTerms.definition: The logical problem claims God and evil are strictly inconsistent (Mackie); the evidential problem claims evil makes God’s existence improbable (Rowe).
keyTerms.example: Rowe’s fawn, burned in a forest fire and suffering for days, is a standard evidential example.
keyTerms.origin: J. L. Mackie, ‘Evil and Omnipotence’ (1955); William Rowe (1979).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The problem of divine hiddenness — which concerns the lack of obvious evidence for God rather than suffering.

keyTerms.definition: The argument that a loving God would make his existence evident to everyone capable of a relationship with him, so God’s not doing so shows he does not exist.
keyTerms.example: J. L. Schellenberg’s version; Feser replies that not all theists hold God seeks such a relationship, that a greater good may be served, and that most people have in fact believed.
keyTerms.origin: J. L. Schellenberg, *Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason* (1993); John Hick’s ‘epistemic distance’ is a related theistic idea.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Agnosticism — hiddenness is offered as an argument for atheism, not as a report of uncertainty.

keyTerms.definition: An explanation that posits God to fill a current gap in scientific knowledge, allowing that a natural explanation might later replace it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Science can’t yet explain the bacterial flagellum, so God designed it’ — the kind of reasoning Feser says his demonstrations are not.
keyTerms.origin: A 20th-century phrase, used by both scientists and theologians critically.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical demonstration — which claims no non-divine explanation is possible in principle, from premises any science presupposes.

keyTerms.definition: On the Aristotelian view, a law of nature is a summary of how things tend to behave given their natures or essences, not an external rule imposed on them.
keyTerms.example: ‘Water freezes at 32°F’ describes water’s disposition, which can be blocked; hence Oderberg’s slogan that the laws of nature are the laws of natures.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle; defended today by David Oderberg and the ‘new essentialists’ (Ellis, Cartwright).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Humean regularity laws (mere descriptions of patterns) and Platonic laws (abstract entities things obey) — neither of which can be an ultimate explanation either.

keyTerms.definition: An interpretation of relativity on which past, present and future are equally real, so that time is like a spatial dimension and nothing really changes.
keyTerms.example: Feser replies that the evidence for relativity comes through changing experiences, and a changeless block would still need a cause of its being actual.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with Hermann Minkowski’s geometric reading of Einstein’s special relativity.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine timeless eternity — God’s knowing all times at once does not imply that the world itself is a four-dimensional block.

keyTerms.definition: Existence outside time altogether, without succession, as opposed to mere endless duration within time. This is what Feser means by calling God ‘eternal’.
keyTerms.example: Like an author who conceives the whole story in one flash of insight, God causes the whole temporal world in a single act.
keyTerms.origin: Classical formulation by Boethius (‘the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life’); defended by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Sempiternity (everlastingness) — existing at all times, which would still involve change and parts, and so cannot be God’s mode of being.

keyTerms.definition: The pattern shared by all five proofs: Stage 1 argues for the existence of something fitting a precise description; Stage 2 argues that whatever fits that description must have the divine attributes.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 1’s Stage 1 reaches a purely actual actualizer (formal steps 1–14); its Stage 2 derives unity, immutability, eternity and the rest (steps 15–47).
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s own method, explained in the Introduction.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Two separate arguments — the stages form one continuous deduction; Stage 2 unpacks what Stage 1 established rather than adding faith to it.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of there being, and in principle being able to be, only one God. It is established by showing that nothing could differentiate two purely actual, simple, self-existent beings.
keyTerms.example: Two dogs differ by their matter and two species by their specific differences; a purely actual being has neither, so there could not be two.
keyTerms.origin: Classical monotheism; Feser’s ‘Unity’ section opens the account of the attributes in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplicity — unity means ‘only one’; simplicity means ‘without parts’. Feser argues the two are inseparable.

keyTerms.definition: Unchangeability. God is immutable because change is the actualization of potential, and God has no potential to actualize; he also has no parts that could be gained or lost.
keyTerms.example: God’s becoming Creator is not a real change in God but a Cambridge change in the world.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *immutabilis*, ‘unchangeable’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or inactivity — an immutable God acts (creates, knows, loves) without being changed by acting.

keyTerms.definition: Being without matter and without a body. What is purely actual and simple cannot be material, since matter involves parts and potentiality to change.
keyTerms.example: Even fundamental particles, which have no smaller parts, have distinct attributes and come into and go out of existence, so they are not simple in the relevant sense.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *materia*, ‘matter’, and *corpus*, ‘body’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being a ‘spirit’ in the sense of a ghost or invisible body — incorporeality excludes any body at all, however subtle.

keyTerms.definition: Lacking no feature proper to a thing’s nature. What is purely actual has no unrealized potential and no privation, so it is perfect.
keyTerms.example: A squirrel hit by a car is imperfect because it can no longer realize capacities its nature calls for; pure actuality has nothing unrealized.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *perficere*, ‘to complete’ — the perfect is the ‘thoroughly made’ or complete.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Maximizing some quantity (the most powerful, the biggest) — perfection concerns the absence of lack, not size or degree.

keyTerms.definition: On the classical view, a thing is good to the extent that it actualizes the potentials its nature sets for it; badness is privation. God, as pure actuality, is fully good and the source of all goodness.
keyTerms.example: A carefully drawn triangle is a better triangle than one scrawled on a moving bus; a tree with strong roots is a good tree.
keyTerms.origin: The Platonic, Aristotelian and Scholastic ‘convertibility’ of being and goodness.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Subjective preference — on this account ‘good’ and ‘bad’ are objective facts about how well a thing realizes its nature.

keyTerms.definition: All-powerfulness: the power to actualize any potential that can be actualized. God is omnipotent because all power derives from him and nothing limits his acting.
keyTerms.example: The ‘paradox of the stone’ fails because a stone too heavy for God to lift describes no possible capacity, like a round square.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *omni-* (‘all’) + *potens* (‘powerful’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ability to do literally anything, including contradictions — omnipotence concerns what is possible, not the self-contradictory.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing all truths. God knows everything not by observation but by knowing himself as the cause of all that is and could be.
keyTerms.example: An author knows every event of the story he has conceived by knowing his own plan, not by watching the characters.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *omni-* (‘all’) + *sciens* (‘knowing’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Foreknowledge as prediction — God does not peer ahead in time; he is outside time and knows the world as its cause.

keyTerms.definition: The capacity to grasp abstract concepts, combine them into judgments, and reason from one judgment to another; most basically, to have the form of a thing without being that thing.
keyTerms.example: Grasping the concept man, forming the thought that all men are mortal, and inferring that Socrates is mortal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *intellectus*, from *intelligere*, ‘to understand’ (literally ‘to read between’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Computation or brain activity — for Aristotelians the core of intellect is grasping universals, which Feser argues is not a material process.

keyTerms.definition: Rational appetite: inclination toward what the intellect apprehends as good. God has something analogous to will and it is free, since nothing inside or outside him compels him to create one world rather than another, or any at all.
keyTerms.example: The concepts of lion and unicorn are both in the divine intellect; God willed to create lions, not unicorns, without being compelled.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *voluntas*; the Aristotelian hierarchy of natural, sensory and rational appetite.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Arbitrary choice requiring potentiality — Feser argues free choice as such does not require passing from potency to act.

keyTerms.definition: Willing the good of another. God loves creatures because in creating them he wills their existence and all the good that follows from it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Tough love’ and love of enemies show that love is essentially an act of will, not a passing feeling.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* I.20.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Emotional affection or being moved by the beloved — which would require passivity and change.

keyTerms.definition: The impossibility of fully understanding God. We know that he is, much of what he is not, and can speak truly of him by analogy, but we cannot comprehend him as we understand things by their parts, genus and difference.
keyTerms.example: God is hard to understand precisely because he is simple, just as physics’ talk of curved space outruns our ordinary concepts.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *comprehendere*, ‘to grasp completely’; Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* I.12.7.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Unknowability — incomprehensibility is compatible with real, demonstrated knowledge about God.

keyTerms.definition: A general pattern or nature that can be shared by many particular things.
keyTerms.example: Redness is shared by stop signs, fire engines and strawberries; triangularity by billiard racks, pyramids and dinner bells.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *universalis*, ‘pertaining to the whole’; the ‘problem of universals’ runs from Plato and Aristotle through the medieval debates.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A general word — nominalists reduce universals to words, but a word is itself a universal (one type, many tokens).

keyTerms.definition: The Platonic idea of a realm of abstract objects existing outside space, time and all minds, in which particular things ‘participate’.
keyTerms.example: On Platonism, the Form of Triangle exists in the third realm and billiard racks are triangular by imperfectly resembling it.
keyTerms.origin: Plato’s Forms; the phrase ‘third realm’ is associated with Frege’s account of thoughts.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The divine intellect of Scholastic realism — which is a mind, not a mind-independent realm.

keyTerms.definition: A substance exists in its own right; a property (in the Thomist sense) flows necessarily from its essence; an accident is a feature it can have or lack. All are constituents of the thing, not Platonic entities.
keyTerms.example: Socrates is a substance; his capacity to be amused is a property of human nature; his skin color is an accident; being Plato’s teacher is a mere relation.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *Categories*; Scholastic metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Property’ in Plantinga’s broad sense, which covers anything predicated of a thing — the conflation Feser says distorts divine simplicity.

keyTerms.definition: An efficient cause brings about a thing’s existence or a change in it; a formal cause is a thing’s nature, which makes it the kind of thing it is and grounds its characteristic behavior.
keyTerms.example: A Pb-210 atom’s nature is the formal cause of its probability of decaying; whatever generated it and keeps it in being are its efficient causes.
keyTerms.origin: Two of Aristotle’s four causes (with material and final causes).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The modern narrow sense of ‘cause’ as a prior event triggering a later one.

keyTerms.definition: A power or tendency a thing has, by its nature, to act or react in certain ways under certain conditions; it can be present without being manifested.
keyTerms.example: Water’s disposition to freeze at 32°F can be blocked, as when liquid water is supercooled.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *dispositio*; central to the ‘powers’ ontology of C. B. Martin, Mumford and Anjum, and the new essentialists.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mere regularity — a disposition is a real feature of a thing that explains regularities.

keyTerms.definition: The view that some events are not fixed in advance by prior conditions, so their causes make them probable rather than inevitable.
keyTerms.example: Radioactive decay: a Pb-210 atom has a certain probability of decaying in the next minute.
keyTerms.origin: Associated especially with the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncausedness or unintelligibility — an indeterministic event can still have causes and be made intelligible by a thing’s nature.

keyTerms.definition: Newton’s first law: a body continues at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a force. Sometimes cited as showing change without a cause.
keyTerms.example: Feser replies that the law presupposes the existence of the bodies it describes and, as mathematical physics, abstracts from causal questions.
keyTerms.origin: Isaac Newton, *Principia* (1687).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Existential inertia — a thesis about things’ continuing to exist, not about motion.

keyTerms.definition: Physics’ method of describing only those aspects of nature that can be expressed mathematically, leaving out qualities, causal powers and intrinsic natures.
keyTerms.example: Like a black-and-white line drawing that cannot show color, physics’ equations cannot show causation — which is no evidence that it is absent.
keyTerms.origin: C. B. Martin’s term ‘mathematicization’ (a ‘partial consideration’); James Weisheipl on the principle of inertia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A complete description of reality — the method’s success at what it attends to does not make it exhaustive.

keyTerms.definition: A form of argument that supports a claim by showing that denying it leads to absurdity or self-contradiction.
keyTerms.example: Feser defends PSR indirectly: denying it would undercut any rational grounds for denying it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘reduction to the absurd’; Garrigou-Lagrange says PSR can be demonstrated this way.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Direct proof from prior premises — a reductio argues from the incoherence of the alternative.

keyTerms.definition: The fallacy of rejecting an argument because of the arguer’s character, motives or interests rather than its merits.
keyTerms.example: Dismissing arguments for God as ‘rationalizations’ of what theists wanted to believe.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘to the person’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Legitimate criticism of reasoning — pointing out a false premise is not ad hominem; attacking motives is.

keyTerms.definition: Arbitrarily exempting a favored case from a rule one applies to everything else.
keyTerms.example: The charge that first-cause arguments say ‘everything has a cause’ but exempt God — which fails because none of the proofs uses that rule.
keyTerms.origin: Originally a legal term for arguing only one side’s special circumstances.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled exception — the proofs exempt God because he lacks the very feature (potency, parts, received existence) that requires a cause.

keyTerms.definition: Misrepresenting an opponent’s position in a weaker form and refuting that instead. Feser argues the ‘everything has a cause’ version of the cosmological argument is a straw man no major defender ever held.
keyTerms.example: Robin Le Poidevin admits no one defended his ‘basic cosmological argument’ yet uses it as a stepping-stone.
keyTerms.origin: Informal-logic term; W. Norris Clarke’s 1970 article traced this particular straw man to Hume.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A simplification for teaching — which is fine as long as it preserves the argument’s actual premises.

keyTerms.definition: Knowable independently of experience (a priori) versus knowable only through experience (a posteriori).
keyTerms.example: The Aristotelian proof is not a priori, since we know change occurs through experience; yet no possible experience could overturn that premise.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘from what comes before’ and ‘from what comes after’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Certain vs. uncertain — Feser’s demonstrations can start from experience and still be certain.

keyTerms.definition: Supernatural: having a cause outside the entire natural order, which only God is. Preternatural: extraordinary but still within created nature broadly — e.g., what an angel might do.
keyTerms.example: A resurrection would be supernatural; a finite spirit’s marvel would be merely preternatural.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *super* (‘above’) and *praeter* (‘beyond, besides’) *naturam*; Anselm Ramelow’s usage in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Supernatural’ as ‘spooky’ — in this sense it means ‘caused by God as outside the order of created causes’.

keyTerms.definition: Believing something because God has revealed it — where there must be evidence (above all miracles) that he really has revealed it.
keyTerms.example: Accepting a prophet’s teaching because miracles certify it as from God.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas’ account of faith as assent on divine authority.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Belief without evidence or against evidence — which Feser calls a common misconception.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge about God that depends on a claimed divine revelation, such as the doctrine of the Trinity; it begins where natural theology leaves off.
keyTerms.example: Whether God sent prophets to Israel or inspired a scripture is a question for revealed, not natural, theology.
keyTerms.origin: The traditional contrast between the ‘light of reason’ and the ‘light of revelation’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Natural theology — which uses only premises available to reason alone.

keyTerms.definition: The misreading of the PPC as saying that causes hand down their own features to effects, like a family heirloom.
keyTerms.example: Cottingham’s objection; a Thomist author notes that a boy need not have a black eye to give one to his neighbor.
keyTerms.origin: John Cottingham’s phrase in his book on Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The PPC itself — which allows effects to be in their causes virtually or eminently, not only formally.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever in reality makes a true statement true.
keyTerms.example: Welty argues a drawing of Socrates hammering nails could represent but not make true that Socrates could have been a carpenter; an idea in an omnipotent mind could.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary analytic metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A representation — something can depict a possibility without grounding it.

keyTerms.definition: John Hick’s idea that God created us at a cognitive distance from himself so that we would be free to choose whether to relate to him.
keyTerms.example: Feser thinks Hick overstates the distance, but that finite minds and free will explain why some people fail to see God’s existence.
keyTerms.origin: John Hick, *Evil and the God of Love*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Religious ambiguity (the world supports theism and atheism equally) — a stronger thesis Hick holds and Feser rejects.

keyTerms.definition: The view that some necessary truths, or moral truths, depend on God’s will rather than his nature or intellect.
keyTerms.example: Leftow suggests ‘water = H₂O’ is necessary because God so willed; Feser says assuming this begs the question against deity theories.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *voluntas*, ‘will’; associated with some late medieval and early modern thinkers.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Scholastic realism — which grounds necessary truths in the divine intellect and nature, not arbitrary choice.

keyTerms.definition: William Vallicella’s claim that everything is a mind, a mental content, a physical thing or an abstract object, used in chapter 2 to show the One is a mind.
keyTerms.example: The One is not abstract (inert), not physical (composite), not a mental content (dependent) — so it is a mind or most like one.
keyTerms.origin: William Vallicella, *A Paradigm Theory of Existence* (2002).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Plotinus’ own view — which placed intellect in a second divine reality after the One.

keyTerms.definition: Any argument from the existence, change or contingency of things in the world to a first or ultimate cause. Four of Feser’s five proofs are cosmological arguments.
keyTerms.example: The Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic and rationalist proofs; Aquinas’ first three Ways; Leibniz’s and Clarke’s arguments.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *kosmos*, ‘world’; the name was popularized by Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The kalām argument specifically, or the straw-man ‘everything has a cause’ version.

keyTerms.definition: An argument, usually probabilistic, from complex, functionally ordered features of nature to an intelligent designer, by analogy with human artifacts.
keyTerms.example: William Paley’s watch; Intelligent Design appeals to the eye or bacterial flagellum.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with Paley’s *Natural Theology* (1802) and modern Intelligent Design theory.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s proofs — which do not appeal to complexity or probability; a pebble is as good a starting point as an eye.

keyTerms.definition: Hypotheses on which our universe is one of many, possibly in a beginningless series of universes. Feser grants such scenarios for the sake of argument.
keyTerms.example: A Big Bang caused by the implosion of an earlier universe, and so on forever back.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary cosmology; Aristotle himself held the world had no beginning.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A refutation of first-cause arguments — hierarchical dependence here and now is unaffected by how far back the linear series goes.

keyTerms.definition: A kind of thing whose members share a real, mind-independent essence, rather than being grouped by convention.
keyTerms.example: Each chemical element (gold, copper) is a natural kind with its own distinctive properties, as Brian Ellis argues.
keyTerms.origin: Term from 19th-century philosophy of science; central to ‘new essentialism’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Artifact kinds like carburetors or can openers, whose essences are partly set by human purposes.

keyTerms.definition: The claim, developed in chapter 6, that the five proofs reach one and the same God, because pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity entail one another and can belong to only one being.
keyTerms.example: Like five trails up one mountain, or ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ naming Venus.
keyTerms.origin: Feser, chapter 6 (‘Unity’), anticipated in each chapter’s Stage 2.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A probabilistic ‘cumulative case’ — the convergence is itself deduced, not a sum of likelihoods.

keyTerms.definition: The finding that elementary particles exhibit properties of both waves and particles — used by Feser as an analogy for why the ultimate level of reality should strain our concepts.
keyTerms.example: If physics must stretch ‘particle’ and ‘wave’ to describe electrons, natural theology must stretch ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ further to describe a simple God.
keyTerms.origin: Early 20th-century quantum physics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Evidence for God — Feser uses it only as a parallel about the limits of concepts.

keyTerms.definition: Logical necessity belongs to propositions true by logic or definition; metaphysical necessity, as Feser uses it of God, belongs to a being that cannot fail to exist because it is purely actual, simple and identical with its existence.
keyTerms.example: Kant and Grayling assume a necessary being must exist ‘by definition’; Feser replies that God’s necessity is metaphysical, neither definitional nor merely conditional.
keyTerms.origin: Standard distinction in modal metaphysics; Grayling contrasts logical, metaphysical and conditional necessity.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conditional necessity (being required for something else to exist), which Grayling wrongly treats as the only alternative.

keyTerms.definition: Having the explanation of one’s existence in one’s own nature. This is possible, whereas being self-caused is not, since a cause must be distinct from its effect.
keyTerms.example: The difference between God and the world is not that one has an explanation and the other lacks it, but that one is self-explanatory and the other is not.
keyTerms.origin: The rationalist tradition; Descartes and Spinoza loosely called God ‘self-caused’ (*causa sui*) when they meant self-explanatory.
keyTerms.confuseWith: *Causa sui* taken literally as efficient self-causation — which is incoherent and which the tradition denied of God.

keyTerms.definition: Belief in one God. For Feser, monotheism is necessarily true, not merely true in fact, since there cannot in principle be two purely actual beings.
keyTerms.example: Even if Zeus became the only god on Olympus, his nature would not change — a sole god of a genus is not the God of classical theism.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *monos* (‘single’) + *theos* (‘god’); *poly-* ‘many’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Having exactly one member of the genus ‘gods’ — classical monotheism denies God is in any genus at all.

keyTerms.definition: Treating something as belonging to a logical type or category it does not belong to.
keyTerms.example: Treating triangularity as one more triangle alongside those drawn on chalkboards, or the God of classical theism as one more god alongside Zeus.
keyTerms.origin: Phrase popularized by Gilbert Ryle (1949).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A factual error — a category mistake misunderstands what kind of thing is under discussion, whatever the facts.

distinctions.name: Linear vs. hierarchical causal series

left.label: Linear (per accidens)
left.desc: Members are ordered through time and each has causal power of its own once it exists; an earlier member can vanish without the later one ceasing to act. Feser grants such a series might have no beginning.

right.label: Hierarchical (per se)
right.desc: Every member other than the first acts only with power borrowed, here and now, from a prior member; remove the source and the whole series stops. Such a series must have an underived first member.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This single distinction disarms three of the commonest objections at once: that the argument assumes a beginning of the universe, that an infinite regress could explain everything, and that Hume showed first causes unnecessary. All four causal proofs run on hierarchical series.

distinctions.name: ‘First’ in time vs. ‘first’ as underived

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest member of a sequence — the one at the head of the queue, such as a supposed first moment of the Big Bang.

right.label: Underived (primary)
right.desc: The member whose causal power is its own rather than borrowed, and on which every other member depends for its power at every moment, however many intermediaries there are.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Critics often hear ‘first cause’ as ‘earliest cause’ and reply with beginningless cosmologies. Feser’s first cause is first the way the painter is first relative to an infinitely long brush handle.

distinctions.name: Demonstration vs. probabilistic hypothesis

left.label: Best-explanation / probabilistic reasoning
left.desc: Like design arguments and ‘god of the gaps’ reasoning: a hypothesis judged more likely, simpler or better-fitting than rivals, which could be displaced by a better scientific account.

right.label: Metaphysical demonstration
right.desc: A deduction from premises about what any possible empirical theory presupposes (change, composition, contingency, abstract truths), claiming that no alternative is possible even in principle.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Objections from parsimony, from ‘science will fill the gap’, and from Dawkins’ ‘the designer is more complex’ assume the first model. To refute a demonstration one must show a premise false or an inference invalid.

distinctions.name: Cause vs. sufficient reason

left.label: Cause
left.desc: That which actualizes a potential; it must be distinct from its effect, so nothing can cause itself.

right.label: Sufficient reason (explanation)
right.desc: Whatever makes something intelligible. Every cause is an explanation, but not every explanation is a cause, so something can be self-explanatory without being self-caused.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It explains why PSR says everything has an explanation without making an exception for God, and why the causal principles never say ‘everything has a cause’. Hume’s confusion of the two, per Norris Clarke, launched the ‘What caused God?’ straw man.

distinctions.name: Univocal vs. analogical predication

left.label: Univocal (and its opposite, equivocal)
left.desc: Univocal: exactly the same sense in both uses (‘Fido is a dog’, ‘Rover is a dog’). Equivocal: wholly unrelated senses (‘baseball bat’, ‘bat in the attic’).

right.label: Analogical
right.desc: Related but not identical senses, still literal: by attribution (healthy George, healthy food) or by proper proportionality (seeing a tree, seeing a theorem).

distinctions.whyItMatters: If we spoke of God univocally he would be a creature; if equivocally we would say nothing. Analogy is what lets the proofs give real, positive knowledge of God while preserving his simplicity — and it is what Plantinga’s critique of simplicity overlooks.

distinctions.name: Classical theism vs. theistic personalism

left.label: Theistic personalism (neo-theism)
left.desc: God as the greatest member of a genus of persons, with distinct properties, possibly changeable and in time, differing from us chiefly in degree.

right.label: Classical theism
right.desc: God as absolutely simple, purely actual, immutable, eternal subsistent being itself — personal in having intellect and will, but not ‘a being’ within any genus.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only the classical God is what the five proofs reach. Feser argues that denying simplicity reduces God to a superangel that would itself need a cause — and that critics who attack ‘God’ as one more item in the universe are attacking theistic personalism, not the God of the proofs.

distinctions.name: Real change vs. Cambridge change

left.label: Real change
left.desc: A thing itself gains or loses some feature, actualizing a potential — Socrates growing hair.

right.label: Cambridge change
right.desc: A new description becomes true of a thing only because something else changed — Socrates becoming shorter than Plato because Plato grew.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It shows how an immutable God can be Creator, can ‘begin’ to be related to a world, and can have contingent truths hold of him (e.g., that he created this world) without any real change or composition in him.

distinctions.name: Platonic realism vs. Scholastic realism

left.label: Platonic realism
left.desc: Abstract objects exist in a third realm outside all minds and matter; things ‘participate’ in them.

right.label: Scholastic realism
right.desc: Abstract objects exist only in things (as instantiated) or in intellects (as abstracted) — and, for necessary truths and pure possibilities, in the necessarily existing divine intellect.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The Augustinian proof’s pivotal move is getting a realist from the first to the second. Many mathematically minded skeptics are already realists; the question becomes where abstract objects can live, and Feser argues only a mind can house them.

illustrations.title: Five trails, one summit
illustrations.body: Picture a mountain approached by five trails from five different valleys: one begins at a river (change), one at a quarry (composition), one at an observatory (mathematical truth), one at a nursery full of living things that might not have existed (essence and existence), and one at a library full of explanations (intelligibility). Hikers on each trail describe the summit differently — ‘the source of all motion’, ‘the undivided peak’, ‘the place where all maps are kept’ — but when they arrive they are standing on the same rock. Use this to explain Stage B of the convergence argument: the descriptions differ in sense, the summit is one.

illustrations.title: The paintbrush with an infinitely long handle
illustrations.body: A brush pushes paint across a canvas only because a hand moves it. Make the handle a mile long, or infinitely long — it still has no power of its own to move. Length is irrelevant; what the series needs is a source with ‘built-in’ power. This is Feser’s key image for a hierarchical series, and why ‘first’ means underived, not earliest. The cup on the desk on the floor on the foundation makes the same point for holding up; the lamp on the chain on the ceiling makes it in the other direction.

illustrations.title: Mirrors, and IOUs
illustrations.body: An infinite row of mirrors, each reflecting the one before, still needs an actual face somewhere outside the series; there cannot be only reflections. An infinite chain of IOUs never amounts to real money unless someone at some point actually pays. Both images (chapters 1, 4 and 7) show why an infinite hierarchical regress explains nothing: every member has only what it received.

illustrations.title: Leibniz’s endlessly copied geometry book
illustrations.body: Suppose a geometry textbook was copied from an earlier copy, that one from another, and so on forever. Each copy has an immediate cause, yet we still have no answer to why the series contains geometry rather than Shakespeare or a car manual, or why the series exists at all. Chapters 5 and 7 use this to show that ‘each member is explained by the previous one’ does not explain everything — and that it is the critic who commits the fallacy of composition by thinking it does.

illustrations.title: Red Lego blocks and heavy stones
illustrations.body: If every stone in a pile weighs under an ounce, the pile need not; but if every Lego block is red, whatever you build from them is red. Whether part-to-whole reasoning works depends on the property. Contingency behaves like color: a collection of contingent things is, if anything, more contingent — ‘doubly contingent’ — than its members. Use it whenever someone says ‘fallacy of composition!’

illustrations.title: Morning star, evening star
illustrations.body: Ancient astronomers named ‘the morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ separately before learning both were Venus. The expressions differ in sense but share a referent. Feser uses Frege’s distinction to explain how God’s omnipotence, intellect and goodness can be one reality in a simple being — and the same idea explains how five proofs with five different conclusions can name one God.

illustrations.title: Three ways to have $20
illustrations.body: I can give you $20 because I have a bill in my wallet (the effect is in the cause formally), because I have $20 in my account (virtually), or because I can have genuine bills printed (eminently). The principle of proportionate causality says an effect must be in its total cause in one of these ways. It is how Stage 2 infers intellect: the cause of every possible thing must contain their forms — not as a cat contains catness, but as a mind contains ideas.

illustrations.title: The author and the story
illustrations.body: An author can conceive a whole story in one flash of insight — beginning, middle and end — while within the story events unfold in order. The author knows every event not by observing it but by knowing his own creative plan. And a character who plots a murder does so freely even though the author wrote it; the author is not a hypnotist inside the story. Chapter 6 uses this to illuminate eternity, omniscience, and the compatibility of divine causality with human freedom.

illustrations.title: The metal detector and the drunk under the lamppost
illustrations.body: A metal detector’s flawless record at finding coins does not show that only metal exists; a drunk who searches for his keys only under the streetlight, because that is where he can see, has no evidence they are nowhere else. Physics is spectacularly successful precisely because it restricts itself to what can be mathematically modelled; its silence about causation, purpose or the intrinsic nature of matter is an artifact of its method, not a discovery. Chapters 1 and 7 deploy these images against Russell, quantum objections and scientism.

illustrations.title: White light and the prism
illustrations.body: All the colors are contained, in a unified way, in white light before a prism separates them. Similarly, all the limited ways of being actual — being a stone, a tree, a dog — are contained in unlimited actuality, and to know pure actuality perfectly would be to know every way it could be limited. Chapter 6 offers this (with the image of cookie dough and cutters) as a way to think about how God knows all things without composition in his knowledge — while warning that God is not a material stuff that creatures are made of.

objections.title: 1. “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”
objections.whoRaises: Hume, Russell, Hospers, Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hitchens, Krauss — the single most common objection
objections.objection: The cosmological argument says everything needs a cause. Then God needs one too. If you exempt God, you are special pleading — and if God can be uncaused, so can the universe.
objections.reply:
1. None of the five proofs has the premise ‘everything has a cause’. The principles are narrower: whatever goes from potential to actual (ch. 1), whatever is composite (ch. 2), whatever has an essence distinct from its existence (ch. 4), or whatever is contingent (ch. 5) needs a cause.
2. The exemption for God is not arbitrary; it is the *conclusion*. Each proof identifies the feature that makes things need a cause and shows there must be something that lacks that very feature — pure actuality, simplicity, essence identical with existence, necessity.
3. So the question becomes ‘What actualized the potentials of that which has no potentials?’ or ‘What combined the parts of that which has no parts?’ — which makes no sense.
4. Against the rationalist proof it is weaker still: PSR says *everything* has an explanation, God included; his is found in his own nature.
5. The Augustinian proof is not a causal argument, so the objection does not even touch it.
objections.pushback: If the critic says the distinction is an ad hoc dodge, note (ch. 1) that motives are irrelevant to soundness (ad hominem), that the ‘potential to actual’ formulation has been the claim for over two millennia, and that it follows from the analysis of change independently of theology. If he asks where the ‘everything has a cause’ version comes from, chapter 7 traces it, following W. Norris Clarke, through Russell and the Mills to Hume’s conflation of ‘cause’ with ‘sufficient reason’ in Descartes and Spinoza — and not one major defender of the argument ever used it. Then invite him to say which premise of an actual proof he rejects.

objections.title: 2. “The argument assumes the universe had a beginning”
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; Rosenberg and Krauss (multiverse); many textbook summaries
objections.objection: Cosmology is unsettled. Maybe there was no Big Bang ‘first moment’ — an eternal universe, an oscillating cosmos, or a beginningless multiverse. Then there is no first event for God to cause.
objections.reply:
1. The four causal proofs grant, for the sake of argument, a beginningless universe or multiverse (ch. 1, 2, 4, 5). Aristotle himself thought the world had no beginning.
2. The concern is not what started things but what **sustains** them at every moment: the concurrent actualization of the coffee’s existence (ch. 1), the concurrent combination of the chair’s parts (ch. 2), the imparting of existence to Fido here and now (ch. 4), the persistence of any contingent thing now (ch. 5).
3. Such dependence forms a hierarchical series, which needs an underived first member however long the universe has existed.
4. Only the kalām cosmological argument (not defended in the book) tries to prove a beginning.
objections.pushback: If the critic insists that ‘first cause’ must mean first in time, show the paintbrush: an infinitely long handle still needs a hand. If he says every present state is explained by the previous state, distinguish explaining how something *got here* from explaining what keeps it *existing now* (ch. 1’s water example; ch. 4’s Fido). Chapter 7 repeats the point against the multiverse.

objections.title: 3. “Why can’t an infinite regress do all the explaining?”
objections.whoRaises: Hume (Dialogues); Graham Oppy; Krauss (endless layers of laws)
objections.objection: If each member of a causal series is explained by the one before it, every member is explained. An infinite series leaves nothing unexplained, so no first cause is needed. Mathematics is full of infinite series; why not causes?
objections.reply:
1. For **linear** series Feser agrees: they may in principle be infinite (ch. 1).
2. But in a **hierarchical** series every member other than the first has only borrowed power. Adding more borrowers never produces a lender. Infinite mirrors still need a face; infinite IOUs never become money; an infinitely long brush handle cannot move itself (ch. 1, 4, 7).
3. Barry Miller’s point (ch. 4): the explanation has the form ‘A is caused by B inasmuch as B is caused by C inasmuch as …’, and the sentence can only be completed by naming a first member.
4. Mathematical infinite series involve no instrumental causation at all, so they are not counterexamples (ch. 1).
5. For the rationalist proof, the whole series still needs explaining (why it exists, why this content — Leibniz’s geometry books), and explaining it by further contingent causes only creates a higher-order series with the same problem (ch. 5).
objections.pushback: If the critic says calling the intermediate causes ‘instrumental’ begs the question (Jordan Howard Sobel), reply (ch. 1) that ‘instrumental’ just means ‘deriving its power from something else’ — anyone can see a stick has no power of its own to push a stone — and nothing in that description presupposes that the regress terminates. For Krauss’s layers of laws, note that levels of laws form exactly such a hierarchy (ch. 7).

objections.title: 4. “First-cause arguments commit the fallacy of composition”
objections.whoRaises: Hume, Russell, A. C. Grayling
objections.objection: Each brick may weigh a pound without the wall weighing a pound. Likewise, each thing in the universe may need a cause without the universe as a whole needing one.
objections.reply:
1. Most of the proofs make no claim about the universe as a whole as a premise; they start from one thing — a cup of coffee, Fido, a stone. That God causes everything is a conclusion (ch. 1, 4, 7).
2. Not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious: if every Lego block is red, the wall is red. It depends on the property (ch. 4, 5).
3. Contingency behaves like color, not weight: a collection of contingent things is if anything *more* contingent — dependent on its members and on their being assembled (ch. 5).
4. In fact the critic commits the fallacy: from ‘each stick’s motion is explained by the next stick’ it does not follow that the motion in the whole series is explained (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If he replies that the ‘universe’ is not a thing but just a label for its members, then there is nothing extra to explain away — and the proofs, which start from any single contingent thing’s existence here and now (ch. 5’s second route), go through anyway.

objections.title: 5. “Hume showed something could come into being without a cause”
objections.whoRaises: Hume; Grayling; many analytic philosophers
objections.objection: I can conceive of a coffee cup suddenly appearing out of nothing, with no cause. What is conceivable is possible. So the principle of causality is not necessarily true.
objections.reply:
1. Conceiving of A *without conceiving of* B is not conceiving of A *existing without* B. I can conceive of a trilateral without thinking ‘triangle’, or of a man without thinking of his height; it does not follow that either could exist without the other (ch. 1, 7).
2. Elizabeth Anscombe’s point: what makes the imagined scenario a case of *coming into being* rather than being teleported from elsewhere? Only reference to the kind of cause — which brings causation back in (ch. 1, 7).
3. Empirically, the principle is as well confirmed as anything: we find causes when we look, and hotels and elephants do not pop onto our lawns (W. Norris Clarke) (ch. 1).
4. As Gerson notes, ‘maybe there is no explanation’ is not an alternative to an explanation that has been given (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic retreats to Kant — the principle may hold within experience but cannot be applied beyond it — reply that we affirm causes not because things are experienced but because they are potential until actualized, a completely general truth; compare Euclidean geometry, learned from black ink drawings but true of figures of any color (ch. 1).

objections.title: 6. “Quantum mechanics shows events without causes”
objections.whoRaises: Stenger, Dennett, Rosenberg; popular science writing
objections.objection: Radioactive decay and vacuum fluctuations happen at random. Physics has discovered genuinely uncaused events, so the principle of causality and PSR are false.
objections.reply:
1. Causation does not require determinism; a cause need only make its effect intelligible (ch. 1). On standard interpretations every quantum transition has causal antecedents (Koons).
2. A Pb-210 atom decays with a certain probability because of what it is — its nature is a formal cause — and something generated it and keeps it existing now; Phil Dowe notes physicists speak of decay ‘producing’ mercury (ch. 1).
3. Physics is a mathematical abstraction that by method leaves out potentiality and causation; the absence of a cause in the representation is not a representation of its absence — like the lack of color in a line drawing (ch. 1).
4. Quantum events occur only given the laws of quantum mechanics and a universe that follows them, which are themselves what needs explaining (ch. 5, 7). Chance presupposes non-chance regularities — the farmer who finds buried treasure (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If pressed on Bell correlations or particles appearing in a vacuum, note the variety of available interpretations, but return to the deeper point: interpretation of quantum theory cannot decide a metaphysical question it methodologically brackets. Heisenberg himself compared quantum states to Aristotle’s *potentia* (ch. 1).

objections.title: 7. “Modern physics has eliminated causation and change”
objections.whoRaises: Early Russell (‘On the Notion of Cause’); appeals to Newton’s law of inertia, Einstein’s block universe, Eddington’s ‘two tables’
objections.objection: Physics describes the world with equations, not causes. Inertia shows motion needs no mover; relativity suggests past and future are as real as the present, so nothing really changes; and physics tells us the table is a cloud of particles, not a solid thing holding up a cup.
objections.reply:
1. Russell’s argument proves too much: ‘law’, ‘event’ and ‘explanation’ are not in the equations either (Schaffer). Particles have dispositions (C. B. Martin), other sciences use causal notions, and naturalists rely on causal theories of perception and meaning (ch. 1).
2. Physics captures only mathematically describable structure; the later Russell admitted it is silent about the intrinsic nature of what changes (ch. 1, 7).
3. Newton’s law presupposes the existence of the bodies it describes, so it cannot explain their existence; and on an Aristotelian reading a law describes how a thing behaves given its nature (ch. 1).
4. Even if the block universe were true, the experiences on which physics rests involve change (Richard Healey), and the sheer existence of such a universe would still need an actualizer (ch. 1).
5. The particle picture merely supplies the mechanism by which the desk holds up the cup; the examples only introduce act/potency and hierarchical series, which apply at any level (ch. 1).
objections.pushback: If the critic says Aristotelianism in general was refuted by modern science, separate the outdated physics (geocentrism, natural places) from the metaphysical thesis that change is actualization of potential, which science presupposes rather than refutes (ch. 1). If he insists simultaneity of cause and effect is impossible, note that ‘simultaneous’ does not mean ‘instantaneous’, and the immediate cause and effect are one event (Mumford and Anjum) (ch. 1).

objections.title: 8. “Maybe the universe itself (or the laws, the Big Bang, the multiverse) is the necessary, uncaused thing”
objections.whoRaises: Hume; Dawkins, Dennett, Grayling, Krauss, Rosenberg, Stenger
objections.objection: Grant that explanation must stop somewhere. Why stop at God? Stop at the universe, or at the laws of physics, and you have saved a step.
objections.reply:
1. The stopping point is principled. What ends the regress must be purely actual, simple, identical with its own existence and necessary (ch. 5, 6, 7).
2. The universe changes (so it has potency), has parts (so it is composite), and is contingent; so do the Big Bang, each stage of a multiverse and each quantum event (ch. 5, 7).
3. Laws cannot be ultimate on any account of them: as mere descriptions of regularities they explain nothing; as Platonic entities we would need to explain why the world participates in these rather than others; as descriptions of how natures behave they presuppose the things that have the natures (ch. 7).
4. If the universe really were necessary, uncaused and self-explanatory, it would have divine attributes — the result would be pantheism, not atheism (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic replies with Kant that a necessary being presupposes the ontological argument, answer (ch. 7) that God’s necessity is not ‘existence by definition’ but the metaphysical necessity of what is purely actual, simple and self-existent; Aquinas rejects the ontological argument while accepting the cosmological. And Grayling’s dilemma (logical vs. merely conditional necessity) is a false one. If the critic appeals to numbers as non-divine necessary beings, chapter 3 argues they cannot exist apart from a mind (ch. 5, note).

objections.title: 9. “PSR is false — reality can end in brute facts”
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Mackie, Bertrand Russell; van Inwagen, Rowe (the big conjunctive contingent fact)
objections.objection: We can explain phenomena by laws and those by deeper laws, but the deepest laws are simply there. Besides, PSR leads to paradox: the conjunction of all contingent truths can be explained neither by a necessary truth (which entails only necessary truths) nor by a contingent one (which would be part of what needs explaining).
objections.reply:
1. Denying PSR undercuts perception (Pruss, Koons) and even the rational grounds of one’s own beliefs, including disbelief in PSR (ch. 5).
2. A regress of laws ending in a brute fact makes every explanation illusory: a book on a shelf that stays up for no reason has not been explained — the brackets cannot be let go in mid-air (ch. 5, 7).
3. Della Rocca: critics use explicability arguments everywhere else and have no non-question-begging reason to exempt existence (ch. 5).
4. The big-conjunction puzzle assumes propositions are Platonic objects needing explanation and that explanation requires entailment. For a Scholastic realist, once concrete things and the minds that entertain propositions are explained, nothing is left over; and scientific explanations do not entail their explananda (ch. 5).
5. Brute-fact appeals are ad hoc, adopted only to avoid theism (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘maybe there’s just no explanation’, answer with Gerson: an explanation has been given; to reject it you must show what is wrong with it (ch. 2, 7). If he demands that PSR be proved directly, explain that it is known indirectly, by *reductio*, because it is more evident than any premise for or against it (ch. 5).

objections.title: 10. “Even if there’s a first cause, it needn’t be God”
objections.whoRaises: Dawkins, Grayling (‘the usual big jump’), Krauss; a staple of popular criticism
objections.objection: At best you get some cause of the universe — perhaps impersonal, perhaps finite, perhaps one of many. Nothing licenses omnipotence, omniscience, goodness or unity.
objections.reply:
1. Every chapter’s Stage 2 derives the attributes from the Stage 1 description: pure actuality yields immutability, eternity, immateriality, perfection, goodness, omnipotence; the PPC yields intellect and omniscience; the impossibility of differentiating purely actual beings yields uniqueness (ch. 1–5).
2. Chapter 6 develops each attribute at length and shows the five routes reach the same being.
3. Historically, proponents always argued for the attributes — Aquinas devoted a vast stretch of the *Summa* to them, and Samuel Clarke’s book is largely about them (ch. 7).
4. The objection is usually made in ignorance that these arguments exist.
objections.pushback: If the critic says a first cause could have potentials that are simply not being exercised, answer (ch. 1) that a first actualizer of existence with unactualized potential would need something further to actualize it, so it would not be first; a partly potential ‘first cause’ collapses into a regress. If he says ‘impersonal’, point to intellect via the PPC and chapter 3, and to will and love in chapter 6.

objections.title: 11. “A thing’s parts might unify themselves”
objections.whoRaises: Critic of the Neo-Platonic proof (considered by Vallicella and Gerson)
objections.objection: Why assume an external cause must combine a composite’s parts? Perhaps one of its parts does the unifying, or its unity is an irreducible fact, or laws of nature explain it.
objections.reply:
1. If part C unifies parts A and B, what unites C with them? Positing D just repeats the problem; the regress compounds rather than solves it (ch. 2).
2. ‘Irreducible fact’ means either the composite causes its own unity — which makes it both cause and effect of its composition, incoherent — or its unity has no cause at all, which is not an alternative explanation but the absence of one (ch. 2).
3. Laws of nature plus the things they govern form a further composite whose composition needs explaining; and on the Aristotelian view laws presuppose the combination of form and matter (ch. 2).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘fine, there is no explanation’, repeat Gerson’s response: an explanation has been offered, and one needs a non-question-begging reason to reject it (ch. 2). Note also that for the rationalist proof the same demand follows from PSR (ch. 5).

objections.title: 12. “The essence/existence distinction is merely conceptual”
objections.whoRaises: Anthony Kenny; analytic critics appealing to Frege’s quantifier view and to intensional contexts
objections.objection: That I can know what a lion is without knowing whether lions exist shows only that the concept of a lion differs from the concept of its existence — just as I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing that acetylsalicylic acid does. And existence is just the quantifier ‘there is an x such that…’, not something a thing has.
objections.reply:
1. Klima: substitution fails in intentional contexts only when the concepts are logically independent. A *complete* grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would include its being acetylsalicylic acid; no complete grasp of a lion’s essence ever includes its existence (ch. 4).
2. Judging that lions do not exist is judging falsely, not misconceiving what a lion is — unlike judging a lion is not a cat (ch. 4).
3. Contingency and plurality give independent grounds: things could fail to exist, and there can be many of a kind (ch. 4).
4. Kenny assumes a real distinction requires separability (radius and circumference refute that) and that quantifier-existence is the only respectable notion. But ‘there is an x that is a cat’ leaves open what makes it true that something falls under the concept — which is precisely existence as act (Knasas, Klima) (ch. 4).
objections.pushback: If the critic doubts that things have real essences at all, point to the unity of natural kinds and individuals, the practice of physics looking for natures under controlled conditions (Cartwright), the discrete kinds of chemistry (Ellis), and Crawford Elder’s argument that conventionalism about all essences — including the mind’s — is incoherent (ch. 4).

objections.title: 13. “Abstract objects don’t need a divine mind”
objections.whoRaises: Platonists; nominalists and conceptualists; Yandell and Craig (divine ideas aren’t abstract); Brian Leftow; Patrick Grim
objections.objection: Either abstract objects are Platonic entities existing necessarily in no mind, or they are human constructs. Ideas in God would be concrete mental items, not abstract objects. And omniscience is incoherent anyway — Cantor’s theorem shows there is no set of all truths.
objections.reply:
1. Nominalism and conceptualism are self-undermining (resemblance regress; words are universals; shared meaning and communication; psychologism refutes itself) (ch. 3).
2. Platonic objects would be causally inert and unknowable, and a Form would have to be both universal and an individual — animality itself neither rational nor nonrational (ch. 3).
3. The ‘not really abstract’ objection begs the question: for Aristotelians and Scholastics an abstract object *is* what an intellect forms by abstracting; there is no consensus notion that settles the matter against them (Welty) (ch. 3).
4. Grim’s argument proves too much — there would be no set of all propositions, yet we truly say all propositions are true or false (Plantinga); omniscience needs only that there is no truth God fails to know (Simmons); and simplicity means God’s knowledge is not a set of discrete ideas (Wainwright) (ch. 3).
5. Leftow’s worry that God would ‘depend’ on water being H₂O is no worse than arithmetic ‘depending’ on rocks (ch. 3).
objections.pushback: If the critic, like Coffey, says we cannot know possibilities are eternal without first knowing God, note that even atheist Platonists affirm eternal possibilities; the argument simply denies they can be housed in a third realm (ch. 3). Welty’s relevance condition helps too: a Platonic possible world, like a drawing, cannot make it true that Socrates could have been a carpenter; an idea in an omnipotent mind can.

objections.title: 14. “Divine simplicity is incoherent”
objections.whoRaises: Alvin Plantinga; Thomas Morris; theistic personalists
objections.objection: If God is identical with each of his properties, then all his properties are identical — power is mercy — and God himself is a property, a mere abstract object. Also, some truths about God are necessary (he is omnipotent) and some contingent (he created this world), so they cannot all be one.
objections.reply:
1. Plantinga reads the doctrine through his own assumptions: a very broad notion of ‘property’, properties as Platonic abstracta, and univocal predication. Classical theists reject all three (ch. 6).
2. Distinguish essence, properties (in the Thomist sense), accidents and relations; these are constituents of a thing, not Platonic entities (ch. 6).
3. God’s power and knowledge differ in sense but are one reality, as with the morning and evening star; we speak of them analogically (ch. 2, 6).
