4. Morris’s point is met by Geach’s and Miller’s ‘Cambridge properties’: God’s having created the world is a Cambridge property, involving a real change only in the world; simplicity identifies only God’s real properties (ch. 6).
5. Without simplicity God would need a cause and could have rivals — a superangel, not God (ch. 6).
objections.pushback: If the critic says theism can do without simplicity, reply that the causal proofs are ipso facto proofs of a simple cause; deny simplicity and you deny what the proofs reach, and even the uniqueness of God becomes a contingent fact (ch. 6). Dawkins’ ‘God would be complex’ is the same mistake from the atheist side (ch. 7).

objections.title: 15. “An immutable, timeless God couldn’t create, act, know, love or choose freely”
objections.whoRaises: Swinburne, Pike (timelessness); Kretzmann, Rowe (freedom); process theists (love)
objections.objection: Acting changes the agent; creating is a transition from not-creating to creating; causing things at different times puts God in time; love means being affected; free choice means actualizing one potential rather than another; and a perfectly good God would have to create the best possible world, so he isn’t free.
objections.reply:
1. That agents in our experience change when they act is a **fallacy of accident** if taken as essential; what is essential to acting is producing an effect (Brian Davies) (ch. 1, 6).
2. Becoming Creator is a Cambridge change (ch. 6).
3. From ‘God causes X to exist at t1’ it does not follow that ‘at t1 God causes X’; God causes a whole temporal world in one act, like an author conceiving a story (ch. 6). Eternity is not a point in time that could be simultaneous with Socrates and with Obama.
4. Love is essentially willing the good of another, not emotion; God wills creatures’ good in creating them (ch. 6).
5. Freedom needs no passive potency, only the absence of compulsion from within or without; there is no obligation to create, and there is no best possible world, since for any world with x forests there is one with x + 1 (ch. 6).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘I can’t understand free choice without potency’, concede that it is hard to grasp positively — Davies suggests reading it partly as negative theology — and note that difficulty is expected when reasoning reaches the ultimate level of reality, just as with wave-particle duality (ch. 2, 6). If he argues that God would be more perfect by creating a better world, answer that God’s perfection follows from what he is, not what he makes, like a perfect diamond whether or not it cuts glass (ch. 6).

objections.title: 16. “If God knows the future, we aren’t free”
objections.whoRaises: Nelson Pike; a very common lay worry
objections.objection: If God infallibly knows I will go to work tomorrow, I cannot fail to go; and since God knows by causing, he causes my choices. Either way my freedom is an illusion.
objections.reply:
1. Knowledge of an action, however certain, does not cause it: my knowing you sit in the next room doesn’t make your sitting unfree, and the same holds if I somehow know it in advance (ch. 6).
2. God is the cause of the world as an author is the cause of a story, not as a hypnotist inside the story; a character can freely commit a crime in a novel the author wrote (ch. 6).
3. Because God is outside time, he does not ‘foreknow’ by peering ahead; he knows the whole world by knowing himself as its cause (ch. 6).
4. Concurrence: like a child whose hand is guided by a parent teaching him to write, our free choice makes a real contribution even though nothing happens without God’s action (ch. 6).
objections.pushback: If the critic says the author analogy works only because characters are fictional, reply that the point concerns the *logical kind* of relation — primary cause of the whole versus one cause among others — and that treating God’s causality univocally with creaturely causality is exactly the error analogy avoids (ch. 6).

objections.title: 17. “It’s a god of the gaps — science will explain it (it already has: a universe from nothing)”
objections.whoRaises: Hitchens, Dawkins, Harris; Krauss; Hawking and Mlodinow
objections.objection: God is posited to fill a gap in scientific knowledge. Parsimony says prefer a physical explanation; indeed physics shows the universe can arise from nothing thanks to laws like gravity.
objections.reply:
1. The proofs are not gap-fillers or probabilistic hypotheses but demonstrations claiming no non-divine explanation is possible in principle (ch. 7).
2. Their starting points — change, composition, essence-existence, contingency — are presupposed by any empirical theory, so no empirical discovery could remove them (ch. 7).
3. Hawking and Mlodinow’s ‘law like gravity’ is not nothing; Krauss’s candidates (empty space with energy, quantum laws, layers of laws) are admittedly not nothing either, as the philosopher of physics David Albert pointed out (ch. 7).
4. Nothing is not an exotic stuff; it is the absence of anything.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘we don’t yet know how the universe began’, remind him the proofs do not depend on how or whether it began (ch. 1, 7). If he says only scientific explanations count, move to objection 18.

objections.title: 18. “Science is the only genuine source of knowledge”
objections.whoRaises: Alex Rosenberg; New Atheists generally (scientism)
objections.objection: Physics’ predictive and technological success shows its methods are the right ones for all knowledge. Metaphysics produces no technology and no consensus. Natural theology isn’t science, so it isn’t knowledge.
objections.reply:
1. Dilemma: the claim ‘only science gives knowledge’ is not itself a scientific result, so it is self-refuting; if ‘science’ is stretched to include philosophy, the claim becomes trivial and natural theology could count as science too (ch. 7).
2. Physics abstracts from everything unquantifiable, so it cannot in principle give a complete description of reality — as Russell admitted, it gives structure, not intrinsic nature (ch. 1, 7).
3. Laws cannot provide ultimate explanation on any theory of what laws are (ch. 7).
4. The success argument is like inferring from metal detectors’ success that only metal exists, or from straight A’s in easy classes that other subjects aren’t worth studying (ch. 7).
5. The science/conceptual-analysis dichotomy is a version of Hume’s fork, which refutes itself; logic and mathematics fit neither prong (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘fine, but philosophy never settles anything’, reply that insisting only consensus-yielding questions matter is itself a philosophical claim needing philosophical defense, and that restricting ‘science’ to what is predictable guarantees trivially that science is a success story (ch. 7).

objections.title: 19. “Evil (and God’s hiddenness) shows there is no good God”
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Mackie (logical), William Rowe (evidential — the fawn), J. L. Schellenberg (hiddenness)
objections.objection: An omnipotent, perfectly good God would eliminate evil — or at least pointless suffering like a fawn burning slowly in a forest fire. And a loving God would make his existence obvious. Neither is the case.
objections.reply:
1. Mackie’s premises fail: omnipotence does not include doing contradictions, and a good being need not eliminate every evil if that would eliminate goods logically requiring it — forgiveness and mercy require wrongdoing; courage requires danger; compassion requires suffering (ch. 7). Mackie himself later conceded the logical argument fails.
2. Evil is privation, not a positive thing God must contain (ch. 6).
3. Rowe’s argument is only as strong as the claim that no greater good is served; anyone with independent demonstrations of a good, omnipotent God has reason to believe there is one, even when we cannot say what it is (ch. 7).
4. An afterlife, which is at least possible, could outweigh all earthly evils, as adulthood makes sense of childhood’s trials (ch. 7).
5. Hiddenness: not all theists hold that God seeks a personal relationship (Aristotle’s God), and most humans have in fact believed in the divine; the ‘epistemic distance’ that exists stems from finite minds and free will (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says this is cold comfort to sufferers, agree that a *defense* (showing consistency) is not a *theodicy* (explaining specific evils) and not pastoral care — Feser explicitly offers only a defense (ch. 7). If he asks why we should expect to be ignorant of God’s reasons, point to the child-adult analogy and to the incomprehensibility of God (ch. 6, 7).

objections.title: 20. “Go one god further” / “That’s not the God people actually worship”
objections.whoRaises: Dawkins, Colin McGinn; critics who contrast the ‘God of the philosophers’ with the God of religion
objections.objection: You reject Zeus, Thor and Quetzalcoatl; atheists just reject one more god. And the abstract ‘ground of being’ of the proofs is not the personal God ordinary believers pray to.
objections.reply:
1. There are demonstrations for classical theism’s God and none for Zeus (ch. 7).
2. More deeply, it is a category mistake: classical theism’s God is not a member of a genus ‘gods’ (he would then have parts — genus and difference), not ‘a being’ among beings, but subsistent being itself. Comparing him to Zeus is like treating triangularity as one more, better-drawn triangle, or the Form of the Good as one more good thing (ch. 6, 7).
3. On the ‘God of the philosophers’: even if true it would be irrelevant — atheism would still be false. And it is false: Catholic teaching, for example, holds that the God known by reason and by revelation is the same; ordinary believers hold the same God in a less sophisticated way, as laymen believe in atoms without the physicist’s understanding (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says the classical God is too abstract to be personal, point out that classical theists attribute intellect, will and love to God (ch. 6) — they deny only that personhood makes God one member of a genus. If he raises a specific religion’s claims, note that natural theology deliberately stops short of revealed religion; miracles would be the bridge (ch. 6).

misconceptions.myth: The proofs argue that the universe had a beginning and that God lit the fuse of the Big Bang.
misconceptions.correction: All four causal proofs grant a beginningless universe or multiverse for argument’s sake; they concern what sustains things in existence here and now through hierarchical causal series. Only the kalām argument, not defended in the book, tries to show a beginning.

misconceptions.myth: The proofs rest on the premise that everything has a cause.
misconceptions.correction: They rest on narrower principles — whatever goes from potential to actual, is composite, has essence distinct from existence, or is contingent needs a cause — and PSR, which says everything has an explanation (God’s lying in his own nature). No major defender of cosmological arguments ever used ‘everything has a cause’.

misconceptions.myth: The five proofs point to five different ultimate beings, or at best to a vague ‘first cause’.
misconceptions.correction: Chapter 6 shows that being purely actual, simple, subsistent existence and necessary entail one another, that a necessary intellect is purely actual, and that there can be only one such being. Every chapter’s Stage 2 derives the full set of divine attributes.

misconceptions.myth: They are scientific hypotheses — ‘God did it’ as a rival to physics, to be judged by parsimony and evidence.
misconceptions.correction: They are metaphysical demonstrations starting from what any scientific theory presupposes; they do not compete with physics at physics’ own level, and a scientific discovery could not overturn their premises.

misconceptions.myth: God, in these arguments, is the biggest and most powerful being in the universe — one item alongside others.
misconceptions.correction: God is not ‘a being’ within any genus but subsistent being itself, the source of the being and causal power of everything else. That is why ‘one god further’ and ‘who designed the designer?’ miss the target.

misconceptions.myth: Divine simplicity means God is simple-minded, has just one property, or is himself a property.
misconceptions.correction: Simplicity means God has no parts — no matter and form, genus and difference, essence distinct from existence, or really distinct attributes. His power, knowledge and goodness are one reality known under different descriptions, spoken of analogically.

misconceptions.myth: If language about God is analogical, it must be metaphorical or merely negative.
misconceptions.correction: Analogical predication is literal: ‘good’ in ‘good wine’ and ‘good man’ is neither identical nor unrelated. Much of our knowledge of God is negative, but analogy of attribution and of proper proportionality give real positive content.

misconceptions.myth: An immutable, timeless God would be inert, unfeeling and unable to act, know, choose or love.
misconceptions.correction: Being changed is not essential to acting, living, choosing or loving; to assume otherwise is a fallacy of accident. God acts without being acted upon, loves by willing the good of creatures, and is Creator by a Cambridge change in the world.

misconceptions.myth: Miracles would be violations of the laws of nature by a God who otherwise leaves the world to run on its own.
misconceptions.correction: God conserves and concurs with everything at every moment, so he cannot literally ‘intervene’. A miracle elevates a nature beyond its powers or suspends its operation by God’s refraining from conserving or concurring — more like a musician improvising than a mechanic forcing a machine.

misconceptions.myth: A real proof would convince every intelligent person who hears it; since many reject these, they aren’t proofs.
misconceptions.correction: A demonstration is a valid deduction from certain premises; it may require substantial work to understand and defend, and fair-minded people can fail to see its force. Controversy is not refutation — no one treats arguments for materialism that way.

misconceptions.myth: Classical theists deny that God is personal; their God is an impersonal force or principle.
misconceptions.correction: Classical theists attribute intellect, will and love to God (chapters 3 and 6) and therefore regard him as personal. What they deny is that God is a member of a genus ‘person’ alongside humans and angels — that would make him composite.

misconceptions.myth: Natural theology replaces faith, or faith is simply belief without evidence.
misconceptions.correction: For Feser, faith is believing something because God has revealed it, and whether God has spoken is itself a matter for evidence — above all miracles. Natural theology establishes the God who could reveal; it does not replace revelation.

explain.tweet: Feser’s case: change, parts, abstract truths, the gap between what things are and that they are, and the demand for explanation each lead — here and now, not back in time — to something purely actual, simple and necessary. There can be only one such thing. That’s God.
explain.elevator: Feser gives five independent arguments. Each starts from something undeniable — that things change, that they have parts, that math is objectively true, that nothing in the world exists by its own nature, that things have explanations — and shows that, right now, everything depends on a cause that has no potential, no parts and no dependence at all. He then shows that anything like that must be unique, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing and good. Five roads, one destination: the God of classical theism.
explain.twoMinute:
Most people think arguments for God go like this: everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, so God — and then they ask what caused God. Edward Feser’s *Five Proofs* argues that no serious philosopher ever argued that way.

Instead, he offers five separate arguments with the same shape. Each starts with something you can’t really deny. Things **change** — your coffee cools. Things have **parts** — a chair needs its legs held together. **Mathematical truths** are objective — two plus two was four before anyone noticed. For every ordinary thing, **what it is** doesn’t include **that it is** — you can know what a lion is without knowing lions exist. And things have **explanations** — we never accept ‘it just happened’ in science.

Then each argument asks not ‘what started the universe?’ but ‘what keeps this going *right now*?’ Your coffee exists only because its molecules are actually water rather than separate gases, which depends on atoms, which depends on particles, and so on — a chain where every link has borrowed power, like a paintbrush in a painter’s hand. A chain of borrowed power can’t go on forever with no lender; however long a brush handle is, it can’t move itself. So there must be something at the bottom with nothing borrowed: something purely actual, with no parts, whose very nature is to exist.

The second stage shows such a thing must be one of a kind — there’d be nothing to tell two of them apart — unchanging, outside time, immaterial, all-powerful, and, because it’s the source of every pattern in things, an intellect that knows everything. Chapter 6 shows the five conclusions are the same being described five ways, like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ both naming Venus.

That’s why ‘what caused God?’ misses: the whole point is that there must be something that doesn’t need a cause because it lacks the very feature — potential, parts, borrowed existence — that makes other things need one. You can still disagree. But you have to find the false premise.
explain.eli12:
Think about a stack of books on your desk. The top book stays up because the book under it holds it. That book stays up because the next one holds it, and so on down to the desk, the floor, the ground. None of them holds itself up — each one is only borrowing its ‘holding-up power’. If everything in a stack were only borrowing, nothing would be holding anything up at all!

Feser says everything in the world is a bit like that. Your body keeps existing only because your cells hold together, which depends on molecules, which depends on atoms, and on and on — right now, this very second. So there has to be something at the bottom that isn’t borrowing anything: something that just **is**, all on its own, with no parts to fall apart and nothing that could change.

He finds this ‘bottom’ five different ways — by thinking about change, about parts, about math, about why things exist at all, and about why everything has a reason. And every way ends up at the same thing. There can only be one of it, it can’t change, it isn’t made of stuff, it’s the source of all power, and — since every idea of every possible thing comes from it — it’s a mind that knows everything. That’s what people have always meant by God.

> A good question to ask back if someone says ‘Then who made God?’: ‘Who holds up the thing that isn’t borrowing anything?’
whiteboard: Draw five boxes across the bottom labeled CHANGE, PARTS, MATH/ABSTRACT TRUTHS, ESSENCE ≠ EXISTENCE, PSR. Say: ‘Five undeniable starting points, five chapters.’

Above each box draw a vertical ladder of arrows (cup ← desk ← floor…). Label it ‘hierarchical series: here and now, borrowed power’. Next to it draw a horizontal time-line with ‘could be infinite — Feser grants it’. Stress: the ladders, not the timeline, are what matter.
At the top of each ladder write its terminus: PURE ACT; THE ONE (simple); NECESSARY INTELLECT; SUBSISTENT EXISTENCE; NECESSARY BEING. Say: ‘Stage 1 gets you here.’

Draw double-headed arrows linking the five top labels: act ⇔ simple; act ⇔ existence itself; all ⇔ necessary; necessary intellect → act. Then draw a single circle around all five: ‘There can’t be two — nothing could distinguish them.’
Inside the circle list the Stage 2 attributes: one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, omnipotent, intellect, omniscient. Say: ‘These follow from the description — no leap of faith.’
Draw a thin arrow from the circle down to every box: ‘conservation and concurrence — everything depends on it at every moment, and really acts through its power.’
Off to the side, draw a crossed-out bubble ‘Everything has a cause → universe has a cause’ and a crossed-out ‘Big Bang = first cause’. Say: ‘These are the straw men chapter 7 dismantles.’
Finish with a box labeled ‘Revelation? Miracles?’ above the circle, outside the frame: ‘Where natural theology stops and the debate among theists begins.’
explain.keyAnalogy: **The paintbrush with an infinitely long handle** (with the ‘five trails, one summit’ image for the convergence). A brush moves paint only because a hand moves it; lengthening the handle — even infinitely — adds no power of its own. That is the logic of every causal proof: a series whose members have only borrowed power needs an underived source, however long it is, and whether or not the universe had a beginning. Use it the moment someone says ‘infinite regress’ or ‘Big Bang’. Then add the summit: each of the five proofs is a different trail from a different valley, and chapter 6 shows the hikers end up standing on the same rock — the purely actual, simple, necessary source of everything.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes the whole book click is **dependence here and now**. Every causal proof asks not ‘what happened first?’ but ‘what is this thing relying on, at this very moment, simply to exist and act?’ Once someone sees that the cup relies on the desk, the desk on the floor, the water on its molecules, and that an endless chain of borrowers never produces a lender, the rest follows: there must be something that borrows nothing — no potency to be actualized, no parts to be held together, no existence to be received — and such a thing can only be one and has to be God.

The usual reason it fails to click is that listeners hear ‘first cause’ as ‘earliest cause’ and ‘God’ as ‘a very big being’. They then reach for beginningless cosmologies or ‘who made God?’, both of which answer an argument no one made. Your first job, in almost every conversation, is to replace those two pictures: *first* means underived, and *God* means subsistent being itself, not the largest item in the inventory.

audiences.startingPoint: Trusts physics as our best picture of reality; suspects theology of gap-filling; often assumes the argument is about the Big Bang.
audiences.approach: Lead with the **Aristotelian** proof and everyday examples. Emphasize at once that the argument grants a beginningless universe and has nothing to predict or measure — it concerns what any physical theory presupposes. Distinguish explaining how something got here from what keeps it existing now (the water in the coffee). When quantum mechanics or inertia comes up, use the line-drawing and metal-detector images: physics’ silence about causation is an artifact of mathematical abstraction, not a discovery. Offer the **Neo-Platonic** ‘what holds it together right now?’ as a second route.
audiences.openingQuestion: When a physicist explains why this table holds up that cup, is she explaining what happened in the past, or what’s going on right now?
audiences.avoid: Don’t attack science, cite scientific ‘evidence for God’, or use fine-tuning; don’t let the conversation become about whether the universe had a beginning.

audiences.startingPoint: Already believes in objective, necessary, discovered truths; may happily accept abstract objects existing ‘nowhere’.
audiences.approach: Use the **Augustinian** proof. Start by agreeing: realism about numbers and propositions is right, and nominalism and conceptualism fail. Then press the question of *where* abstract objects can exist: if they are causally inert, how do we know them and how do they make things what they are? Show the animality problem for Forms and Welty’s relevance condition. Once they concede abstractions live only in minds, move to necessity (contingent minds can’t ground eternal truths), the interlocking system, and pure actuality.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would 2 + 2 = 4 have been true if no human had ever existed — and if so, what kind of reality does that truth have?
audiences.avoid: Don’t treat Platonism as silly; don’t skip the argument that a necessary intellect must be purely actual, or you’ll end with a ‘cosmic library’ rather than God.

audiences.who: Analytic philosophy student (Humean or Kantian training)
audiences.startingPoint: Knows Hume on causation, Kant on the cosmological argument, Frege on existence and possible-worlds modal reasoning; expects the arguments to be refuted in a textbook paragraph.
audiences.approach: Engage the premises precisely. Use the **Thomistic** and **rationalist** proofs. Answer the conceivability argument with trilateral/triangle and Anscombe’s point; answer Kenny with Klima and Knasas; answer Kant by distinguishing metaphysical necessity grounded in pure actuality from ‘existence by definition’; answer the big conjunctive fact by rejecting Platonic propositions and entailment-only explanation. Show that the textbook ‘basic cosmological argument’ is a straw man even Le Poidevin admits no one held.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which contemporary critic can you name who quotes an actual defender of the cosmological argument using the premise ‘everything has a cause’?
audiences.avoid: Don’t bluff about technical literature; don’t appeal to authority or to how many historical philosophers agreed — engage the argument on its merits.

audiences.who: Casual skeptic raised on New Atheist talking points
audiences.startingPoint: ‘Who made God?’, ‘science explains everything’, ‘one god further’, ‘faith is belief without evidence’.
audiences.approach: Spend the first minutes removing caricatures, calmly and with good humor: no ‘everything has a cause’, no Big Bang premise, no god of the gaps, no design argument. Then give one short proof — often the Aristotelian with the cup and desk — and show why ‘who made God?’ asks what actualized the potentials of that which has none. Use the triangularity analogy for ‘one god further’.
audiences.openingQuestion: If I could show you that the most famous objection to these arguments attacks something none of their defenders ever said, would you be willing to look at what they actually say?
audiences.avoid: Don’t be smug or quote Feser’s sharpest put-downs; don’t try to cover all five proofs or jump to religion-specific claims.

audiences.who: Believer with a ‘very powerful person in the sky’ picture of God
audiences.startingPoint: Believes in God but imagines him as a big being among beings, in time, with changing moods; may find arguments unnecessary or even irreverent.
audiences.approach: Use the **Neo-Platonic** proof and chapter 6 on simplicity, analogy and immutability. Show that a composite, changing god would need a cause and could have rivals — a superangel, not God. Explain that analogy lets us speak truly of God’s love and knowledge without shrinking him. Present natural theology as ‘faith grounded in reason’ (chapter 6 on miracles and faith), not as a rival to faith.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God were made of parts, what would hold those parts together?
audiences.avoid: Don’t make them feel their piety is naive; don’t present immutability as God being cold or unresponsive — stress that love is willing the good, not a passing emotion.

audiences.startingPoint: Senses a sacred ground of everything; resists a ‘separate’ God; may identify the divine with the universe or with consciousness.
audiences.approach: Affirm the insight that everything depends on a ground of being — that is the heart of the proofs. Then show why that ground cannot be the universe itself: the world changes, has parts and is contingent, while the ground must be simple, unchanging and necessary (chapter 6 against pantheism and panentheism). Stress conservation: God is more intimately present to everything than anything else, because he is keeping it in existence now.
audiences.openingQuestion: Can something that is always changing and made of parts be the ultimate reason anything exists at all?
audiences.avoid: Don’t caricature their view or rush to institutional religion; don’t describe God as distant — the doctrine of conservation makes him maximally present.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I know the argument: everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, and that’s God. But then what caused God? You can’t have it both ways.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Agreed — that argument would be hopeless. But none of the five proofs in Feser’s book uses it. Take the first one. It never says everything has a cause. It says whatever goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to actualize it. Your coffee can’t cool itself; the air does it. Do you think a mere potential could make itself actual?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: No, but that’s a convenient redefinition. You pick a rule that lets God slip through. And anyway, maybe the universe had no beginning. Some cosmologists think the Big Bang came out of an earlier universe.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The rule isn’t new — it’s Aristotle’s analysis of change, two thousand years old and used for nothing theological at first. And Feser grants you the beginningless universe. The question isn’t what started things; it’s what’s keeping this cup of coffee in existence right now. Its water exists only because its matter is actually water rather than loose hydrogen and oxygen — which depends on the atoms, which depends on particles, all at this very moment. That’s a chain where each link borrows its power from the next, like a desk holding a cup only because the floor holds the desk.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Physics doesn’t talk about ‘actualizing potentials’. It has equations. And quantum mechanics has events with no cause at all — radioactive decay is random.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Physics describes the world mathematically and leaves out whatever can’t be quantified — the later Russell admitted it tells us structure, not what the structured stuff is. Absence of a cause from the equations is like absence of color from a line drawing: an artifact of the method. And a lead atom decaying at random still decays because of what it is, and still exists only because something keeps it existing. Indeterministic isn’t unintelligible.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, suppose the chain needs a bottom. Why not let the bottom be the universe itself, or the laws of physics? Why add God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because whatever ends the chain can’t be borrowing anything — no potential waiting to be actualized, no parts needing to be held together. The universe changes and has parts; so do the Big Bang and a multiverse. Laws are either descriptions of how things behave, which presuppose the things, or something the universe must somehow participate in, which needs explaining. And notice: if the universe really were necessary and uncaused, it would have divine attributes. You’d be a pantheist, not an atheist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Or there’s no bottom. Each state of things is explained by the one before, forever. Every member explained; no need for anything extra.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: For chains through time — your grandfather, your father, you — Feser actually agrees that could go back forever. But the chain I’m describing isn’t through time; it’s the stack holding you up right now. A mirror reflecting a mirror reflecting a mirror, infinitely, still needs a real face somewhere. An infinite pile of IOUs is never money. A brush handle a mile long, or infinitely long, still can’t move itself. Adding borrowers doesn’t produce a lender.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Honestly, this all sounds like a god of the gaps. We don’t know yet what underlies particles. Give science time.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: A gap argument says, ‘we can’t explain this yet, so God.’ This says: whatever science finds underneath, it will be something that changes, has parts and could have been otherwise — because those are features of anything physical. The premise isn’t a gap in our knowledge; it’s what any possible scientific discovery would still presuppose. Let me try a different road: do you think everything has an explanation, even if we never find it?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Most things. But I’m happy to say the universe is just there. A brute fact. Explanation has to stop somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Stop there and every explanation built on it becomes an illusion. Suppose a book stays up because it rests on a shelf, and the shelf stays up for no reason at all — have you explained the book? The shelf has nothing to lend. And you’d never accept ‘it just happened, no reason’ in a lab. Why accept it only for the question of why anything exists? That’s the rationalist proof in a nutshell.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s where I actually am: I’m a mathematician. I’m sure 2 + 2 = 4 is true whether or not anyone thinks it. But that’s just Platonism. It doesn’t need God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then you’re already halfway down the Augustinian road — you reject nominalism and conceptualism, and so does Feser. The question is where such truths can live. If they float in a third realm, they can’t do anything — so how do they make triangles triangular, and how could we ever know them? And ‘animality itself’ would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which no individual thing can be. Abstract things exist only in things or in minds. Truths that would hold if no humans existed need a mind that isn’t contingent — a necessary intellect.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So now you’ve got a cosmic mathematician, an unmoved mover, a necessary being. That’s three different things. Maybe a committee.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Chapter 6 takes that on directly. Anything with parts has potential, so what’s purely actual is simple; anything with potential has parts, so what’s simple is purely actual. A necessary mind can’t depend on being actualized, so it’s purely actual too. And two purely actual beings couldn’t differ — any difference would be a part or a potential. So it’s one reality described five ways, like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ both naming Venus.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then it’s the most complex thing imaginable — it knows everything, can do anything. Dawkins’ point: a designer would be more complex than what it designs, so it needs explaining even more.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Dawkins aims that at design arguments — eyes, flagella, probabilities. These proofs agree with him that anything complex needs a cause. That’s precisely why they conclude to something absolutely simple. The atheist’s alternatives — universe, laws, multiverse — are the complex ones.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: But ‘simple’ and ‘omniscient and omnipotent and good’? Those are different properties. That’s incoherent.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Different descriptions, same reality. ‘Power’ and ‘knowledge’ are distinct in us because we’re composite. Applied to God they’re used analogically — literally, but not in exactly our sense. It’s strange, but physics has taught us to expect strangeness at deep levels: something can behave like both a wave and a particle. The ultimate level of reality would stretch our concepts even further.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even if the metaphysics works, children die of cancer. An all-good, all-powerful being would stop that. Your God is contradicted by the world.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s the most serious question you’ve asked, and I won’t pretend it’s easy to feel. But logically, omnipotence doesn’t include doing contradictions, and some goods — mercy, courage, compassion, forgiveness — can’t exist without evils to face. Mackie, who pressed the logical version hardest, eventually conceded it fails. The probabilistic version says we can’t see a reason, so there probably isn’t one. But if there are sound independent proofs of a good, all-powerful God, then there is a reason, even when we can’t see it — the way a child can’t yet see why some hard things were good for him.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: It still feels like you believed first and built arguments to fit.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Maybe some believers do; and Thomas Nagel admitted he hoped there is no God and suspected that fear shapes a lot of secular thinking. Either way, motives don’t make premises true or false. So — which premise do you actually reject? That change is real? That a potential can’t actualize itself? That an infinite chain of borrowed power needs a lender?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’m not convinced. But I’ll admit I was attacking arguments nobody makes. Suppose I granted it all — does it prove Christianity?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: No, and Feser says so. Natural theology stops at one simple, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, good cause of everything. Whether that God has revealed himself is the next question — that’s where miracles and history come in, and where the real debate among theists begins. If you want, let’s take just one proof — the Thomistic one, about the difference between what a thing is and that it is — and go through it slowly next time.

socratic: Could a merely potential state of affairs — coldness that isn’t yet there — do anything at all, including make itself actual?
Is explaining how your coffee got into the cup the same as explaining what keeps it existing as coffee right now?
If a stick has no power of its own to move a stone, does making the stick longer — even infinitely long — give it any?
Can something be held together by one of its own parts, without our then asking what holds that part to the rest?
Would the Pythagorean theorem have been true a billion years ago, before any human mind existed? Where was it true?
If I describe a unicorn to you perfectly, have I thereby told you whether unicorns exist? What does that suggest about a thing’s existence?
Would you ever accept, in a laboratory, the explanation ‘there’s no reason — it just happened’? What would make the existence of things different?
If every block in a pile is red, is the pile red? If every thing in a collection could fail to exist, could the collection?
How could we tell two beings apart if neither had any parts, any potential or anything the other lacked?
If God were made of parts, what would put those parts together?
If ‘God’ meant a being alongside other beings, would anything be left to explain why there are beings at all?
When physics gives a mathematical description of a system, does it tell us everything about the system — or only what can be described mathematically?

traps.trap: Opening with the Big Bang or ‘the universe must have had a beginning’.
traps.fix: Say up front that every causal proof grants a beginningless universe; the issue is dependence here and now. Use the cup-desk-floor or water-molecule example.

traps.trap: Saying ‘everything has a cause’ as shorthand.
traps.fix: Always state the precise principle: whatever goes from potential to actual, whatever is composite, whatever has its existence from another, or whatever is contingent needs a cause; everything has an explanation.

traps.trap: Presenting the proofs as the ‘best explanation’ or most probable hypothesis.
traps.fix: Frame them as demonstrations whose premises any scientific theory presupposes; invite the listener to identify a false premise or invalid step rather than to weigh probabilities.

traps.trap: Describing God as a very big, very powerful being — a cosmic engineer or superperson.
traps.fix: Describe God as subsistent being itself, purely actual and simple — not a being among beings — which is exactly why ‘who made God?’ and ‘one god further’ misfire.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there is a first cause’ and conceding it might not be God.
traps.fix: Always include Stage 2: from pure actuality (or simplicity, or necessity) derive uniqueness, immutability, eternity, immateriality, goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience.

traps.trap: Firing all five proofs at once, or piling on jargon.
traps.fix: Choose one proof suited to the listener, anchor every term in an everyday example, and mention the convergence only after one proof has landed.

traps.trap: Jumping from natural theology to specific doctrines (Trinity, scripture, Resurrection) as if the proofs established them.
traps.fix: Be explicit that the proofs establish classical theism only; revealed claims need further argument, with miracles as the bridge.

traps.trap: Adopting Feser’s combative tone — calling objections ‘incompetent’ or critics ignorant.
traps.fix: Keep his content, drop the heat: show that an objection targets a caricature, then ask what the person thinks of the actual premise. Confidence belongs in the argument, not the adjectives.

connections.note: The introduction sets out the book’s method (informal two-stage statement, formal statement, objections), the five proofs’ sources, and the claim that the real debate is among theists; the capstone’s summary of the project and the two-stage structure builds directly on it.

Supplies the toolkit — act and potency, the principle of causality, hierarchical series, the PPC, the meaning of ‘first’ — and the template Stage 2 derivation of the attributes that every later proof reuses; the ‘pure actuality’ node of the convergence argument.

The ‘simplicity’ node of the convergence argument; also introduces the sense/reference distinction and analogical predication that make the identity of the five conclusions and the unity of the attributes intelligible.
The only non-causal proof and the ‘divine intellect’ node; it explains how the first cause has intellect and why abstract objects cannot serve as non-divine necessary beings.

The ‘subsistent existence itself’ node; its essence/existence distinction is, for Feser, the deepest explanation of why creatures depend on God at every moment, and it answers Hume’s ‘why a first cause?’ and the composition charge.
The ‘necessary being’ node; it grounds the demand for explanation (PSR) that underlies all the causal principles and notes how the five proofs complement one another.

Chapter 6’s background principles (PPC, agere sequitur esse, analogy of being) and the Unity section, which proves the five proofs reach one and the same God — the backbone of Stage B of the capstone argument — plus simplicity, immutability, eternity and necessity.

The remaining attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility) and God’s relation to the world — conservation, concurrence, the rejection of pantheism, occasionalism and deism, and miracles as the bridge to revealed religion.

The first half of the objection chapter — the ‘What caused God?’ straw man and its history, the universe as necessary being, no-cause and no-beginning objections, composition, the attributes gap, and the ontological and god-of-the-gaps charges — feeds items 1–10 and 17 of the objection handbook.

The second half — scientism, brute-fact laws, the ‘more complex designer’, ‘one god further’, the God of the philosophers, evil, hiddenness, rationalization, and what counts as a demonstration — feeds items 18–20 and the capstone’s section on demonstration and controversy.

quiz.q: Which of the five proofs is not a causal argument, so that Feser says the ‘What caused God?’ objection is not even prima facie relevant to it?
options: The Aristotelian proof
The Thomistic proof
The Augustinian proof
The rationalist proof
quiz.explanation: The Augustinian proof starts from the reality of abstract objects and concludes to a necessary intellect in which they exist; it does not reason from effects to a cause. The rationalist proof is tempting because it speaks of explanation, but it does argue to a necessary being as the cause of contingent things.

quiz.q: In a hierarchical causal series, what does it mean to call a cause ‘first’?
options: It is the member that came earliest in time, such as the Big Bang
It has its causal power in an underived way, and all other members borrow their power from it
It is the member nearest to the effect being explained
It is the largest and most powerful member of the series
quiz.explanation: ‘First’ means primary or underived, not temporally earliest. Even an infinitely long brush handle needs a hand with its own power. The temporal reading is the most common misunderstanding of first-cause arguments.

quiz.q: What does Stage 2 of each proof aim to establish?
options: That the universe had a beginning in time
That the cause reached in Stage 1 is the God of a particular revealed religion
That the argument’s starting point is empirically confirmed
That whatever fits the Stage 1 description must have the key divine attributes
quiz.explanation: Stage 1 reaches something fitting a key description (pure actuality, simplicity, etc.); Stage 2 derives unity, immutability, eternity, immateriality, goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience from that description. It stops short of any revealed religion.

quiz.q: A friend says: ‘Cosmologists think our universe may have branched from an eternal multiverse, so first-cause arguments are dead.’ Which response best reflects the book?
options: The four causal proofs grant a beginningless universe or multiverse for argument’s sake; they concern what sustains things in existence here and now
The multiverse hypothesis is unscientific, so it can be ignored
Only the rationalist proof survives, because it is about necessity rather than causation
Feser argues that the Big Bang proves the universe began, so the multiverse must be false
quiz.explanation: Feser repeatedly grants a beginningless universe or multiverse. The proofs are about hierarchical dependence at every moment, which a beginningless past does nothing to remove. Feser does not dismiss cosmology or argue for a beginning.

quiz.q: Why can there not be two purely actual beings?
options: Because the universe could not contain two infinite beings
Because two such beings would compete and one would defeat the other
Because distinguishing them would require a feature one has and the other lacks, which implies potentiality or parts
Because Aristotle defined God as unique
quiz.explanation: Plurality requires differentiation — a specific difference, matter, or some perfection one lacks — and any such differentiator involves parts or unactualized potential, which what is purely actual cannot have. The argument is metaphysical, not about competition or definition.

quiz.q: Which pair of claims establishes that the Unmoved Mover of chapter 1 and the One of chapter 2 are the same kind of being?
options: Whatever changes is material, and whatever is material is composite
Whatever is composite has potency (its parts only potentially compose it), and whatever has potency is composite (an actual and a potential ‘part’)
Whatever is necessary is eternal, and whatever is eternal is timeless
Whatever has intellect has will, and whatever has will is personal
quiz.explanation: The two-way entailment ‘purely actual iff simple’ is the link. The first option gives only a one-way chain about material things and does not reach pure actuality; the others concern different attributes.

quiz.q: The Thomistic proof begins from which feature of the things of our experience?
options: The real distinction between their essence and their existence
Their being composed of form and matter
Their being explicable by the laws of physics
Their beauty and order
quiz.explanation: Chapter 4 argues that what a thing is and that it is are really distinct in everything we experience. Form and matter figure in the Neo-Platonic proof as one kind of composition; order and beauty belong to design arguments Feser does not use.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think the lion/pterodactyl/unicorn example supports a real distinction between essence and existence?
options: Because unicorns are impossible, while lions are possible
Because one can fully describe what each animal is without that description revealing which exists, has existed, or never existed
Because existence is a property lions have and unicorns lack
Because the existence of animals can be known only through science
quiz.explanation: If existence were identical with essence, knowing the essence would reveal the existence; it does not. Unicorns are possible, not impossible, in the example, and Feser denies that existence is a property or accident.

quiz.q: A critic says: ‘I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does, yet they are identical; so knowing a lion’s essence without knowing its existence shows nothing.’ Which reply follows Klima, as Feser presents it?
options: Aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid are not really identical
Intentional contexts never block substitution of identicals
A complete grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would include its being acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence includes its existence
Existence is merely a second-order property of concepts, as Frege held
quiz.explanation: Substitution fails only where the concepts are logically independent or incompletely grasped. The Fregean option actually states the critic’s side (Kenny’s ‘specific existence’), not the reply.

quiz.q: Which statement expresses the principle of sufficient reason as Feser defends it?
options: Everything has a cause distinct from itself
Every event is determined by prior events
Every true proposition is logically entailed by a necessary proposition
Everything is intelligible — whatever exists has an explanation of its existence and attributes
quiz.explanation: Feser’s Thomistic PSR concerns intelligibility. It is not ‘everything has a cause’ (causes must be distinct from effects), not determinism, and explicitly not the requirement that explanations entail what they explain.

quiz.q: Why can PSR say that everything has an explanation without making an exception for God, when the principle of causality cannot say that everything has a cause?
options: Because PSR is only an empirical generalization
Because a cause must be distinct from its effect, but an explanation can lie in a thing’s own nature
Because God is a proposition rather than a thing
Because PSR applies only to contingent things
quiz.explanation: Nothing can cause itself, but something can be self-explanatory. All causes are explanations; not all explanations are causes. PSR applies to everything, God included — his explanation lies in his nature.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is ‘What caused God?’ even less effective against the rationalist proof than against the others?
options: Because the rationalist proof holds that God does have an explanation — in his own nature — so there is no exception to be charged with special pleading
Because the rationalist proof concludes only to a necessary being, not to God
Because the rationalist proof admits that some things have no explanation
Because Leibniz answered the objection before Hume raised it
quiz.explanation: The rationalist proof makes no exception at all: the difference between God and the world is that one is self-explanatory and the other is not. The second option is false because Stage 2 identifies the necessary being with God.

quiz.q: Leibniz’s example of an infinite series of geometry books, each copied from the previous one, is meant to show that:
options: an infinite series of copies is impossible
books are contingent while geometry is necessary
citing each member’s immediate cause still leaves unexplained why the series exists and has the content it has
geometry must have been invented by the first copyist
quiz.explanation: The example grants the infinite series and shows that tracing immediate causes forever does not explain the whole. It is used in chapters 5 and 7 against Hume’s claim that explaining each member explains everything.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think inferring the contingency of a collection from the contingency of its members is not a fallacy of composition?
options: Because the universe is identical with each of its members
Because all part-to-whole inferences are valid
Because contingency is like weight — it adds up
Because contingency, like the redness of Lego blocks, carries over to the whole; a collection of contingent things is if anything more dependent
quiz.explanation: Whether part-to-whole reasoning is valid depends on the property. Weight does not transfer (stones), color does (Lego), and contingency behaves like color — a collection is doubly contingent. Feser does not claim all such inferences are valid.

quiz.q: What are the three versions of realism about abstract objects that the Augustinian proof considers?
options: Platonic, Aristotelian and Scholastic realism
Nominalism, conceptualism and psychologism
Direct, indirect and scientific realism
Naive, critical and structural realism
quiz.explanation: After defeating nominalism and conceptualism (the second option lists anti-realist views), Feser compares Platonic, Aristotelian and Scholastic realism and argues only the last is adequate.

quiz.q: Why is Aristotelian realism, without a divine intellect, judged inadequate in chapter 3?
options: It denies that universals exist in things
It cannot ground possibilities and necessary truths that would hold even if no material world or human minds existed
It places universals in a Platonic third realm
It treats universals as mere words
quiz.explanation: Aristotelian realism locates universals in things and in the minds that abstract them, so pure possibles (unicorns) and necessary truths that would hold without any world or human mind are left ungrounded. The other options describe Platonism or nominalism.

quiz.q: Why must the necessarily existing intellect of the Augustinian proof be purely actual?
options: Because only a purely actual being could be worshipped
Because every intellect is purely actual
Because if its existence depended on the actualization of some potential, it would exist contingently on that actualization
Because abstract objects are themselves purely actual
quiz.explanation: Necessity excludes dependence on any actualizer. That step links the Augustinian conclusion to chapter 1 and brings uniqueness, omnipotence and the other attributes. Human intellects are clearly not purely actual.

quiz.q: Patrick Grim argues that Cantor’s theorem rules out a set of all truths, and hence omniscience. Which of these is NOT among the replies Feser reports?
options: The argument proves too much, since we can truly generalize about all propositions
Omniscience requires only that there be no truth God fails to know
Divine simplicity means God’s knowledge is not a set of discrete ideas
Cantor’s theorem has been shown to be false for infinite sets
quiz.explanation: Feser reports Plantinga’s ‘proves too much’ reply, Simmons’ point that no set is needed, and Wainwright’s appeal to simplicity. He does not dispute Cantor’s theorem.

quiz.q: In Feser’s $20 illustration of proportionate causality, having the power to get genuine bills printed corresponds to having the effect in the cause:
options: formally
virtually
eminently
accidentally
quiz.explanation: A bill in the wallet is ‘formally’; money in the bank is ‘virtually’; the more fundamental power to make bills is ‘eminently’. ‘Accidentally’ is not one of the three modes.

quiz.q: How does Stage 2 of the Aristotelian proof infer that the purely actual actualizer has intellect?
options: By noting that only minds can move matter
By inferring from the order of the universe to a designer
By arguing that the ability to cause entails the ability to feel
Since it causes every possible thing, the forms of all things must exist in it (by the PPC) — not concretely but abstractly, the way forms exist in an intellect
quiz.explanation: The argument combines the PPC with the fact that the cause is immaterial: forms can exist concretely (in things) or abstractly (in minds), and only the second is possible here. It is not a design inference.

quiz.q: Cottingham objects that a sponge cake has a sponginess not present in its eggs, flour and butter. What is Feser’s main reply?
options: The PPC concerns the total cause (including the mixing and baking), not just the material ingredients, and it does not require causes to have their effects’ features formally
Sponginess is an illusion
The PPC applies only to God, not to cakes
The objection succeeds, so the PPC must be restricted
quiz.explanation: Attacking a version limited to material factors is a straw man, and the ‘heirloom’ reading ignores the virtual and eminent modes. Feser also notes the PPC is implicitly used by naturalists and respected by evolutionary explanation.

quiz.q: What does the principle agere sequitur esse state?
options: Existence precedes essence
A thing’s activity follows from and reflects what it is
Every effect resembles its cause
Being and goodness are convertible
quiz.explanation: ‘Action follows being.’ It is the formal-cause counterpart of the PPC and is used to argue for omnipotence, concurrence and against occasionalism. The first option is a slogan of existentialism, not Scholasticism.

quiz.q: Why does Feser hold that terms like ‘good’ and ‘powerful’ must be applied to God analogically?
options: Univocal use would make God a creature like us and equivocal use would say nothing; analogical use is literal yet not identical
Because all talk of God is metaphorical
Because God’s attributes are unknowable in every respect
Because only negative statements about God are true
quiz.explanation: Analogy is a literal middle ground between univocal and equivocal predication. Feser stresses that it is not metaphor and that it gives real, positive knowledge, while acknowledging much knowledge of God is negative.

quiz.q: According to Feser, Plantinga’s objection to divine simplicity misfires chiefly because it:
options: denies that God exists
reads the doctrine through a broad notion of ‘property’, a Platonist view of properties and univocal predication, all of which classical theists reject
assumes that God is material
relies on the principle of sufficient reason
quiz.explanation: Given those three assumptions, simplicity would indeed make God a property. But classical theists distinguish essence, properties, accidents and relations as constituents of things and predicate analogically. Plantinga is a theist, so the first option is wrong.

quiz.q: What is a ‘Cambridge change’, and how does it help with divine immutability?
options: A change in God’s mind prompted by prayer
A slow, gradual change too small to detect
A new description becoming true of something only because something else changed — as God becomes Creator by a change in the world, not in himself
A change that occurs only in abstract objects
quiz.explanation: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows. Likewise God’s being Creator involves real change only in the world, so God can be Creator without real change or composition.

quiz.q: An objector argues that since God causes things to exist at t1 and at t2, God must be acting at t1 and at t2, and so be in time. What is the best reply from chapter 6?
options: God acts only at the first moment of time
From ‘God causes X to exist at t1’ it does not follow that ‘at t1 God causes X’; God causes a whole temporal world in one timeless act, as an author conceives a whole story
Time is an illusion, so the problem does not arise
God is in time but unchanging
quiz.explanation: The inference confuses the time of the effect with a time of the cause’s action. Feser’s author analogy shows how a single act can produce a sequence. He does not deny the reality of time or place God in time.

quiz.q: Which analogy does Feser use to show that God’s causing and knowing all events is compatible with human free will?
options: A clockmaker winding a clock
A hypnotist directing a subject
A chess master predicting a novice’s moves
An author writing a novel in which a character freely commits a crime
quiz.explanation: The author is not a character inside the story interfering with others; the hypnotist would be exactly the wrong model, because he undermines freedom from within the story.

quiz.q: Why, on Feser’s view, does the principle of proportionate causality not imply that evil exists in God?
options: Because evil is an illusion
Because God is not the cause of everything
Because badness is a privation — an absence — rather than a positive feature that must be in the cause
Because evil is caused only by angels
quiz.explanation: The PPC concerns positive features of effects. Evil is real, but its reality is that of a lack, like blindness; making a world with evil is making good things while refraining from making others.

quiz.q: The concurrentist view of divine causality is a middle position between:
options: occasionalism and mere conservationism
pantheism and panentheism
deism and polytheism
nominalism and realism
quiz.explanation: Occasionalism denies creatures any real causal power; mere conservationism gives them power independent of God. Concurrence says creatures are real but secondary causes that act only with God’s concurrence.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say occasionalism is self-undermining for someone who accepts the proofs?
options: It contradicts the possibility of miracles
It makes God dependent on the world
By agere sequitur esse, things that truly do nothing would not truly exist — yet the proofs start from real changing, composite things, so occasionalism kicks away the ladder it climbed
It entails that God is material
quiz.explanation: Occasionalism implies only God truly exists, which contradicts both our knowledge that we exist (and are not God) and the starting points of the causal proofs. Feser’s image is climbing a ladder and then blasting it away.

quiz.q: What is Feser’s response to the thesis of ‘existential inertia’?
options: He accepts it for material things but not for souls
No composite, act-potency, essence-existence thing could tend to persist on its own, and its defenders never explain what would give it that feature
It is refuted by the second law of thermodynamics
It is true but irrelevant to the proofs
quiz.explanation: Existential inertia would let things exist without being conserved by God. Feser argues the proofs show no such thing could have this feature and that merely suggesting it ignores the arguments.

quiz.q: On the Thomistic account presented in chapter 6, a miracle is best described as:
options: an elevation of a nature beyond its own powers, or a suspension in which God refrains from conserving or concurring — not a violation of natural law
a violation of a law of nature
an event with no cause
an unusual natural event we cannot yet explain
quiz.explanation: Since laws describe the tendencies of natures, they are not ‘broken’. A resurrection adds to nature’s course; the unburnt young men in the furnace involve a subtraction. God cannot literally ‘intervene’ in his own continuous work.

quiz.q: Why does the ‘god of the gaps’ charge miss Feser’s arguments?
options: Because God is invoked only where science has already succeeded
Because Feser concedes that science will never progress
Because the proofs appeal to biological complexity
Because the proofs are strict demonstrations from starting points any empirical theory must presuppose, not probabilistic hypotheses filling a gap in current science
quiz.explanation: A gap argument allows that a non-divine explanation might be correct. These arguments claim none is possible in principle, and they start from change, composition, essence-existence and contingency — features of anything science could discover.

quiz.q: A student cites Krauss: ‘Physics shows a universe can arise from nothing.’ Which reply follows chapter 7?
options: Krauss’s physics is mathematically flawed
The universe did not arise at all but has always existed
Krauss’s ‘nothing’ — empty space with energy, or the laws of quantum physics — is not nothing, and laws cannot be ultimate explanations
Physics can never say anything about the history of the universe
quiz.explanation: Feser does not dispute Krauss’s physics; he points out that a quantum vacuum and laws are something, which Krauss himself concedes, and that laws presuppose what they govern.

quiz.q: Feser’s dilemma against scientism is that the thesis ‘only science yields genuine knowledge’ is either:
options: self-refuting (it is not itself a scientific claim) or trivial (if ‘science’ is broadened to include philosophy, in which case natural theology could qualify)
empirically confirmed or merely assumed
too narrow (excluding biology) or too broad (including astrology)
incompatible with quantum mechanics or with relativity
quiz.explanation: The scientistic claim cannot be established by scientific method, so it refutes itself; stretching ‘science’ to escape that makes the thesis vacuous and removes its force against natural theology.

quiz.q: Feser compares the argument ‘physics is predictively successful, so what physics reveals is probably all that is real’ to:
options: inferring from a metal detector’s success that only metallic things exist
a thermometer’s success at measuring heat
engineering’s success at building bridges
a map’s being smaller than its territory
quiz.explanation: A method that attends only to certain aspects of reality (the mathematically modellable) can be perfectly successful without those aspects being all there is. Feser also uses the drunk under the lamppost and the student who takes only easy classes.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think treating the most fundamental laws of nature as brute facts is incoherent?
options: Because laws of nature do not exist
Because brute facts violate the law of non-contradiction
Because physicists have already explained the fundamental laws
Because an unexplained foundation has nothing to impart, so every explanation resting on it becomes illusory — like a book on a shelf that stays up for no reason
quiz.explanation: A regress of laws is like a hierarchical series: higher laws explain only by borrowing from lower ones. Let go of the brackets in mid-air and nothing stays up. Feser also calls the move ad hoc and contrary to PSR.

quiz.q: Dawkins argues that a designer of the universe would be more complex than the universe and so need explanation. Feser’s central reply is that:
options: complexity is an illusion
the proofs agree complex things need causes, which is exactly why they conclude to an absolutely simple cause; the objection targets design arguments
God is only moderately complex
the universe is actually simple
quiz.explanation: The objection presupposes a probabilistic design argument from biological complexity. The five proofs are demonstrations, and their conclusion is divine simplicity; it is the atheist’s alternatives that are complex.

quiz.q: Why does Feser call the ‘one god further’ objection a category mistake?
options: Because Zeus and Thor might actually exist
Because atheists believe in no gods at all
Because it confuses polytheism with pantheism
Because classical theism’s God is not a member of a genus ‘gods’ but subsistent being itself — like treating triangularity as one more drawn triangle
quiz.explanation: Zeus-like gods are limited beings among beings; the God of the proofs is the source of all being and cannot belong to any genus without having parts. Feser also notes there are demonstrations for this God and none for Zeus.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think William Rowe’s evidential argument from evil (the burned fawn) poses no challenge to the book’s arguments?
options: Because animals do not really suffer

Because Rowe concludes only that God probably does not exist, and anyone with independent demonstrations of a good, omnipotent God has reason to believe a greater good is served, even if it is unknown
Because the fawn’s suffering is deserved
Because suffering is logically necessary for every good
quiz.explanation: Rowe concedes we cannot prove there is no greater good; so if the proofs succeed, we have reason to think there is one. To challenge the proofs, the evidential argument would first have to refute them.

quiz.q: According to W. Norris Clarke’s account, which Feser endorses, the ‘everything has a cause’ straw man arose mainly because:
options: Aquinas stated it in the First Way
Leibniz used it in his Monadology
Hume conflated the rationalist claim that everything has a sufficient reason with the claim that everything has an efficient cause distinct from itself
Aristotle held that God is self-caused
quiz.explanation: Descartes and Spinoza spoke loosely of God as ‘self-caused’, meaning self-explanatory. Hume read this as efficient causation, and the caricature passed through the Mills to Russell. No major defender used the premise.

quiz.q: A critic, following Kant, says the cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument. The best reply is that:
options: the ontological argument is sound after all

the necessity the proofs attribute to God is metaphysical — grounded in pure actuality, simplicity and the identity of essence and existence — not existence by definition; Aquinas rejected the ontological argument while defending cosmological ones
necessity is just a matter of linguistic convention
God exists contingently
quiz.explanation: Kant’s charge works only if ‘necessary being’ means ‘exists by definition’. Grayling’s dilemma between that and merely conditional necessity is a false one. The third option is Findlay’s objection, which chapter 6 rejects.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason, from the book, that the universe cannot be the necessary being?
options: The universe is too large to be necessary
The universe began with the Big Bang
The universe is not conscious
The universe changes, has parts and is contingent, while a necessary being must be purely actual, simple and subsistent existence itself
quiz.explanation: The reason is principled and independent of cosmology. The second option relies on a beginning the proofs never assume; the third would at best show an impersonal necessary being.

quiz.q: You are talking with a mathematician who is a convinced Platonist about numbers. Which proof is the most natural entry point?
options: The Augustinian proof
The Aristotelian proof, since mathematicians like physics
The rationalist proof, since it begins with PSR
The Thomistic proof, since numbers have essences
quiz.explanation: A Platonist already accepts realism about abstract objects — the first half of the Augustinian proof. The work is showing that abstract objects can exist only in a mind, and necessary ones only in a necessary mind.

quiz.q: What does Feser mean by calling the arguments ‘demonstrations’?
options: That they are experimentally testable
That they convince every rational hearer immediately
That their conclusions are highly probable
That their conclusions follow necessarily from premises that are certain and cannot be overturned by further empirical inquiry
quiz.explanation: A demonstration is a strict deduction, not a probabilistic or best-explanation inference. Feser explicitly denies that a demonstration must convince everyone immediately; controversy is not refutation.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that every linear causal series presupposes hierarchical ones?
options: Because things can change only if they exist, and each thing’s existence at every moment requires a concurrent series of actualizers
Because linear series cannot be infinite
Because hierarchical series always occur earlier in time
Because Aristotle’s physics required celestial movers
quiz.explanation: The coffee cannot cool unless it exists, and its existence here and now depends on a hierarchy of actualizers. Feser allows linear series to be infinite, and hierarchical series are not defined by temporal priority.

quiz.q: In the capstone’s convergence argument, which step secures that the Augustinian conclusion refers to the same being as the conclusions of the four causal proofs?
options: The premise that a necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual (step 18)
The principle of proportionate causality (step 21)
The premise that the things of experience are composite (step 3)
The final premise that such a being is what is meant by God (step 25)
quiz.explanation: Once the necessary intellect is shown to be purely actual, the biconditionals and the uniqueness argument apply to it. The PPC is used to infer intellect in the other proofs, not to identify the Augustinian conclusion with them.

quiz.q: What would Feser reply to someone who says: ‘Kant showed that causal principles apply only within possible experience, so they can’t take us to an unobservable first cause’?
options: That Kant was a theist and did not mean this seriously

That we affirm causes not because things are experienced but because they are potential until actualized — a general truth, as Euclidean geometry learned from inked diagrams applies to figures of any color
That the first cause is in fact observable through laboratory effects
That the objection is correct but applies only to the rationalist proof
quiz.explanation: Chapter 1: the principle is grounded in the nature of potentiality, which is completely general; confining it to experienced things is like confining geometry to black-ink figures.

quiz.q: Which distinction does the objection ‘Physics says the desk is a cloud of particles, so it doesn’t really hold up the cup’ ignore?
options: The distinction between essence and existence
The distinction between contingent and necessary being
The distinction between the mechanism by which something happens and whether it happens — the particle story describes how the desk holds up the cup
The distinction between univocal and equivocal terms
quiz.explanation: Eddington’s two tables are not competitors; physics supplies the mechanism. And the examples only introduce act/potency and hierarchical series, which apply at any level of description (chapter 1).

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that Parmenides’ argument against the reality of change is self-refuting?
options: Because Parmenides lived before Aristotle
Because the senses cannot err about change
Because Parmenides admitted that the heavens change
Because reasoning through the argument from premises to conclusion is itself a change in the mind
quiz.explanation: Even if the senses deceived us (Descartes’ dream), the succession of thoughts is change. Feser’s second, deeper reply is Aristotle’s: a potential is not nothing, so change is not something from nothing.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly matches one of Feser’s opening examples in chapter 1 to its kind of change?
options: A swatted fly dying — substantial change
A puddle growing — qualitative change
A leaf falling — quantitative change
Coffee cooling — change of place
quiz.explanation: A living thing giving way to dead matter is substantial change. The puddle is quantitative, the leaf is local (change of place), and the coffee is qualitative.

quiz.q: A critic says: ‘There’s always a tiny time lag between the stick moving and the stone moving, so hierarchical series don’t exist.’ Which reply fits chapter 1?
options: Relativity shows time lags are illusions
Simultaneous does not mean instantaneous — the immediate cause and effect are one event, however long it lasts; and what defines a hierarchical series is derived power, not simultaneity
Feser concedes the point and relies on linear series instead
The stick and stone are really one object
quiz.explanation: Following Norris Clarke and Mumford and Anjum, pushing a chair takes time, but there is no time between the pushing and the being-pushed. And the argument can rest on the sheer existence of a thing at an instant.

quiz.q: In chapter 2, how does Feser (following William Vallicella) argue that the One is a mind?
options: Only minds can be simple, since matter always has parts
The One is the source of all order, which implies a designer

Everything is a mind, a mental content, a material thing or an abstract object; the One cannot be abstract (causally inert), material (composite) or a mental content (dependent), so it is a mind or most like one
Plotinus identified the One with intellect, and Feser follows him
quiz.explanation: It is an argument by elimination. The last option is a tempting error: Plotinus actually placed intellect in a second divine reality after the One, and Feser notes he need not follow Plotinus on that detail.

quiz.q: Why does Feser appeal to wave-particle duality in chapter 2?
options: To show that God is made of energy
To show that physics has proved divine simplicity
To argue that quantum mechanics requires a divine observer
To show it is unsurprising if concepts stretched to the most fundamental level of reality yield conclusions hard to grasp, such as a simple being with many attributes
quiz.explanation: Physics stretches everyday concepts to describe remote phenomena and gets strange results we still have reason to accept; natural theology stretches them further still, so difficulty is to be expected.

quiz.q: What is the ‘words are universals too’ problem for nominalism?
options: The nominalist says there are only general words, but a word like ‘red’ is itself one type with many tokens — a universal
Words change meaning over time, so they cannot be universal
Words exist only in minds, which supports conceptualism
Different languages use different words for the same thing
quiz.explanation: If you, I and Socrates all utter the same word, we have a one-over-many; saying we utter only resembling words is absurd, makes communication impossible, and restarts Russell’s resemblance regress.

quiz.q: A relativist says logic and mathematics are merely products of evolution and culture, with no objective validity. What is Feser’s chief reply in chapter 3?
options: Evolution is false
Any account of how evolution or culture shaped our minds must itself use universals, scientific principles and logic, so the view undermines itself
Logic is a matter of convention, but mathematics is not
Different cultures in fact share the same logic
quiz.explanation: This is the incoherence of psychologism. Even Kant’s milder version faces a dilemma: to claim knowledge of how our minds necessarily work is to claim the objective knowledge the view denies.

quiz.q: Brian Leftow argues that if God’s nature grounds the necessity of ‘water = H₂O’, God’s existence would depend on facts about water. How does Feser respond?
options: He denies that water is necessarily H₂O
He concedes the point but says it is harmless
By parity: arithmetic entails necessary truths about rocks without depending on mineralogy; and there is no coherent scenario in which a necessary truth fails to be necessary
He argues that God’s will, not his nature, grounds such truths
quiz.explanation: The ‘dependence’ is only entailment of necessary truths, not vulnerability to hydrology. The last option is Leftow’s own voluntarism, which Feser says begs the question against deity theories.

quiz.q: According to Greg Welty’s ‘relevance’ condition, why is a Platonic possible world a poor truthmaker for ‘Socrates could have been a carpenter’?
options: Because Platonic worlds are too numerous to be real
Because Socrates never really existed
Because possible worlds are material objects
