Because, like a drawing of Socrates hammering nails, a third-realm object could represent the possibility without making it true; an idea in an omnipotent creator’s mind could make it true
quiz.explanation: Scholastic realism ties possibilities to a divine intellect, will and power able to create what it conceives, giving them a relevance to the actual world that a third realm lacks.

quiz.q: What is the point of Barry Miller’s formula ‘A is being caused to G by B inasmuch as B is being caused to G by …’ in chapter 4?
options: The sentence describing such a series can only be completed by naming a first member, so a hierarchical regress must terminate
It shows that causal series are always finite in time
It proves that God is the only cause of anything
It shows that causation is a merely linguistic relation
quiz.explanation: However many ‘inasmuch as’ clauses you add, the sentence stays incomplete until a term naming a first member is supplied; and only subsistent existence can nonarbitrarily be that member.

quiz.q: A student claims that all essences are merely conventional labels. Which argument (drawing on Crawford Elder) most directly answers him?
options: Physics has already discovered the essence of every natural kind
If all essences were mind-dependent, the mind’s own essence would be too, making the mind both prior and posterior to itself, which is incoherent
Conventional essences cannot be expressed in language
Aristotle demonstrated that essences exist in the Physics
quiz.explanation: Mind-dependence presupposes a mind that is prior to what depends on it. The last option is a trap: Aristotle thought it absurd to try to prove things have natures, because it is more obvious than any argument.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say Anthony Kenny’s critique of the real distinction begs the question?
options: Because Kenny relies on Aquinas’ own texts
Because Kenny denies that God exists
Because it assumes that a real distinction requires separability and that quantifier-style ‘specific existence’ is the only respectable notion of existence — assumptions the Thomist rejects
Because Kenny confuses essence with accident
quiz.explanation: Following Gyula Klima and John Knasas, Feser argues that Fido’s essence and individual existence can be really distinct though inseparable, and that ‘there is an x’ leaves open what makes something fall under a concept.

quiz.q: What is Michael Della Rocca’s argument, as used in chapter 5?
options: PSR can be deduced from the laws of logic alone
Quantum mechanics confirms PSR
Brute facts are logically impossible
Critics who accept explicability arguments elsewhere have no non-question-begging way to reject them for the existence of things — so accepting any commits one to PSR
quiz.explanation: Rejecting all explicability arguments would gut much of science and philosophy; accepting some but not those about existence looks arbitrary. Feser pushes further: even rejecting all of them undermines argument itself.

quiz.q: A friend objects: ‘Take the conjunction of all true contingent propositions. A necessary truth can’t explain it and a contingent one would be part of it — so PSR fails.’ Which reply fits Feser?
options: On Scholastic realism, propositions are not extra objects needing explanation once concrete things and the minds that entertain them are explained; and explanation need not be logical entailment
The conjunction of all contingent truths is itself necessary
PSR applies only to physical objects, so propositions are exempt by stipulation
Such a conjunction would be infinitely long and so cannot exist
quiz.explanation: The objection presupposes Platonism about propositions and an entailment model of explanation that even scientific explanation does not meet (planetary orbits and gravity).

quiz.q: Why does Feser hold that the principle of proportionate causality is not trivial, even though it allows effects to be in causes ‘virtually’ or ‘eminently’?
options: Because it can be verified by laboratory measurement
Because explanations in terms of potentialities are minimally but genuinely informative, and naturalists like Paul Churchland rely on the principle in their own arguments
Because it applies only to God
Because it entails determinism
quiz.explanation: Churchland argues that material causes can yield only material effects, assuming the PPC; the dualist accepts the same principle and reverses the inference. So both sides treat it as substantive.

quiz.q: What does Feser’s argument for the analogy of being turn on?
options: That God and creatures are exactly alike in being
That ‘being’ is a genus with species
That potentiality is real yet really distinct from actuality, so it must have being neither univocally nor equivocally but analogically
That all language about God is metaphorical
quiz.explanation: Denying potency’s reality (Parmenides) or actuality’s (Heraclitus) is incoherent; univocal being would collapse the distinction and equivocal being would make potency unreal. ‘Being’ is not a genus, since nothing outside being could differentiate it.

quiz.q: An objector says: ‘If God is timeless, Socrates’ existence and Obama’s existence are both simultaneous with God’s eternity, hence with each other — absurd.’ What is Feser’s reply?
options: Socrates and Obama are indeed simultaneous from God’s point of view
God exists at every time rather than outside time
The relation of simultaneity is not transitive
The objection treats eternity as a point in time; a timeless being is not simultaneous with any time at all
quiz.explanation: Only a point in time could be simultaneous with points in time. God causes, from outside time, a world in which Socrates exists in 469 B.C. and Obama in A.D. 1961.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is God not obliged to create the best possible world?
options: Because there is no best possible world — for any world, a better one is possible — and God wrongs no one by not creating
Because the actual world is the best possible world
Because God lacks the power to create a better world
Because goodness is simply whatever God commands
quiz.explanation: A world with x forests can always be bettered by x + 1; and nonexistent things cannot be harmed. God’s perfection follows from what he is, not from what he makes, like a perfect diamond whether or not it cuts glass.

quiz.q: A believer asks why God, being sexless, is traditionally called ‘he’. What does Feser’s appendix to chapter 6 say?
options: That God is in fact male
That God has intellect and will, so ‘it’ is inappropriate, and his relation to the world — active, unchanging, independent and distinct — resembles a father’s role more than a mother’s
That the usage is purely conventional and ‘she’ would be equally apt
That only Scripture can settle the matter
quiz.explanation: Feser argues maternal imagery would suggest change in God or continuity with the world (pantheism or panentheism), whereas paternal language fits pure actuality, independence and distinctness.

quiz.q: According to Feser, what is the role of miracles relative to natural theology?
options: They are the primary evidence for God’s existence
They show that the natural order is defective and needs repair
They are the rational bridge to revealed theology — the sign that a purported revelation really comes from God
They are violations of natural laws that prove God stronger than nature
quiz.explanation: Feser says the ordinary course of nature, not miracles, is the most direct evidence of God as First Cause; miracles serve to authenticate revelation. They are not violations or repairs.

quiz.q: Someone argues: ‘So many intelligent people reject these arguments that they can’t be demonstrations.’ Which of Feser’s points most directly exposes the double standard?
options: Most philosophers are atheists, so their opinion is biased
Genuine demonstrations must be a priori
Hume refuted such arguments once and for all
Arguments for materialism or against free will are not declared failures just because they have critics; a demonstration can be controversial and still sound
quiz.explanation: Feser (citing Hilary Putnam) notes that no philosophical argument meets the standard of convincing every rational hearer. Controversy shows the need for defense, not failure.

shortAnswer.q: Describe the two-stage structure shared by Feser’s five proofs and explain why it undercuts the objection that ‘even if there is a first cause, it need not be God’.
shortAnswer.model:
Each proof’s **Stage 1** argues from an evident starting point to something fitting a precise description: a purely actual actualizer (ch. 1), an absolutely simple cause (ch. 2), a necessarily existing intellect (ch. 3), subsistent existence itself (ch. 4), a necessary being (ch. 5). **Stage 2** shows that whatever fits that description must have the divine attributes. For example, what is purely actual cannot change, so it is immutable and hence outside time; being immutable and eternal, it cannot be material; since imperfection and badness are failures to actualize potential, it is perfect and fully good; nothing could distinguish two purely actual beings, so it is unique; all power derives from it, so it is omnipotent; and by the principle of proportionate causality the forms of all possible things must exist in it in the abstract way they exist in an intellect, so it is intelligent and omniscient.

The objection assumes Stage 1 yields a bare ‘cause’ about which nothing further can be said. But Stage 1 yields a cause of a very specific kind, and the attributes are deduced from that kind, not added by faith. So the objector must attack a specific Stage 2 inference, not merely assert a ‘gap’. Chapter 6 develops the attributes further, and chapter 7 notes that defenders of cosmological arguments have always argued for the attributes at length (Aquinas, Clarke).
rubric: Identifies the distinctive Stage 1 description for at least three proofs
Explains that Stage 2 deduces attributes from that description
Gives at least three concrete attribute derivations (e.g., immutability, uniqueness, intellect via PPC)
Explains why the objection therefore misfires and where the burden now lies

shortAnswer.q: Compare and contrast the Aristotelian and Thomistic proofs. What does each take as its starting point, and why does Feser think they arrive at the same cause?
shortAnswer.model:
The **Aristotelian** proof starts from change, analyzed as the actualization of potential, and then from the fact that a changing thing’s very existence at each moment involves the concurrent actualization of potentials (the water in the coffee existing as water). The regress of actualizers is hierarchical and ends in a purely actual actualizer.

The **Thomistic** proof starts from the real distinction between essence and existence in everything we experience, argued from knowledge (we can know what a lion is without knowing whether lions exist), from contingency, and from the fact that there can be only one thing whose essence is existence. A thing whose existence is distinct from its essence cannot give itself existence, so it must receive it from another at every moment; the hierarchical regress ends in subsistent existence itself.

Both concern dependence here and now rather than a temporal beginning, and both use the hierarchical-series argument. They converge because essence and existence relate as potency and act: a purely actual being cannot have an essence distinct from its existence, and subsistent existence cannot depend on any actualization. Since there can only be one of either, they are the same cause. The Thomistic proof arguably goes deeper, explaining *why* things have a potency for existence in the first place.
rubric: States each proof’s starting point accurately
Notes the shared hierarchical, here-and-now structure
Explains the potency/act relation between essence and existence
Uses uniqueness to conclude identity
Notes at least one difference in depth or emphasis

shortAnswer.q: The Neo-Platonic proof reasons from composition and the rationalist proof from contingency. How are these starting points related, according to Feser?
shortAnswer.model:
The **Neo-Platonic** proof argues that anything composite depends at every moment on something that combines its parts, since no whole can compose itself; the hierarchical regress ends in an absolutely simple One. The **rationalist** proof argues from PSR: contingent things must be explained by something else, and no contingent thing or series of them can explain why contingent things exist or persist, so there must be a necessary being.

Feser links them explicitly. In chapter 5 he says the deeper reason why things are contingent — why they need explanation outside themselves — is that they are mixtures of actuality and potentiality, are composed of parts, and have essences distinct from their existence; and the deeper reason why such things need causes is that otherwise they would be unintelligible, contrary to PSR. In chapter 6 he shows that something is necessary if and only if it is simple (and purely actual, and subsistent existence). So composition is one of the roots of contingency, and the One and the necessary being coincide. The proofs complement one another: the Neo-Platonic proof supplies a metaphysical reason for contingency, while the rationalist proof supplies the principle (intelligibility) that underwrites the demand for a cause of composition.
rubric: Summarizes both proofs accurately
Cites Feser’s claim that composition (and act/potency, essence/existence) underlies contingency
Cites the biconditional between simplicity and necessity
Explains how each proof supports the other

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct the Augustinian proof in about ten steps and identify the premise you think a critic is most likely to attack. How would Feser defend it?
shortAnswer.model:
1. There are three accounts of abstract objects: realism, nominalism, conceptualism.
2. Strong arguments support realism (one over many, geometry, mathematics, propositions, science, possible worlds).
3. Nominalism fails (resemblance regress; words are universals).
4. Conceptualism fails (shared concepts and communication; psychologism refutes itself).
5. So realism is true, in one of three forms: Platonic, Aristotelian, Scholastic.
6. Platonic realism fails: third-realm objects would be causally inert and unknowable, and a Form would have to be both universal and individual.
7. Aristotelian realism alone fails: it cannot ground necessary truths and pure possibilities that would hold without any world or human mind.
8. So Scholastic realism is true: abstract objects exist in at least one necessarily existing intellect.
9. Since abstract objects form an interlocking system, one necessary intellect grasps them all.
10. A necessary intellect is purely actual, hence unique, fully omniscient, omnipotent, good, immutable, immaterial, eternal — God.

The most attacked premise is usually step 6 (a sophisticated Platonist is comfortable with abstract objects existing necessarily in no mind). Feser’s defense: causally inert objects could explain neither why things instantiate them nor how we know them; ‘animality itself’ would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which no individual can be; Platonism makes trees and humans mere imitations; and (with Welty) third-realm possibilities are no better truthmakers than a drawing. Only an intellect can be the home of what is abstract, since abstraction is an intellectual activity.
rubric: Presents a logically ordered reconstruction covering realism, the elimination of rivals, and Scholastic realism
Includes the interlocking-system and pure-actuality steps
Identifies a plausible target premise
Gives Feser’s actual defense of that premise with at least two specific arguments

shortAnswer.q: Explain, step by step, why Feser holds that the five proofs arrive at one and the same God rather than five different ultimate realities.
shortAnswer.model:
The argument (chapter 6, ‘Unity’, anticipated in each Stage 2) rests on two-way entailments. First, anything with parts is a mixture of act and potency, since parts only potentially compose a whole until combined; and anything with potency is composite, having an actual and a potential constituent. So **purely actual ⇔ simple**, uniting the Unmoved Mover and the One. Second, essence relates to existence as potency to act, so a purely actual being cannot have an essence distinct from existence; and subsistent existence cannot depend on actualization without becoming derivative. So **purely actual ⇔ subsistent existence**, uniting chapter 4 with chapters 1 and 2. Third, contingency means depending on actualized potency, combined parts or existence added to essence; so **necessary ⇔ purely actual, simple, subsistent**, uniting chapter 5. Fourth, a necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual (chapter 3). Finally, there can be only one such being, since any plurality needs a differentiator — which would be a part or a potency.

So the five descriptions have one referent, as ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ both name Venus. Feser’s conclusion: the five proofs are not proofs of distinct deities but distinct paths to one God.
rubric: States the act/simplicity biconditional with its justification
States the act/subsistent-existence biconditional
Links necessity to the other three
Links the necessary intellect via pure actuality
Uses the uniqueness argument to conclude identity

shortAnswer.q: Explain the distinction between linear and hierarchical causal series and show how it answers both the ‘the universe may have no beginning’ objection and the ‘an infinite regress explains everything’ objection.
shortAnswer.model:
In a **linear** (per accidens) series, members are ordered through time and each has causal power of its own: the air conditioner keeps cooling after you leave; a son can beget a child after his father dies. In a **hierarchical** (per se) series, every member except the first has power only derivatively, here and now: the cup is held up by the desk only as long as the floor holds the desk, like a stone moved by a stick moved by a hand. Such a series needs a first member in the sense of an underived source; even an infinitely long brush handle cannot move itself.

Against the **no-beginning** objection: Feser grants that linear series — even the history of the universe or a multiverse — might have no beginning. The proofs concern the hierarchical dependence of things’ existence at each moment, which a beginningless past does nothing to remove. Against the **infinite-regress** objection (Hume): in a linear series, explaining each member by the previous one may be adequate, but in a hierarchical series every member only passes on borrowed power, so an infinite regress explains nothing — infinite mirrors still need a face, infinite IOUs never become money. Barry Miller adds that the explanatory sentence can only be completed by naming a first member.
rubric: Defines both kinds of series with an example of each
Explains ‘first’ as underived and uses an image (brush, mirrors, IOUs)
Applies the distinction to the no-beginning objection
Applies it to the infinite-regress objection

shortAnswer.q: Show how each of the five proofs answers ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
shortAnswer.model:
The objection targets a premise none of the proofs uses. In each case the need for a cause is tied to a specific feature that God lacks:

- **Aristotelian:** what goes from potential to actual needs an actualizer; what is purely actual has no potential to actualize, so it neither needs nor could have a cause.
- **Neo-Platonic:** what is composite needs something to combine its parts; the One has no parts.
- **Thomistic:** what has an essence distinct from its existence needs existence imparted; subsistent existence itself has nothing to receive.
- **Rationalist:** contingent things need an explanation in another; the necessary being is explained by its own nature, so PSR applies to God without exception.
- **Augustinian:** it is not a causal argument, so the question does not even arise.

Thus ‘What caused God?’ amounts to asking what actualized the potentials of that which has none, or combined the parts of what has none. Chapter 7 adds that the ‘everything has a cause’ version is a straw man descending from Hume’s conflation of cause and sufficient reason, and that the exemption is principled rather than ad hoc — it was the tradition’s claim from the start.
rubric: Gives the correct principle for each causal proof
Identifies the feature God lacks in each case
Notes the rationalist proof makes no exception and the Augustinian proof is non-causal
Mentions the straw-man history or the non-ad-hoc character of the principle

shortAnswer.q: Evaluate the charge that first-cause arguments commit the fallacy of composition. Consider both the Thomistic and the rationalist proofs.
shortAnswer.model:
The charge: from ‘each part needs a cause’ it does not follow that ‘the whole needs a cause’, just as bricks weighing a pound do not make a one-pound wall.

**Thomistic proof:** it does not reason from parts to whole at all. It starts from any single thing whose essence is distinct from its existence — Fido — and argues that this thing needs a cause of its existence here and now. That God causes the whole universe is a consequence (since subsistent existence is unique and everything else depends on it), not a premise. Feser adds that the space-time universe, being made of such things and itself having essence distinct from existence, would need a cause anyway.

**Rationalist proof:** one version does ask why the whole series of contingent things exists. But part-to-whole reasoning is not always fallacious (Lego blocks all red make a red wall). Contingency behaves like color: a collection of contingent things is if anything doubly contingent. And the second version of the proof avoids the issue by asking why any single contingent thing persists now. Finally, chapter 7 argues the critic commits the fallacy: from each stick’s motion being explained by the next, it does not follow that the motion of the series is explained (sticks, mirrors, Leibniz’s books). The charge fails.
rubric: States the objection fairly
Explains that the Thomistic proof starts from one thing and treats the universe as conclusion
Explains why contingency transfers to wholes (Lego/color vs. weight)
Notes the rationalist proof’s alternative single-thing route
Mentions that the critic arguably commits the fallacy himself

shortAnswer.q: A science-educated friend says: ‘Quantum mechanics and relativity have shown that causation and change aren’t real features of the world, so the first proof collapses.’ Write Feser’s response.
shortAnswer.model:
First, physics describes nature mathematically and by method leaves out whatever cannot be quantified — including potentiality and causation. An absence in the representation is not a representation of absence, as colorlessness in a line drawing does not show the scene is colorless; the later Russell admitted physics gives abstract structure, not the intrinsic nature of what changes.

On **quantum mechanics**: causation does not require determinism, only intelligibility. A Pb-210 atom decays with a certain probability because of its nature (formal cause), was generated by something (efficient cause), and exists now only because something keeps it in existence. Quantum events occur only given quantum laws and a universe that follows them, which themselves need explaining. Heisenberg even likened quantum states to Aristotle’s *potentia*.

On **relativity’s block universe**: the evidence for any physical theory comes through experiences that succeed one another — prediction, then observation — so denying all change is incoherent (Healey). And even a changeless block would need a cause of its being actual rather than some other world.

Finally, the proofs concern what any physical theory presupposes, not rival physics; physics affects how we apply act and potency, not whether we must.
rubric: Makes the ‘mathematical abstraction / absence in representation’ point
Distinguishes indeterminism from uncaused-ness with an example
Answers the block-universe objection (experience of change; existence of the block)
Notes that the proofs concern presuppositions of any physical theory

shortAnswer.q: What is divine simplicity, why does Feser consider it nonnegotiable, and how does he answer Plantinga’s claim that it makes God a property?
shortAnswer.model:
Divine simplicity is the doctrine that God has no parts of any kind — no matter and form, no genus and specific difference, no essence distinct from existence, no really distinct attributes. His power, knowledge and goodness are one reality described in different ways.

It is nonnegotiable because whatever is composite needs a cause of its composition and could in principle have rivals; a non-simple God would be a very powerful creature, a ‘superangel’, not the ultimate cause. The causal proofs are, as proofs of a first cause, proofs of a simple cause; deny simplicity and you deny what they reach. It has been affirmed by pagans, Jews, Muslims and Christians, including councils and Protestant reformers.

Plantinga argues that if God is identical with each of his properties, all properties are identical and God is a property, an abstract object. Feser replies that this reads the doctrine through Plantinga’s own assumptions: a broad notion of ‘property’ covering any predicate, a Platonist view of properties as abstract objects, and univocal predication. Classical theists distinguish essence, properties, accidents and relations as constituents of things, predicate analogically (God’s power and knowledge differ in sense but share one referent), and never say God is a property. Morris’s necessary-vs-contingent-properties worry is answered by treating contingent truths like ‘God created this world’ as Cambridge properties.
rubric: Defines simplicity accurately
Explains why it is essential to God’s ultimacy and uniqueness
States Plantinga’s objection
Identifies the three assumptions Feser says Plantinga imports
Mentions analogy and/or Cambridge properties in the reply

shortAnswer.q: How can an immutable, timeless God create, know and love the world, and how does divine causality leave room for human freedom?
shortAnswer.model:
Feser’s strategy is to diagnose a **fallacy of accident**: in our experience agents change as they act, but change is not essential to acting; what is essential is producing an effect. So God can cause without being changed. His becoming Creator is a **Cambridge change**, a real change only in the world. As timeless, he does not cause at t1 and then again at t2; he causes a whole temporal world in one act, as an author conceives a whole story at once.

God **knows** the world not by observing it but by knowing himself as its cause, as an author knows his story by knowing his plan; this is why he cannot be mistaken and why his knowledge requires no change. He **loves** because love is essentially willing the good of another, not undergoing emotion, and in creating things he wills their good.

On **freedom**: knowing an act does not cause it, even with certainty. And God’s causality is like an author’s relation to a character who freely commits a crime in the novel — not like a hypnotist inside the story. By concurrence, creatures are real secondary causes; like a child whose hand is guided by a parent learning to write, our free choice makes a real contribution though nothing occurs without God. Feser admits these matters are hard to grasp positively, as expected at the ultimate level of reality.
rubric: Explains the fallacy of accident and Cambridge change
Uses the author analogy for eternity and/or knowledge
Defines love as willing the good
Addresses foreknowledge and causal determination separately
Mentions concurrence or the hypnotist/author contrast

shortAnswer.q: Summarize Feser’s response to the problem of evil. Distinguish his ‘defense’ from a ‘theodicy’ and explain why the evidential argument does not threaten the book’s proofs.
shortAnswer.model:
A **defense** shows that God and evil are logically consistent; a **theodicy** tries to explain why God permits the evils that exist. Feser offers a defense.

Against Mackie’s **logical** argument (an omnipotent God could and a good God would eliminate all evil): omnipotence does not include doing contradictions, and a good being need not eliminate an evil if that would eliminate a good logically requiring it. Even granting Mackie that free creatures could always choose rightly, some goods — forgiveness and mercy (requiring wrongdoing), courage (requiring danger), compassion (requiring suffering), sacrifice — cannot exist without evil. Mackie later conceded the logical argument fails. Chapter 6 adds that evil is privation, so God does not ‘make’ it as a positive thing.

Against Rowe’s **evidential** argument (some suffering, like the fawn’s, is probably pointless): Rowe admits there might be a greater good we cannot see. Anyone with independent demonstrations of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God has reason to believe there is such a good. To challenge the proofs, the evidential argument would first have to refute them. Our ignorance is expected: if there is an afterlife, which is possible, its goods could outweigh earthly evils, and we are like children who cannot yet understand the point of hardships.
rubric: Defines defense vs. theodicy
Answers the logical problem with goods that logically require evils
Mentions privation and/or Mackie’s later concession
Explains why independent proofs defeat the evidential argument
Mentions the afterlife/child analogy as support for expected ignorance

shortAnswer.q: What do the five proofs NOT establish, and how does Feser relate natural theology to revealed religion?
shortAnswer.model:
The proofs establish that there exists one simple, purely actual, necessary, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good cause of all things, which conserves and concurs with everything. They do **not** establish that God sent prophets, inspired a scripture, is a Trinity, became incarnate, or any other doctrine of a particular religion. Nor do they show the universe began, rest on ‘everything has a cause’, or treat God as a being among beings.

Feser regards this as a strength, not a weakness: if the proofs succeed, atheism is false, and the remaining question — which kind of theism is true — is the real debate, among Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus and philosophical theists. Chapter 6 explains how that debate could proceed. A miracle, understood not as a violation of natural law but as an elevation or suspension of nature by its first cause, could only come from God, so miracles would be the rational ‘seal’ on a purported revelation — the bridge from natural to revealed theology. Faith, on this view, is belief on God’s authority where there is evidence that God has spoken, not belief without evidence. Natural theology also constrains religions: any that deny God’s unity, distinctness from the world, intellect and will, immateriality or unlimited power are thereby shown false.
rubric: Lists what the proofs do establish and at least two things they do not
States that the real debate is among theists
Explains miracles as the bridge to revelation
Mentions faith as grounded in reason and/or natural theology’s constraint on religions

shortAnswer.q: Present Feser’s case against scientism and explain why it matters for natural theology.
shortAnswer.model:
Scientism holds that science is the only genuine source of knowledge. Feser raises four problems. (1) It is **self-refuting or trivial**: the claim is not itself established by science (science presupposes an external world, regularities and reliable faculties, which only philosophy can defend); if ‘science’ is broadened to include philosophy, the thesis becomes empty — and natural theology could then count as science. (2) Science cannot give a **complete description** of reality: physics studies only what can be quantified, as aircraft engineers consider passengers only as weights; as Russell admitted, it gives structure, not intrinsic nature, and structure implies something that has it. (3) **Laws cannot provide ultimate explanation** on any view of what laws are — regularities (describe rather than explain), Platonic entities (why these?), divine decrees (theological), or tendencies of natures (presuppose the things). (4) The **argument from success** is a non sequitur: metal detectors’ success does not show only metal exists; the drunk under the lamppost. The ‘science or mere conceptual analysis’ dichotomy is a version of Hume’s fork, which refutes itself; logic and mathematics fit neither prong.

This matters because scientism is usually a way of dismissing natural theology unheard. Once it fails, the arguments must be answered on their merits.
rubric: States the self-refuting/trivial dilemma
Explains the abstraction/incompleteness point
Explains why laws cannot be ultimate explanations
Explains the metal-detector (or similar) non sequitur
Connects the critique to the evaluation of natural theology

shortAnswer.q: Why must the first actualizer of chapter 1 be unmovable (purely actual), not merely unmoved? Include Feser’s response to the claim that every actualizer must itself change.
shortAnswer.model:
The regress chapter 1 is concerned with is a regress of actualizers of the **existence** of things. The first member is first because it can actualize others’ existence without its own being actualized. Suppose it had some potential needing actualization. If something else actualized it, that something would be the true first actualizer. If a purely actual part of it did, that part would be the true first actualizer and the potential ‘part’ merely its first effect. If a mixed part did, we would need something to actualize that part, restarting the regress. So a genuine first actualizer must be purely actual — unmovable, not merely unmoved — and so has all the attributes that follow from pure actuality.

To the objection that anything which actualizes must itself change, Feser gives three replies. It begs the question, since the argument purports to show a purely actual actualizer exists. It commits a **fallacy of accident**: that actualizers in our experience change as they act is a contingent correlation, like every U.S. president so far having been under seven feet tall. And there is nothing self-contradictory in the idea, unlike an ‘immortal mortal’; our actualizers change while acting precisely because they are limited mixtures of act and potency (my arm must move to move the stick), and pure actuality lacks those limits.
rubric: Explains that the regress concerns actualizers of existence
Runs the trilemma (external actualizer / purely actual part / mixed part)
Concludes that the first actualizer must be purely actual
Identifies the fallacy of accident with an example
Notes the question-begging charge or the non-contradiction point

shortAnswer.q: Summarize chapter 6’s account of conservation and concurrence, and explain why it rules out existential inertia, pantheism, panentheism, occasionalism and deism.
shortAnswer.model:
The causal proofs show that nothing other than God could exist for an instant unless God were keeping it in being — **conservation**: creation is ongoing. This rules out **existential inertia**, since composite, act-potency, essence-existence things cannot tend to exist of themselves, and its advocates never say what would give them that feature. Because things are composite, changing and contingent while God is simple, immutable and necessary, they are distinct from God: this excludes **pantheism** (God is the world) and **panentheism** (God is affected or changed by the world).

Add *agere sequitur esse* and we get **concurrence**. **Occasionalism** says only God acts; but what truly does nothing does not truly exist, so occasionalism implies only God exists — false, since I exist and am not God (I change, err, lack power) — and it undermines the proofs’ starting points, like climbing a ladder and blasting it away. **Mere conservationism** says creatures act independently once conserved; but what cannot exist independently cannot act independently, and the view slides toward **deism**. So creatures are true but secondary causes: the chalk colors the square while the hand produces it; the moon shines with borrowed sunlight; a child’s guided hand really cooperates in writing a letter.
rubric: Defines conservation and connects it to the causal proofs
Explains the rejection of existential inertia
Explains why God is distinct from the world (against pantheism/panentheism)
Explains the arguments against occasionalism and mere conservationism
Illustrates concurrence with an example

shortAnswer.q: Lay out Feser’s case for the principle of sufficient reason and explain why he thinks denying it is self-undermining.
shortAnswer.model:
Feser gives several lines. **Inductively**, PSR is as well supported as any generalization: we find explanations when we look, and when we don’t we can usually explain why (the careful murderer). A world without PSR would teem with inexplicable events, and the intelligibility that makes science and common sense succeed would be a miracle.

But PSR is more certain than an empirical hypothesis; it is defended indirectly by *reductio*. Following **Pruss and Koons**, if PSR is false there might be no connection between our perceptions and the world, and we could not even say a disconnect is improbable. Pushing further, we could have no reason to think our beliefs are caused by the reasons that justify them rather than by nothing; this applies to any grounds for doubting PSR itself — so denying PSR undercuts the denial. **Explanations ending in brute facts** are illusory: a book on a shelf that stays up for no reason is not explained, and a regress of laws resting on a brute law explains nothing. Finally, **Della Rocca**: critics use explicability arguments throughout science and philosophy and have no principled, non-question-begging way to exempt the existence of things; abandoning all such arguments would abandon argumentation. So the burden falls on the critic to show how PSR can coherently be rejected.
rubric: Gives the inductive argument
Gives the perceptual-skepticism argument and its extension to reasoning
Explains why brute-fact termination makes explanations illusory
Presents Della Rocca’s argument
States why the denial is self-undermining

shortAnswer.q: Explain the Thomistic account of miracles defended in chapter 6. Why is ‘violation of a law of nature’ misleading, and how do miracles relate to faith and revealed religion?
shortAnswer.model:
On the Aristotelian view, a **law of nature** describes the dispositions a thing has in virtue of its nature — ‘the laws of nature are the laws of natures’. Dispositions can fail to manifest when blocked or untriggered, so non-manifestation is not a violation; and since laws follow from natures, a genuine violation (water behaving un-water-like while remaining water) is metaphysically impossible. Hume’s definition therefore rests on a crude account of law.

A **miracle** is instead an event with a supernatural cause that either **elevates** a nature beyond its own powers (a resurrection; the multiplication of loaves) or **suspends** its operation — God refraining from conserving or concurring with certain causes, as when the young men in the furnace are not burnt. It is a suspension, not a breach, as when a law is temporarily taken off the books rather than left unenforced. God cannot literally ‘intervene’, because he is already the cause of everything; better images are a musician improvising beyond the score, a director’s cut, or a second edition.

Miracles matter as the **bridge** from natural to revealed theology: only God can work them, so they would be his ‘seal’ on a prophet’s teaching. Faith, then, is believing what God has revealed, grounded in evidence that he has revealed it — not belief without evidence.
rubric: Explains the Aristotelian view of laws and why violations are impossible
Defines miracles as elevation or suspension
Explains why ‘intervention’ is misleading, with an analogy
Connects miracles to revelation and to faith grounded in reason

shortAnswer.q: What is the analogy of being? Explain the kinds of analogy, why analogical language is needed for natural theology, and why it does not make God-talk empty.
shortAnswer.model:
Terms can be used **univocally** (same sense: Fido and Rover are dogs), **equivocally** (unrelated senses: a baseball bat, a bat in the attic), or **analogically** (related senses, still literal: good wine, a good man). Analogy comes in two main kinds. In the **analogy of attribution**, a term applies intrinsically to one primary analogate and to others by relation to it (George is healthy; food and complexion are healthy as causes or signs of his health). In the **analogy of proper proportionality**, a term applies intrinsically to each analogate by a similarity of relations (eyes are to a tree as intellect is to a theorem, so both ‘see’). Metaphor is a third, improper kind.

‘Being’ itself is analogical: potency is real but really distinct from act, so it cannot have being univocally with act (the distinction would collapse) or equivocally (it would be unreal). Being is not a genus, since nothing outside being could differentiate its ‘species’.

For natural theology, univocal predication would make God a creature, while equivocal predication would say nothing — we couldn’t even say he exists or causes. Analogy allows literal, positive claims (God is the primary analogate of power and being; God is to his goodness as a man is to his) while respecting simplicity. Our grasp thins but does not vanish — as physics’ talk of curved space shows, reason can speak truly of what it cannot picture.
rubric: Distinguishes univocal, equivocal and analogical use with examples
Explains attribution and proper proportionality
Explains why being is analogical (act/potency) or not a genus
Explains why analogy is needed for God-talk and remains literal

shortAnswer.q: Explain Feser’s account (following W. Norris Clarke) of how the ‘everything has a cause’ caricature of the cosmological argument arose, and assess why it matters for anyone debating these arguments.
shortAnswer.model:
Feser shows that critics from Russell to Dennett, Warburton and Graham Priest describe the cosmological argument as ‘everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, God’, and then ask ‘what caused God?’ Yet no major defender — from Plato and Aristotle through Avicenna, Aquinas, Scotus, Leibniz and Clarke to Koons, Pruss, Oderberg and Craig — used that premise, and Robin Le Poidevin admits no one defended the ‘basic’ argument he nonetheless uses as a stepping-stone. Feser compares this to Intelligent Design theorists describing ‘basic Darwinism’ as a monkey giving birth to a human.

Following **W. Norris Clarke**, the caricature seems to descend from mid-20th-century textbooks (John Hospers) and Russell’s *Why I Am Not a Christian*, back through J. S. Mill and James Mill to **Hume**. Descartes and Spinoza spoke of God as ‘self-caused’, meaning self-explanatory — a sufficient reason — and Hume took them to mean that everything has an efficient cause distinct from itself, which the tradition always denied of God. The result is a ‘hybrid monster’ neither Scholastics nor rationalists held. Richard Clarke complained of the same misrepresentation in 1889.

For debate, this matters because a critic who uses the caricature has not yet engaged the argument; the productive move is to state the real principles and ask which premise he rejects.
rubric: States the caricature and shows no major defender used it (with Le Poidevin’s admission)
Traces the genealogy through Russell and the Mills to Hume
Explains Hume’s conflation of sufficient reason and efficient cause (Descartes/Spinoza)
Draws a practical lesson for debate

shortAnswer.q: Scenario: you have ten minutes with a thoughtful mathematician who is a Platonist about numbers and an atheist. Plan the conversation using the Augustinian proof, including the two objections you expect and how you will answer them.
shortAnswer.model:
**Opening (common ground):** agree that 2 + 2 = 4 was true before humans existed, that we discover rather than invent mathematics, and that nominalism and conceptualism fail (Russell’s resemblance regress; words are universals; psychologism refutes itself). Her Platonism already rejects the view that math depends on matter or human minds.

**Key question:** where can abstract objects exist? Press the problems for a third realm: such objects would be causally inert, so how do they make anything triangular, and how could we know them? A Form would have to be both universal and an individual — ‘animality itself’ neither rational nor nonrational. Welty’s relevance point: a third-realm possible world, like a drawing, could represent but not make true that Socrates could have been a carpenter. Offer the Aristotelian alternative — abstract objects exist only as abstracted by intellects — and then show it needs a necessary intellect, since necessary truths and pure possibilities (unicorns) would hold with no human minds. Because mathematical and logical truths interlock, one intellect grasps them all; being necessary, it is purely actual, hence unique, omniscient and the rest.

**Expected objections:** (1) ‘Divine ideas aren’t abstract but concrete mental states’ — reply that for the Aristotelian, abstraction just is an intellectual act; the objection assumes a disputed definition (Welty). (2) ‘Omniscience is incoherent — no set of all truths (Grim)’ — reply that the argument proves too much (we generalize over all propositions), omniscience needs no set (Simmons), and simplicity means no set of discrete ideas (Wainwright).

**Close:** invite her to say whether she thinks something abstract could exist unthought by any mind — and leave the convergence with the other proofs for next time.
rubric: Builds on common ground about mathematical realism
Presents the case against Platonism with at least two arguments
Moves correctly to a necessary, unique, purely actual intellect
Anticipates two realistic objections with Feser-based replies
Shows sensitivity to the listener (tone, pacing, ending with a question)

flashcards.front: What are the five proofs and their chapters?
flashcards.back: 1 Aristotelian (change → purely actual actualizer); 2 Neo-Platonic (composition → the One); 3 Augustinian (abstract objects → divine intellect); 4 Thomistic (essence/existence → subsistent existence itself); 5 Rationalist (PSR → necessary being).

flashcards.front: What structure does every proof share?
flashcards.back: Stage 1: from an evident starting point to something fitting a key description. Stage 2: whatever fits it must have the divine attributes. Then a formal statement and objections.
The Augustinian proof — it starts from abstract objects, not from effects needing a cause.
A purely actual actualizer — the Unmoved (indeed unmovable) Mover.
An absolutely simple, noncomposite first cause — the One (Plotinus’ term).
A necessarily existing intellect in which universals, propositions, numbers and possibilities exist — conceptually omniscient.
A cause whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself.
An absolutely necessary being, whose existence is explained by its own nature.
The actualization of a potential. A potential is real but not yet actual — hot coffee can become cold, not chicken soup.
Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. Not ‘everything has a cause’.
Linear: through time, each member has its own power; may be infinite. Hierarchical: here and now, members have borrowed power; must have an underived first member.
Underived — having causal power of its own rather than borrowed — not earliest in time.

flashcards.front: Image: why an infinite hierarchical regress fails?
flashcards.back: An infinitely long paintbrush handle still can’t move itself; infinite mirrors still need a face; infinite IOUs are never money.

flashcards.front: Why does every linear series presuppose hierarchical ones?
flashcards.back: Things can change only if they exist, and their existence at every moment requires a concurrent series of actualizers.
Whatever is in an effect is in its total cause formally, virtually or eminently ($20 in wallet, in bank, or power to print).
‘Action follows being’: what a thing does reflects what it is and cannot exceed it.
Everything is intelligible: whatever exists has an explanation, in its own nature (necessary) or in another (contingent).
Every cause is an explanation, but not every explanation is a cause. Nothing causes itself, but something can be self-explanatory.

flashcards.front: Three arguments for a real essence/existence distinction?
flashcards.back: (1) We know essences without knowing existence (lion, pterodactyl, unicorn); (2) things are contingent; (3) something whose essence is existence could only be one.

flashcards.front: Does a real distinction require separability?
flashcards.back: No — a circle’s radius and circumference are really distinct but inseparable.

flashcards.front: Why must a composite have an external cause of its unity?
flashcards.back: A whole that caused its own composition would be both cause and effect of it — lifting itself by its metaphysical bootstraps.
Platonic (third realm), Aristotelian (in things; abstract only in minds), Scholastic (plus a divine intellect).
Forms would be causally inert (so unknowable and explanatorily idle), and a Form would be both universal and individual (animality neither rational nor nonrational).

flashcards.front: Why a necessary intellect, not human minds?
flashcards.back: Human (and alien, even angelic) minds are contingent; necessary and eternal truths and pure possibilities can’t depend on them.
Abstract objects form an interlocking system — universals presuppose others, propositions stand in logical relations — so one intellect must grasp them all.
It is inductively well confirmed; denying it undermines perception and reasoning (self-undermining); critics can’t principledly limit explicability arguments (Della Rocca).

flashcards.front: Why can’t an infinite series of contingent things explain itself?
flashcards.back: The series is itself contingent (and its features unexplained — Leibniz’s geometry books); appealing to further contingent causes creates a higher-order series with the same problem.
Parts only potentially compose a whole, so composites have potency; anything with potency has an actual and a potential ‘part’.
Essence relates to existence as potency to act; and what depended on actualization would have derived, not subsistent, existence.

flashcards.front: Why there can only be one God?
flashcards.back: Plurality needs a differentiator (specific difference, matter, a perfection lacking), which implies parts or potency — impossible in what is purely actual and simple.

flashcards.front: Frege’s sense/reference point, as Feser uses it?
flashcards.back: ‘Morning star’ and ‘evening star’ differ in sense but both refer to Venus; likewise God’s attributes — and the five proofs’ conclusions — name one reality.
Literal use in related but not identical senses: attribution (healthy food/George) or proper proportionality (seeing a tree/a theorem).
A description newly true of X only because something else changed (Socrates becomes shorter than Plato). God becomes Creator this way.

flashcards.front: Fallacy of accident (as used by Feser)?
flashcards.back: Treating an accidental accompaniment as essential — e.g., ‘actualizers we know change as they act, so every actualizer must’.
Badness is the absence of a perfection a thing’s nature calls for (blindness), so the PPC doesn’t put evil in God.
Conservation: God keeps everything in existence at every moment. Concurrence: creatures are real secondary causes that act only with God’s cooperation.

flashcards.front: Why reject occasionalism and mere conservationism?
flashcards.back: Occasionalism: things that do nothing wouldn’t exist, and it kicks away the proofs’ starting points. Mere conservationism: what can’t exist independently can’t act independently (drifts to deism).

flashcards.front: What is a miracle, for Feser?
flashcards.back: Not a violation of natural law but an elevation of nature beyond its powers, or a suspension by God’s refraining from conserving/concurring.
No proof says everything has a cause; each shows there must be something lacking the very feature (potency, parts, received existence, contingency) that requires a cause.

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘The universe might have no beginning.’
flashcards.back: Granted for argument’s sake; the proofs concern what sustains things here and now through hierarchical series.
The proofs start from single things; and contingency transfers to wholes like color (Lego), not weight.

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘Hume: I can conceive an uncaused event.’
flashcards.back: Conceiving A without B isn’t conceiving A existing without B; and Anscombe: telling coming-to-be from teleportation reintroduces causes.
Indeterministic ≠ unintelligible; the atom’s nature, generator and sustainer remain; physics’ silence about causes reflects its method.

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘The universe/laws could be the necessary being.’
flashcards.back: The universe changes, has parts and is contingent; laws presuppose what they govern; and a necessary universe would be pantheism, not atheism.
Then explanations built on them are illusory (book on a floating shelf), PSR is violated, and the move is ad hoc (Della Rocca, Gerson).

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘A first cause needn’t be God.’
flashcards.back: Stage 2 of every chapter (and all of chapter 6) derives unity, immutability, eternity, goodness, omnipotence, intellect, omniscience.
These are demonstrations from what any empirical theory presupposes, not probabilistic stopgaps; Krauss’s ‘nothing’ isn’t nothing.
Self-refuting or trivial; science abstracts from the unquantifiable; laws can’t ultimately explain; success ≠ completeness (metal detector).
Category mistake: God isn’t a member of the genus ‘gods’ but subsistent being itself — like triangularity vs. drawn triangles.

flashcards.front: What is a demonstration, and does controversy refute one?
flashcards.back: A deduction from certain premises that no empirical inquiry could overturn. No — even fair-minded people can fail to see its force.

flashcards.front: Convergence steps 1–2: what do they claim and why?
flashcards.back: Change is real and changing things exist only by concurrent actualization; so there is a purely actual actualizer — the hierarchical regress of actualizers needs an underived first member (ch. 1).
Things are composite and need something combining their parts now; so there is an absolutely simple One — a composite first member would itself need a cause (ch. 2).
Abstract objects are real and can’t depend on matter, contingent minds or a third realm; so they exist in a necessary intellect grasping their whole interlocking system (ch. 3).
Things’ essence is really distinct from their existence, so they must receive existence at every moment; so there is subsistent existence itself (ch. 4).
PSR is true and no contingent thing or series explains contingent existence; so there is an absolutely necessary being (ch. 5).

flashcards.front: What does convergence step 13 claim and why?
flashcards.back: Purely actual iff simple: parts only potentially compose a whole (so composites have potency), and potency would be a second ‘part’.

flashcards.front: What does convergence step 15 claim and why?
flashcards.back: Purely actual iff subsistent existence: essence relates to existence as potency to act, and derived existence isn’t existence itself.

flashcards.front: What does convergence step 17 claim and why?
flashcards.back: Necessary iff purely actual, simple and existence itself: contingency just is dependence on actualized potency, combined parts or received existence.
That the Augustinian necessary intellect is purely actual — linking chapter 3’s conclusion to the other four.

flashcards.front: What does convergence step 19 claim and why?
flashcards.back: There can be only one purely actual being: any differentiating feature would be a part or a potency.
Via the PPC, the one being contains all forms as a mind does, so it has intellect and omniscience (step 6 reaches this directly).
Conservation and concurrence: nothing else exists or acts for an instant without this being — ruling out inertia, pantheism, occasionalism, deism.
Change = something from nothing, impossible. Reply: the new state was there potentially, and a potential is not nothing. (Also: doubting change is itself change.)

flashcards.front: Four kinds of change, with Feser’s examples?
flashcards.back: Qualitative (coffee cools), local (leaf falls), quantitative (puddle grows), substantial (swatted fly dies).

flashcards.front: Why must the first actualizer be unmovable, not merely unmoved?
flashcards.back: Any unactualized potential in it would need actualizing — by something else, by a purely actual part, or by a mixed part — so it wouldn’t be first.

flashcards.front: Vallicella’s fourfold division — what does it show?
flashcards.back: Everything is a mind, mental content, material thing or abstract object; the One is none of the last three, so it is a mind (or most mind-like).
Resemblance is itself a universal; explaining resemblances by further resemblances just repeats the problem at a higher level forever.
Explaining how evolution or culture built our logic requires universals, science and logic — the very things it says lack objective validity.
If Man-in-general is itself an individual Form, it seems to need a further Form to explain it, and so on — Plato’s own objection to Forms.

flashcards.front: Welty’s six conditions for a theory of abstract objects?
flashcards.back: Objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude, simplicity — best met, he argues, by theistic conceptual (Scholastic) realism.

flashcards.front: Kenny’s two senses of existence — and Feser’s reply?
flashcards.back: Specific (there is an x such that…) and individual (the Pyramid still exists). Reply: real distinction ≠ separability, and ‘there is an x’ doesn’t say what makes it so.

flashcards.front: Barry Miller’s point about hierarchical regresses?
flashcards.back: ‘A is caused by B inasmuch as B is caused by C inasmuch as…’ can only be completed by naming a first member.

flashcards.front: Elder’s argument against conventionalism about essences?
flashcards.back: If all essences were mind-dependent, so would the mind’s be — making the mind prior and posterior to itself.
Critics use explicability arguments everywhere else; exempting the existence of things is arbitrary and question-begging.

flashcards.front: Reply: the ‘big conjunctive contingent fact’ objection to PSR?
flashcards.back: Propositions aren’t extra things needing explanation (Scholastic realism), and explanation needn’t be logical entailment.
No composite, act-potency, essence-existence thing could persist on its own; defenders never say what gives it that power.
The world is composite, changing and contingent; God is simple, immutable and necessary — so God is distinct from and unaffected by it.

flashcards.front: Why can’t God literally ‘intervene’ in the world?
flashcards.back: He is already the cause of everything; nothing is ‘alongside’ him to intervene in (McCabe). Better image: a musician improvising.

flashcards.front: Hume’s fork — and why it refutes itself?
flashcards.back: All knowledge is relations of ideas or matters of fact — but that claim is neither, so it fails by its own standard.

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘A thing’s parts could unify themselves.’
flashcards.back: A unifying part needs unifying too; brute unity is no explanation; laws plus what they govern form another composite (ch. 2).
Plantinga imports a broad ‘property’, Platonic properties and univocal predication; classical theists reject all three (ch. 6).

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘An immutable God couldn’t act or love.’
flashcards.back: Being changed isn’t essential to acting or loving (fallacy of accident); love is willing the good; becoming Creator is a Cambridge change.
Knowing doesn’t cause; God relates to us as an author to free characters, not as a hypnotist inside the story (ch. 6).

flashcards.front: Reply: Mackie’s logical problem of evil.
flashcards.back: Omnipotence excludes contradictions; some goods (mercy, forgiveness, courage, compassion) logically require evils (ch. 7).
Not all theism says God seeks relationship; a greater good may be served; and most people have in fact believed in the divine (ch. 7).
Aimed at design arguments; these proofs agree complex things need causes — that’s why they conclude to a simple cause.

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘The cosmological argument presupposes the ontological’ (Kant).
flashcards.back: God’s necessity is metaphysical (pure actuality, simplicity), not existence-by-definition; Aquinas rejects the ontological argument.
Ad hominem — motives don’t affect soundness; and bias runs both ways (Nagel hoped there is no God).

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘It can’t be a proof if so many doubt it.’
flashcards.back: Many objections are ill-informed; other philosophical arguments aren’t held to that standard; a demonstration can be controversial.
Kalām tries to prove the universe began; Feser’s causal proofs grant it may not have and argue from present dependence.
Differs absolutely, not in degree, from a series that points to it (zero speed isn’t the slowest speed); used for God’s will and goodness.
A genus is divided by differences outside it; the only thing outside being is nothing, which can’t differentiate anything.
Literally sexless; but personal (not ‘it’), and his active, independent, unchanging, distinct relation to the world is more paternal than maternal.
…that citing each copy’s immediate cause leaves unexplained why the series exists and why it contains geometry.

teachBack:
**The ‘whole case’ challenge.** Record yourself giving a 20-minute talk titled *Five Roads, One Summit* to an imagined intelligent friend who has read nothing by Feser and is mildly skeptical. Constraints:

1. **Minutes 0–3:** remove the three big caricatures (everything has a cause; the Big Bang; God as a big being) *without* using the words ‘actuality’, ‘potentiality’ or ‘essence’.
2. **Minutes 3–13:** present all five proofs, two minutes each. Each must include its everyday starting example, its key principle stated precisely, the phrase ‘here and now’ (except the Augustinian), and one Stage 2 attribute derivation.
3. **Minutes 13–16:** draw or describe the convergence — why the five conclusions must be one being — using at least two of the biconditionals and the uniqueness argument.
4. **Minutes 16–20:** answer three objections picked at random from the handbook (have someone choose, or roll dice). Name the chapter that handles each.

**Check yourself:** replay the recording with the comparison table and the objection handbook open. Mark every place where you (a) said ‘everything has a cause’ or implied a temporal first cause, (b) skipped Stage 2, (c) misstated a principle, or (d) answered an objection with confidence rather than an argument. Then do the talk again for a real person and ask them to explain back to you, in one minute, why ‘What caused God?’ misses. If they can, you have taught it.
videoPrompt: Audience: an intelligent adult who has studied all five of Feser’s proofs and wants a synthesis for review and debate prep. Emphasize, in order: (1) the shared two-stage structure — Stage 1 reaches a precise description, Stage 2 derives the divine attributes; (2) the difference between linear and hierarchical causal series, with the paintbrush, cup-on-desk, mirrors and IOUs images, and why ‘first’ means underived, not earliest; (3) each proof in about ninety seconds with its starting example (cooling coffee, a chair’s parts, 2 + 2 = 4, lion versus unicorn, a book on a shelf); (4) why the five conclusions are one being, using the morning-star/evening-star analogy; (5) the top objections — ‘What caused God?’, no beginning, composition, quantum mechanics, scientism, evil — with crisp replies. Correct the myths that the proofs need a Big Bang or claim everything has a cause. Tone: clear, confident, fair to critics, never smug.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This book tries to do something most people assume can’t be done: prove, using reasoning alone, that God exists — not ‘make it seem likely’, but show it follows from facts you already accept. It does this five separate times, from five different starting points: that things change, that things are made of parts, that truths like 2 + 2 = 4 are real, that nothing around us exists just by being what it is, and that things have explanations. Then it asks what God must be like, and finally answers the objections you have probably heard.

Why care? Because whether there is a God is one of the biggest questions there is, and because most public debate about it — on both sides — rests on misunderstandings this book clears away. Even if you end up disagreeing, you will know exactly what you disagree with.

What will you be asked to accept? Mostly very ordinary things: that change happens, that a chair needs its parts held together, that your coffee keeps existing from moment to moment. The work lies in following where those ordinary things lead. You will meet some old technical words — ‘actuality’, ‘potentiality’, ‘essence’ — but each is explained with everyday examples, and this course defines them for you first.

How to approach it as a beginner: read the Introduction first; then read chapter 1 slowly, because it teaches the tools every later chapter uses. In each of chapters 1–5, read the informal ‘Stage 1’ and ‘Stage 2’ carefully, look at the numbered formal statement as a summary, and treat the long objections sections as optional on a first pass — come back to them once the main argument is clear. Keep in mind one idea above all: these arguments are about what keeps things existing *right now*, not about how the universe began.

Reassurance: parts of chapters 3, 4 and 6 are genuinely hard, and Feser himself says every chapter ends in the deep end of the pool. Getting lost in a paragraph is normal. Mark it, keep going, and return after you’ve seen where the chapter is heading — the big picture usually makes the hard paragraph make sense.

knowFirst.plain: Reasoning about God using only logic and ordinary experience, without relying on scripture or religious authority.
What a thing actually is right now, versus what it really could become. Hot coffee is actually hot and potentially cold — change is a potential becoming actual.
Nothing can turn its own potential into reality; something already real has to do it. It does not say ‘everything has a cause’.

A chain where each link works only because the link before it is working at that very moment — like a cup held up by a desk held up by a floor. Such a chain needs something at the bottom that isn’t borrowing its power.

The idea that God has no parts of any kind — not physical parts, and not even distinct ‘pieces’ like separate attributes. His power, knowledge and goodness are one reality described in different ways.
Things like numbers, truths and general qualities (such as ‘redness’) that are real but can’t be seen or touched.
What a thing is, versus the fact that it is. You can know what a unicorn is without knowing whether any exist — so the two are different.
Everything has an explanation — either in itself or in something else. Nothing just happens or exists for no reason at all.
A contingent thing depends on other things and could have failed to exist, like you or a tree. A necessary being exists by its own nature and could not fail to exist.

Using a word in a related but not identical sense, while still speaking literally — as ‘good’ means something different for good wine and a good person. This is how words like ‘wise’ and ‘powerful’ apply to God.

questionsToHold: Is this argument about how the universe began, or about what keeps things existing right now — and how would the difference change the objections I’d raise?
What exactly is the starting fact of this chapter, and do I really accept it?
Where does the argument claim a chain must stop — and what does ‘first’ mean there?
Once the argument reaches its conclusion, how does Feser get from ‘something special exists’ to ‘God exists’?
Would the objection I’m tempted to make still work against the argument as Feser actually states it, or only against a simpler version?
Are the five arguments pointing to five different things, or one thing described five ways?
If these arguments succeed, what questions do they leave open — for example, about which religion, if any, is true?

map.what: Feser explains what the book is (natural theology without historical interpretation), how every argument chapter is structured, previews all seven chapters, and states his confident thesis that the real debate is among theists.
map.tip: Read it all — it is short and gives you the map for everything else. Note the chapter structure: informal Stage 1 and 2, formal statement, objections.

map.what: From everyday change (coffee cooling) to a purely actual ‘Unmoved Mover’: the key tools of actuality/potentiality and hierarchical causal series are introduced here, then the divine attributes are derived, then many objections (Hume, Kant, Russell, Newton, Einstein, quantum mechanics) are answered.
map.tip: Slow right down on pp. 20–29 (the hierarchical series and the move from change to existence) — reread until the cup-desk-floor example is clear. The formal statement is pp. 34–37. On a first read, the physics objections (pp. 43–60) can be skimmed.

map.what: From the fact that things are made of parts to an absolutely partless cause, ‘the One’; introduces analogy and the idea that God’s many attributes are one reality.
map.tip: The shortest proof chapter and a good confidence-builder. Take care with pp. 77–79 on analogical language — you will need it in chapter 6.

map.what: From the reality of numbers, truths and universals to a necessarily existing divine mind; works through the old debate between nominalism, conceptualism and three kinds of realism.
map.tip: The numbered arguments on pp. 90–97 can be read quickly; the crucial pages are 97–102 (why abstract objects can’t float in a ‘third realm’) and 103–106 (why one necessary mind). The objections (pp. 110–116) are technical — skim first time.

map.what: From the distinction between what a thing is and that it exists to ‘subsistent existence itself’ — something whose very nature is to exist — which keeps everything else in being moment by moment.
map.tip: Reread pp. 117–126 carefully; the three arguments for the essence/existence distinction are the heart of it. The objections from Kenny (pp. 135–138) are among the hardest pages in the book — fine to skim on a first pass.

map.what: Defends the principle that everything has an explanation, then argues that contingent things — even an infinite series of them — can only be explained by a necessary being.
map.tip: Pay special attention to pp. 149–153, where Feser argues that denying the principle undermines itself. Leibniz’s geometry-book example (p. 156) is worth remembering.

map.section: 6. The Nature of God and of His Relationship to the World (principles; unity to necessity)
map.what: Three background principles (proportionate causality, action follows being, analogy of being), then why all five proofs reach one God, and God’s simplicity, immutability, immateriality, eternity and necessity.
map.tip: The analogy-of-being section (pp. 176–184) is abstract; get its main point and move on. Pp. 184–189 (why the five proofs reach the same God) are essential — read them twice.

map.section: 6. The Nature of God and of His Relationship to the World (omnipotence to miracles)
map.what: God’s omnipotence, omniscience (and human free will), goodness (evil as absence), will, love and incomprehensibility; then how God keeps the world in being and works through creatures, and what miracles are. A short appendix asks whether God is male.
map.tip: The author-and-story analogy on pp. 213–215 unlocks several puzzles. Pp. 232–238 on conservation and concurrence are important for understanding how God relates to nature.

map.what: ‘What caused God?’ and where that objection came from; the universe as necessary being; uncaused events; beginnings; composition; ‘why call it God?’; ‘which religion?’; the ontological argument; ‘god of the gaps’ and ‘a universe from nothing’.
map.tip: Very readable, and it pulls together objections from earlier chapters. Good to reread right before any real conversation.

map.what: Scientism, brute-fact laws, ‘who designed the designer?’, ‘one god further’, the God of philosophers versus the God of religion, the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, the ‘rationalization’ charge, and what a demonstration is.
map.tip: The scientism section (pp. 273–285) is long but important. The problem-of-evil section (pp. 294–300) is the emotional heart of the chapter — read it slowly. End with the last pages on what a ‘proof’ is (pp. 305–307).

map.what: Feser’s suggestions for going deeper into each argument and related topics.
map.tip: Optional; skim for books on whichever proof you found most interesting.

Pick any proof and state its key principle precisely — then say which objection in the book targets that principle and how Feser replies.
Explain to a friend why the arguments don’t need the universe to have had a beginning.
